# **Amish culture prizes peace − but you wouldn’t necessarily know it from a stop in Amish Country tourist towns**

Published: October 18, 2023 8:31am EDT

![Image 3: A brown-yellow wall features a flag decoration that says '2nd Amendment Is My Gun Permit' and two crosses in the colors of the U.S. flag.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/554112/original/file-20231016-24-fx386t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&rect=0%2C0%2C832%2C555&q=75&auto=format&w=768&h=512&fit=crop&dpr=1)

Print article

Ohio’s Amish Country, located in the northeastern part of the state, [draws over 4 million visitors](https://www.visitamishcountry.com/media-information#:%7E:text=The%20topography%20consists%20of%20low,4%20million%20tourists%20per%20year [link_35].) every year – second only to Cedar Point amusement park as the Buckeye State’s most popular tourist attraction.

October, with its cooler temperatures and spectacular colors, is the region’s peak month for tourist traffic. Hundreds of thousands of tourists descend on the area in the fall to shop for Amish-made furniture, enjoy buggy rides and visit small towns that many Americans romanticize as bucolic escapes from the world.

And what will they find in the shops that line the main streets of towns like Berlin, Sugarcreek and Walnut Creek? Among other things, a plethora of items that feature [Christian nationalist](link_36) motifs, intense patriotism and ominous suggestions of violence – all antithetical to the core values of the Amish.

The reality is that Amish Country tourism has long been at odds with the plain and simple life of the Amish – a discrepancy at the heart of [my 2012 book](link_37) “Selling the Amish: The Tourism of Nostalgia.”

## A life apart

Descended from Anabaptist immigrants who fled religious persecution in Europe, the Amish typically live in rural areas where they seek to [live a different sort of life](link_38), resisting aspects of contemporary American culture that undermine their commitments to church, family and community.

[![Image 4: A simple, open-top horse-drawn carriage with a man and woman inside, going down a paved road.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/554115/original/file-20231016-29-wgyabw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/554115/original/file-20231016-29-wgyabw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

An Old Order Amish couple drive their buggy through an intersection in Berlin, Ohio.Susan Trollinger

To live at a slower pace, they drive horse-drawn buggies instead of cars. To pursue their calling to follow Jesus rather than chase personal ambitions, they [stop school after eighth grade](link_39). To avoid the distractions of consumer culture, they prohibit TVs and internet connections in their homes. And to keep themselves humble, they yield to communal rules about dressing plainly, living in modest homes and keeping their businesses small.

Seeking to follow Jesus, they embrace nonviolence and find inspiration in the story of [a 16th-century Anabaptist](link_40), Dirk Willems, who was imprisoned for his faith. He escaped, but because of his commitments to love his enemy, he turned back when he saw that his captor had fallen through the ice. His captor survived to witness Willems being burned at the stake.

Out of their deep commitment to [separation between church and state](link_41), the Amish refuse to swear oaths, receive Social Security benefits or join the military. That’s why you won’t see an American flag in an Amish school or hear Amish students recite the Pledge of Allegiance.

## The ‘Amish brand’

Yet tourist towns capitalizing on what has become the “[Amish brand](link_42)” are full of gift shops selling merchandise you would not expect to find in an Amish home – Uncle Sam cutouts, Mickey Mouse yard flags, ornate lace curtains and Elvis Presley figurines.

As [a scholar of rhetoric and religion](link_43), I’ve long been curious about Amish Country tourism, since it seemed – at least on the face of it – to have so little to do with the Amish themselves. “[Selling the Amish](link_37)” was my attempt to explain why many Americans found Amish Country so compelling.

My answer was that Amish Country tourism afforded visitors a nostalgic experience of a “simpler time” when Americans could imagine that they were in control of technology; that men were “men” and women were “women”; and that families sat down to Mom’s home-cooked meal every evening.

The region’s tourist towns play into this nostalgic desire that visitors have for a future that resembles an imagined past. In that imagined future, they would, like the Amish, escape cultural forces that they think have compromised America’s ability to be the [Christian nation](link_44) it supposedly once was.

## A glimpse of real life

Since 2008, I’ve taken students from the University of Dayton to the Amish settlement located in Holmes and Wayne counties in northeastern Ohio.

[![Image 5: A simple sign advertising homemade goods and candy outside a white farmhouse.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/554114/original/file-20231016-15-fgokj4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/554114/original/file-20231016-15-fgokj4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

A Swartzentruber Amish farm in Wayne County, Ohio, where tourists can purchase homemade treats and handwoven baskets.Susan Trollinger

In the course of the day, we visit a two-room school run by New Order Amish, whose rules for daily life [are among the least strict among the Amish](link_45). Then we’re off to a candle shop owned and operated by five Old Order Amish sisters, followed by a visit to a Swartzentruber Amish farm. The Swartzentruber are among the strictest Amish groups. In the small shop located between the house and a woodworking shop, a young woman sells woven baskets, homemade preserves and wood furnishings crafted by her father. We also enjoy meals and conversation at two Amish homes.

Of course, the stops we make are [part of the tourism industry](link_46). And many Amish make their living from that industry, whether they are crafting solid wood furniture, serving diners in Amish-style restaurants or preparing hotel rooms for guests.

Importantly, the Amish don’t own the big Amish-style restaurants or gift shops or hotels. And because I want my students to have conversations with the people they have been studying, we spend very little time in these tourist towns.

When I was invited to present a paper last summer on Amish Country tourism – an update of “Selling the Amish,” as it were – I was obliged to spend some time in those tourist towns.

## Guns and crosses

What I saw blew me away. There I was in the heart of [the biggest Amish settlement in the world](link_47), when measured by the number of congregations. This area is home to nearly [40,000 Amish](link_38) people deeply committed to pacifism: people who would rather [suffer solitary confinement and reduced rations](link_48) – as some did during World War I – than participate in “the war machine,” and who would never sing the national anthem.

[![Image 6: Store shelves show pointy, bullet-shaped silver and gold items next to novelty mugs.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/549796/original/file-20230922-15-21mkfk.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/549796/original/file-20230922-15-21mkfk.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

Beverage containers and coffee mugs for sale in Berlin, Ohio, on May 30, 2023.Susan Trollinger

Yet, I saw the Stars and Stripes everywhere: on T-shirts, ball caps, decorative wreaths, candles and, perhaps most strikingly, wooden crosses. There were concrete statues of soldiers kneeling at crosses, patriotic bunting and images of the Founding Fathers, with facsimiles of the Declaration of Independence, the Ten Commandments and the Pledge of Allegiance nearby.

A large display in one Berlin shop featured merchandise from “[Hold Fast](link_49),” a company whose website says its merchandise is designed “for freedom loving Americans who want to see Biblical values preserved and are taking a stand and letting their voices be heard.” Flags figure prominently across the merchandise, along with messages like: “One nation under God. Psalm 33:12. Hold Fast.”

I was even more taken aback by home decor items announcing that the “2nd Amendment is my gun permit,” along with thermoses challenging government authorities to “come and take it” – “it” being a gun – and coffee mugs that listed gun calibers (.22, .380, 9 mm, .40, .45) and proclaiming, “All faster than dialing 911.”

Amish Country tourism has never simply been about the plain and simple life of the Amish. But these days, sites that fuse Christian symbols and sacred texts with a brand of nationalism that celebrates masculine bravado, guns and the military marks a further and dramatic remove from the character of Amish life.

Still, if one ventures down a back road and ends up behind a slow-moving buggy, or ducks into an Amish-owned shop selling bulk foods, handmade brooms or half-moon pies, they can still encounter a people whose life is wildly at odds with so much that characterizes mainstream America today.

# Articles on Ohio

### Displaying 1 - 20 of 60 articles

[![Image 3](https://images.theconversation.com/files/763438/original/file-20261001-50-w7xxyl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&rect=0%2C1073%2C8640%2C4320&q=45&auto=format&w=668&h=334&fit=crop)](https://theconversation.com/christa-pike-survived-a-lethal-injection-attempt-the-latest-person-to-endure-a-failed-execution-293405 [link_29])

 Emergency vehicles arrive at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, Tenn., on Sept. 30, 2026, after Christa Pike’s execution was halted. AP Photo/George Walker IV

 October 1, 2026 

## [Christa Pike survived a lethal injection attempt – the latest person to endure a failed execution](link_29)

[Austin Sarat](link_30), _Amherst College_

The constitutional prohibition of cruel and unusual punishment has shaped legal discourse around failed executions, but courts have not stopped states from attempting to execute the same person again.

[![Image 4](https://images.theconversation.com/files/748981/original/file-20260720-57-opaxa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&rect=865%2C0%2C3468%2C3467&q=45&auto=format&w=240&h=240&fit=crop)](https://theconversation.com/sanctuary-people-redefine-what-it-means-to-protect-immigrants-in-uncertain-times-286932 [link_31])

 Ushers at the First Haitian Evangelical Church of Springfield, Ohio, hold hands during Sunday service on Jan. 26, 2025. AP Photo/Luis Andres Henao

 July 21, 2026 

## [‘Sanctuary people’ redefine what it means to protect immigrants in uncertain times](link_31)

[Gina Perez](link_32), _Oberlin College and Conservatory_

Many faith groups supporting immigrants root their mission in the idea of ‘accompaniment,’ which springs from Catholic social teaching.

[![Image 5](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739869/original/file-20260603-57-l2qdbs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&rect=812%2C0%2C2865%2C2864&q=45&auto=format&w=240&h=240&fit=crop)](https://theconversation.com/cincinnati-where-vance-converted-gives-a-glimpse-of-catholicisms-history-in-americas-heartland-282310 [link_33])

 John Caspar Wild painted ‘View of Cincinnati From Covington’ in 1835, as the city was booming. Cincinnati Museum Center at Union Terminal/Google Art Project via Wikimedia Commons

 June 8, 2026 

## [Cincinnati, where Vance converted, gives a glimpse of Catholicism’s history in America’s heartland](link_33)

[Matthew Smith](link_34), _Miami University_

For more than a century, anti-Catholicism was a powerful force in the region’s culture and politics. But religious pluralism ultimately triumphed in the ‘Queen City.’

[![Image 6](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739825/original/file-20260603-57-67idrr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&rect=372%2C0%2C1419%2C1418&q=45&auto=format&w=240&h=240&fit=crop)](https://theconversation.com/tony-carruthers-recently-survived-a-lethal-injection-attempt-the-latest-man-to-endure-a-failed-execution-284134 [link_35])

 In the past 80 years, at least nine men have survived execution attempts. Bernd Obermann/Getty Images

 June 4, 2026 

## [Tony Carruthers recently survived a lethal injection attempt – the latest man to endure a failed execution](link_35)

[Austin Sarat](link_30), _Amherst College_

The constitutional prohibition of ‘cruel and unusual punishment’ has shaped legal discourse around failed executions, but courts have not stopped states from attempting to execute the same man again.

[![Image 7](https://images.theconversation.com/files/718276/original/file-20260213-56-8b3mkc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&rect=575%2C0%2C2305%2C2304&q=45&auto=format&w=240&h=240&fit=crop)](https://theconversation.com/how-deregulation-made-electricity-more-expensive-not-cheaper-272780 [link_36])

 Plugging in costs more these days. Devonyu/iStock / Getty Images Plus

 February 18, 2026 

## [How deregulation made electricity more expensive, not cheaper](link_36)

[Noah Dormady](link_37), _The Ohio State University_

Deregulation promised competition but delivered middlemen instead.

[![Image 8](https://images.theconversation.com/files/716856/original/file-20260206-66-1fnrs6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&rect=504%2C0%2C3024%2C3024&q=45&auto=format&w=240&h=240&fit=crop)](https://theconversation.com/mapping-cemeteries-for-class-how-students-used-phones-and-drones-to-help-a-city-count-its-headstones-273154 [link_38])

 Miami University students in the author’s advanced GIS course collect headstone data. Robbyn Abbitt

 February 10, 2026 

## [Mapping cemeteries for class – how students used phones and drones to help a city count its headstones](link_38)

[Robbyn Abbitt](link_39), _Miami University_

Cemeteries are a treasure trove of local history and family connection. Technology and ingenuity have made mapping them easier.

[![Image 9](https://images.theconversation.com/files/707506/original/file-20251209-66-kcrwb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&rect=1173%2C0%2C1665%2C1665&q=45&auto=format&w=240&h=240&fit=crop)](https://theconversation.com/pfas-are-turning-up-in-the-great-lakes-putting-fish-and-water-supplies-at-risk-heres-how-they-get-there-271489 [link_40])

 PFAS are now found in all of the Great Lakes, including Lake Superior, pictured. Mario Dias/iStock/Getty Images Plus

 January 28, 2026 

## [PFAS are turning up in the Great Lakes, putting fish and water supplies at risk – here’s how they get there](link_40)

[Christy Remucal](link_41), _University of Wisconsin-Madison_

Some of these ‘forever chemicals’ are toxic at very low levels. They can get into water systems and bioaccumulate in fish, ultimately posing risks to people.

[![Image 10](https://images.theconversation.com/files/707161/original/file-20251208-76-5q293f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&rect=822%2C0%2C3282%2C3280&q=45&auto=format&w=240&h=240&fit=crop)](https://theconversation.com/data-centers-need-electricity-fast-but-utilities-need-years-to-build-power-plants-who-should-pay-271048 [link_42])

 Data centers need lots of power – but how much, exactly? alacatr/iStock/Getty Images Plus

 December 12, 2025 

## [Data centers need electricity fast, but utilities need years to build power plants – who should pay?](link_42)

[Theodore J. Kury](link_43), _University of Florida_

How many data centers will be built – and how much electricity they’ll need – is uncertain. Being prepared costs money, but so does being unprepared.

[![Image 11](https://images.theconversation.com/files/686393/original/file-20250819-66-ahnbcx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&rect=839%2C0%2C2160%2C2160&q=45&auto=format&w=240&h=240&fit=crop)](https://theconversation.com/rural-women-are-at-a-higher-risk-of-violence-and-less-likely-to-get-help-258976 [link_44])

 Rural areas have higher rates of violence against women than suburban and urban places. pocketlight/E+ via Getty Images

 August 25, 2025 

## [Rural women are at a higher risk of violence − and less likely to get help](link_44)

[Walter S. DeKeseredy](link_45), _West Virginia University_

Research shows that rural women in the US are more likely to be killed by their current or former male partners compared to their urban and suburban counterparts.

[![Image 12](https://images.theconversation.com/files/681605/original/file-20250722-56-w5fdmw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&rect=726%2C0%2C3715%2C3715&q=45&auto=format&w=240&h=240&fit=crop)](https://theconversation.com/great-lakes-offshore-wind-could-power-the-region-and-beyond-261311 [link_46])

 The United States’ offshore wind potential isn’t just in the ocean, where these turbines are located, off Rhode Island. John Moore/Getty Images

 July 29, 2025 

## [Great Lakes offshore wind could power the region and beyond](link_46)

[Cora Sutherland](link_47), _University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee_ and [Melissa Scanlan](link_48), _University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee_

States take the lead on regulation of planning, site selection, leasing and other elements of offshore wind projects in the Great Lakes, though the federal government has a role as well.

[![Image 13](https://images.theconversation.com/files/676852/original/file-20250626-74-vxaw84.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&rect=0%2C582%2C454%2C454&q=45&auto=format&w=240&h=240&fit=crop)](https://theconversation.com/toxic-algae-blooms-are-lasting-longer-in-lake-erie-why-thats-a-worry-for-people-and-pets-259954 [link_49])

 A satellite image from Aug. 13, 2024, shows an algal bloom covering approximately 320 square miles (830 square km) of Lake Erie. By Aug. 22, it had nearly doubled in size. NASA Earth Observatory

 June 26, 2025 

## [Toxic algae blooms are lasting longer in Lake Erie − why that’s a worry for people and pets](link_49)

[Gregory J. Dick](link_50), _University of Michigan_

The blooms have become an annual problem in the Great Lakes. DNA studies show what’s growing there and why it’s dangerous.

More than 19 million tourists flock to Amish Country each year, drawn by the opportunity to glimpse "a better time" and the quaint beauty of picturesque farmland and handcrafted quilts. What they may find, however, are elaborately themed town centers, outlet malls, or even a water park. Susan L. Trollinger explores this puzzling incongruity, showing that Amish tourism is anything but plain and simple.

_Selling the Amish_ takes readers on a virtual tour of three such tourist destinations in Ohio’s Amish Country, the world’s largest Amish settlement. Trollinger examines the visual rhetoric of these uniquely themed places—their architecture, interior decor, even their merchandise and souvenirs—and explains how these features create a setting and a story that brings tourists back year after year.

This compelling story is, Trollinger argues, in part legitimized by the Amish themselves. To Americans faced with anxieties about modern life, being near the Amish way of life is comforting. The Amish seem to have escaped the rush of contemporary life, the confusion of gender relations, and the loss of ethnic heritage. While the Amish way supports the idealized experience of these tourist destinations, it also raises powerful questions. Tourists may want a life uncomplicated by technology, but would they be willing to drive around in horse-drawn buggies in order to achieve it?

Trollinger's answers to important questions in her fascinating study of Amish Country tourism are sure to challenge readers’ understanding of this surprising cultural phenomenon.

Millions of people (this reviewer included) visit Ohio's Amish country, but few consider the penetrating insights Trollinger raises... Following an excellent review of Amish history and belief, she looks at what tourists find when they 'connect' with the plain people... A great book!

— Choice 

Trollinger begins Selling the Amish with a praiseworthy overview of Amish history. She enriches her analysis with theories and concepts of tourism: consumer culture, preservation, authenticity, social drama, commemoration, and exotic encounters.

— Steven D. Reschly, Indiana Magazine of History 

The book is highly readable and well documented, making it accessible to students and useful to scholars and those interested in Amish studies.

— Diane Zimmerman Umble, Journal of Mennonite Studies 

Susan Trollinger... covers many Amish Country themes that reveal much about tourists and their ideas of the Amish in her book _Selling the Amish: The Tourism of Nostalgia_... She makes the book accessible to a general audience by writing both as a tourist and as an academic.

— Caroline Brock, H-Net Reviews 

_Selling the Amish_ offers insights into Amish Country tourism that are both original and convincing. Trollinger’s attention to detail, and her judicious use of theory, means nothing less than a fresh new reading of this deeply American phenomenon.

— David L. Weaver-Zercher, coeditor of _The Amish and the Media_

### [UD in the News Sept. 26-Oct. 2 ![Image 3: link-arrow](http://www.udayton.edu/_resources/assets/icons/arrow-link-red-20x20px-outline.svg)![Image 4: link-arrow](http://www.udayton.edu/_resources/assets/icons/arrow-link-red-20x20px.svg)](https://udayton.edu/news/articles/2026/10/ud-news-sept-26-oct-2.php)

 Seventy years ago, Air Force requests for support solving complex technology challenges ignited the formation of the University of Dayton Research Institute. Today, UDRI is a nationally recognized research powerhouse, advancing technologies that strengthen national defense, support industry, and move innovation from the laboratory into the real world. 

![Image 9](https://udayton.edu/news/_resources/img/architecture/campus/archway-entrance-600x400-12122019.jpg)

#### About the site

 Amish Studies is an academic website developed by the [Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies](http://www.etown.edu/centers/young-center/) at [Elizabethtown College](http://www.etown.edu/) to provide reliable information on Amish life and culture. Designed to assist scholars, students and the general public, the site was developed with support from the National Endowment for the Humanities. 
The Amish population statistics are updated annually in the summer. Other information is updated periodically.

For an in-depth discussion of the Amish:

# **‘Sanctuary people’ redefine what it means to protect immigrants in uncertain times**

Published: July 21, 2026 5:09pm EDT

(Twitter)](http://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=%E2%80%98Sanctuary+people%E2%80%99+redefine+what+it+means+to+protect+immigrants+in+uncertain+times&url=https%3A%2F%2Ftheconversation.com%2Fsanctuary-people-redefine-what-it-means-to-protect-immigrants-in-uncertain-times-286932%3Futm_source%3Dtwitter%26utm_medium%3Dbylinetwitterbutton&utm_campaign=none&via=ConversationUS)

Print article

Hundreds of thousands of Haitians in the U.S. are living in uncertain times. On June 25, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the Trump administration could proceed with a plan [to end Temporary Protected Status](https://www.scotusblog.com/cases/noem-v-doe-3/) – a federal program that allows people to stay in the United States when the government considers their own country unsafe – [for around 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/25/us/politics/supreme-court-temporary-protected-status.html). Their work permits are [scheduled to end July 24](https://www.uscis.gov/save/current-user-agencies/news-alerts/update-on-termination-of-temporary-protected-status-for-haiti-release-july-10-2026), leaving TPS holders at risk of deportation.

This uncertainty is not new. In 2010, President Barack Obama [granted TPS to Haitians living in the U.S.](https://www.nytimes.com/2010/01/16/world/americas/16immig.html?eafs_enabled=false)[after an earthquake killed approximately 200,000 people](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/03/10/science/haiti-earthquake-seismometer.html?eafs_enabled=false) in Haiti. The original period was 18 months, but [TPS has been renewed](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/07/01/2024-14247/extension-and-redesignation-of-haiti-for-temporary-protected-status) multiple times because of humanitarian concerns, gang violence and political unrest.

Haitian communities in Ohio, [where I study immigration](https://www.oberlin.edu/gina-perez), have been particularly on edge since 2024, when, during the presidential campaign, Trump and JD Vance [repeated false claims](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/15/us/politics/jd-vance-springfield-pets.html) that Haitians living in Springfield were eating pets. Many of the city’s [estimated 12,000 Haitian residents](https://www.ablelaw.org/areas-of-impact/serving-springfields-haitian-community/) endured harassment, and the city experienced [more than 30 bomb threats](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/30-bomb-threats-made-springfield-ohio-false-pets-claims-rcna171392).

[![Image 4: A woman in a blue uniform stands at the side of a sanctuary, in front of wooden pews with a few people seated in them.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/748988/original/file-20260721-71-26igjt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/748988/original/file-20260721-71-26igjt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

A police officer stands watch to protect churchgoers during a service in support of the Haitian community at St. Raphael Catholic Church in Springfield, Ohio, on Sept. 15, 2024.[AP Photo/Jessie Wardarski](https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/HaitianImmigrantsSpringfield/fa2ec920da9c43a895324ef9a9b796b6/photo?vs=false&displayquery=ohio%20haiti&currentItemNo=27&startingItemNo=50&sourceLocation=Search)

Yet Haitians have built lives here, often with the support of neighbors, nonprofits and churches – groups speaking up as the community prepares for the end of TPS. Days before the Supreme Court decision, Ohio’s Catholic bishops [issued a statement](https://www.ohiocathconf.org/) expressing deep concern for “our Haitian neighbors.” Echoing [a November 2025 statement about immigration](https://www.usccb.org/news/2025/us-bishops-issue-special-message-immigration-plenary-assembly-baltimore) from the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, they told Haitians, “We stand with you in your suffering, since, when one member suffers, all suffer.”

Meanwhile, residents in Springfield have [organized prayer vigils](https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/06/tps-we-want-you-here-springfield-ralliesand-grievesafter-scotus-clears-path-to-deport-haitians/), [rallies](https://www.springfieldnewssun.com/local/forever-interwoven-within-our-springfield-story-hundreds-rally-in-support-of-haitians-after-tps-decision/article_370f8754-52b0-57e0-bc70-00bef3f2b06f.html), food drives and donations for Haitian families. Many groups that have supported immigrants for years are faith-based, [such as G92](https://springfieldg92.org/get-involved/). Another, [Springfield Neighbors United](https://www.wyso.org/news/2025-01-30/springfield-neighbors-united-rally-around-citys-haitians-other-immigrants) describes its work as [centering “love your neighbor values](https://springfieldg92.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Clark-County-Community-Immigrant-Resources.pdf).”

These responses reflect themes in [my research on faith communities supporting immigrants](https://nyupress.org/9781479823932/sanctuary-people/) and how they become “sanctuary people.” In the 1980s, [churches in the sanctuary movement](https://theconversation.com/sanctuary-cities-in-the-us-were-born-in-the-1980s-as-central-american-refugees-fled-civil-wars-257718) prioritized offering physical protection to Central American asylum-seekers. In recent years, however, I have seen faith-based advocates’ sense of sanctuary expand. The idea now encompasses efforts to assist people most affected by immigration policy, as well as other vulnerable groups, and to assure them that they are not alone.

## Catholic roots

This broader understanding of sanctuary is [rooted in Catholic social teaching](https://theconversation.com/why-standing-in-solidarity-with-immigrants-is-an-act-of-accompaniment-in-catholic-philosophy-275224) – especially [the idea of accompaniment](https://orbisbooks.com/products/in-the-company-of-the-poor?srsltid=AfmBOoqRSm0zKG67IKTUBWwDEHJTBj2dz23HRO1nIS6oC2lYlyUm0EvQ), which prioritizes closeness to people who are suffering.

Accompaniment has a long history in faith-based social justice movements in the U.S. and Latin America. One of the most famous examples comes from Archbishop [Óscar Romero](https://kellogg.nd.edu/archbishop-oscar-romero), who was assassinated in 1980 and [declared a saint by Pope Francis in 2018](https://faith.nd.edu/saint/st-oscar-romero/). Romero challenged people to accompany the rural poor amid the violence and persecution of El Salvador’s civil war.

Pope Leo XIV affirmed the importance of accompaniment in meeting migrants’ needs during [his visit to the Italian island of Lampedusa](https://www.ncronline.org/vatican/pope-leo-visits-lampedusa-migrant-hotspot-july-4) on July 4, 2026. “Before any intellectual consideration or ideological conviction,” he said, “the encounter with those who lie before us, stripped of everything, calls us to be close to them.”

[![Image 5: Four women stand outside with signs and shirts that say things like, 'Love your neighbor as yourself.'](https://images.theconversation.com/files/748990/original/file-20260721-57-v1c2i2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/748990/original/file-20260721-57-v1c2i2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

People attend a rally in support of Haitians on June 25, 2026, in Springfield, Ohio.[AP Photo/Patrick Aftoora-Orsagos](https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/SupremeCourtImmigrationRallyOhio/45a08053b7d6435a8efdab1954a9e61d/photo?vs=false&displayquery=ohio%20haiti&currentItemNo=0&startingItemNo=0&sourceLocation=Search)

Accompaniment is [a defining feature of today’s immigrant advocacy](https://jewishcurrents.org/on-accompaniment), embraced by faith-based and secular activists alike. It is also a central value for “sanctuary people” – a term I learned from [Ruben Castilla Herrera](https://cfs.osu.edu/archives/collections/ONLO/ruben-castilla-herrera), an activist in Columbus.

Herrera, [who died in 2019](https://www.dispatch.com/story/news/local/2019/04/08/local-latino-activist-herrera-dies/5495946007), helped create coalitions of support for immigrants. After the 2016 presidential election, he called on secular and faith-based activists to see all of their efforts – including to work to end police violence that disproportionately affects the poor and people of color, and to protect LGBTQ+ rights – as interconnected struggles to create places of safety: to be sanctuary for one another.

“Sanctuary comes from the people,” Herrera somberly observed on Sept. 5, 2017, as a woman named Edith Espinal [entered into sanctuary](https://www.columbusmennonite.org/sanctuary-for-edith/) at the Columbus Mennonite Church. Faced with a deportation order that would separate her from her family, Espinal lived there for more than three years. In February 2021, during President Joe Biden’s administration, she was [granted an order of supervision](https://www.wosu.org/news/2021-02-18/edith-espinal-returning-home-after-three-years-in-sanctuary-at-columbus-church), which allowed her to return to live with her family in Columbus, Ohio.

## Wider sense of ‘sanctuary’

Throughout my research, I have observed how groups across Ohio expanded the idea of sanctuary beyond physical protection for migrants and asylum-seekers, reflecting a national shift.

Organizations like [El Centro de Servicios Sociales](https://www.lorainelcentro.com/) in Lorain, Ohio, for example, worked closely with Sacred Heart Chapel, a Catholic parish, when more than 200 Puerto Rican families [arrived in the city after Hurricane María](https://www.cleveland.com/metro/2018/03/lorain_responds_to_needs_of_pu.html) in September 2017. In the weeks and months that followed, sanctuary people helped secure housing, jobs, language instruction, translation services, health care and guidance enrolling children into local schools.

“Sanctuary people” also supported families left behind following an Immigration and Customs Enforcement [raid at Corso’s Flower & Garden Center](https://www.wosu.org/news/2018-06-12/advocates-helping-families-and-children-impacted-by-ohio-immigration-raid) in northern Ohio on June 5, 2018 – one of the largest ICE actions in the U.S. at the time. The raid prompted the creation of [Los Niños de Corsos](https://www.thenews-messenger.com/story/news/local/2018/06/07/alonso-gathering-donations-los-ninos-de-corsos/683261002/), a grassroots organization led by young people who tried to educate the public about detention’s impact on families and communities and respond to their needs.

[![Image 6: Several people with their hands cuffed behind their backs walk single-file toward a large greenhouse.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/748991/original/file-20260721-57-9qofrg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/748991/original/file-20260721-57-9qofrg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

Workers are led away during an immigration sting at Corso’s Flower and Garden Center in Castalia, Ohio, on June 5, 2018.[AP Photo/John Minchillo](https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=ohio%20raid%20garden&mediaType=photo)

The following year, when 680 workers were [detained in a Mississippi poultry plant](https://www.npr.org/2019/08/07/749243985/mississippi-immigration-raids-net-hundreds-of-workers), Los Niños de Corsos [collected food](https://www.instagram.com/p/B11gEXXHNYW/), diapers, money and clothes to help their families. Members of the organization drove to Mississippi to deliver the items, and accompany people during some of the most challenging moments of their lives.

# **Cincinnati, where Vance converted, gives a glimpse of Catholicism’s history in America’s heartland**

Print article

Ten years after “Hillbilly Elegy” catapulted its author into public view, [JD Vance is publishing a new memoir](https://www.harpercollins.com/products/communion-j-d-vance?variant=45116963192866), “Communion: Finding My Way Back to Faith.” The vice president explains the book as a sort of [self-help guide for the spiritually lost](https://www.harpercollins.com/blogs/press-releases/harper-to-publish-communion-finding-my-way-back-to-faith-a-new-book-by-vice-president-jd-vance): “… by sharing my journey I might be helpful to others – Catholic, Protestant, or otherwise – who are seeking reconciliation with God.”

Scheduled for publication in June 2026, “Communion” promises “an intimate account” of its author’s religious journey. But the Catholicism to which Vance converted in Cincinnati in 2019 is quite unlike the evangelism he encountered in his childhood, famously described in “[Hillbilly Elegy](https://www.harpercollins.com/products/hillbilly-elegy-j-d-vance?variant=32207704424482).”

As a [historian of religion](https://miamioh.edu/regionals/profiles/matthew-smith.html)[in Appalachia and the Midwest](https://tupress.temple.edu/books/the-spires-still-point-to-heaven), I find America’s religious mosaic endlessly fascinating. Vance’s journey from Protestantism, to atheism, to Catholicism, not to mention his [marriage to a Hindu woman](https://religionnews.com/2025/11/03/why-i-hope-she-converts-is-bad-for-usha-vance-for-love-and-for-america/), reflects the diversity of the United States.

My [own experiences](https://theconversation.com/revisiting-middletown-ohio-the-midwestern-town-at-the-heart-of-jd-vances-hillbilly-elegy-234975) teaching in Vance’s hometown of Middletown, Ohio, suggest that America’s Midwestern communities, tarnished by “Rust Belt” stereotypes, are as dynamic and as changing as everywhere else – including in matters of faith.

Nearby Cincinnati, where [Vance was confirmed](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/25/us/jd-vance-catholic-church-conversion.html) at a Dominican priory, is a case in point and a window into Catholicism’s history in the American heartland. For more than a century, anti-Catholicism was a powerful force in culture and politics – yet, time and again, religious pluralism triumphed.

[![Image 4: A brown-haired man looks ahead of him, hands clasped, as he leans his elbows on a padded railing.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739871/original/file-20260603-57-2215m8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739871/original/file-20260603-57-2215m8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

U.S. Vice President JD Vance and his wife, Usha Vance, attend services at St. Peter’s Basilica in the Vatican on Good Friday, April 18, 2025.[Andreas Solaro/AFP via Getty Images](https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/vice-president-jd-vance-and-his-wife-usha-vance-attend-the-news-photo/2210188780?adppopup=true)

## Scots-Irish settlers

“To understand me, you must understand that I am a Scots-Irish hillbilly at heart,” [Vance declared in his first memoir](https://www.harpercollins.com/products/hillbilly-elegy-j-d-vance?variant=32207704424482).

The Scots-Irish played [an outsized role in history](https://search.worldcat.org/title/778618998). Initially, these Protestants were from Scotland, but they moved to Ireland in the 17th century. “[Planted” by the British Crown](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/articles/z2bgsrd) as a form of colonization, these immigrants riled the Catholic majority whose lands they occupied.

Later, many crossed the Atlantic and settled the Colonial American backcountry. Their distinctive influence [shaped the “hillbilly” culture of Appalachia](https://www.lmc.edu/about/news-center/articles/2022/in-the-mountains-the-scots-irish-heritage-in-appalachia.htm).

The faith of these settlers kindled a fervent Protestant piety, found in the [Great Revival](https://npshistory.com/series/symposia/george_rogers_clark/1991-1992/sec5.htm) of the Ohio Valley frontier. In this early 19th-century rebirth of backcountry religion, traveling ministers preached a fiery gospel of grace, stirring large crowds with their open-air sermons.

## Queen City

Boundaries between urban and rural America were always porous. [By 1830](https://ohiostatepress.org/books/titles/9780814208991.html) a quarter of Ohio’s 1 million inhabitants clustered in the state’s southwestern corner. Cincinnati was the heart of this region: the “[Queen City](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/7879298aac6c47c28ab3f75e59b22c6d)” of the United States’ [expanding Western frontier](https://www.cincinnati.com/story/news/2020/12/22/why-cincinnati-called-queen-city/4007103001/).

It had become a hub of Catholic immigrants [from Germany](http://www.cincinnati-cityofimmigrants.com/german/)[and Ireland](http://www.cincinnati-cityofimmigrants.com/irish/) – and a center for anti-Catholic preaching and anti-immigrant politics. In 1835, leading Protestant evangelist [Lyman Beecher infamously denounced immigrants](https://teachingamericanhistory.org/document/a-plea-for-the-west/) “rushing in like the waters of the flood” and argued the Vatican and Catholic schools posed dangers for America.

[![Image 5: A sepia illustration of a wooden building with a small cross on the top.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739875/original/file-20260603-57-sxxl17.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739875/original/file-20260603-57-sxxl17.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

The first Catholic parish in Cincinnati originally met in a small building just outside city lines.[Cincinnati Public Library via Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Christ_Church,_First_Catholic_Church_built_in_Cincinnati--Erected_1821.jpg)

Amid such prejudice, Protestant Irish Americans embraced the [term Scots-Irish](https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/irish-americans-9781608192403/) to distinguish their more established population from recent Catholic arrivals. Many of these Catholic newcomers, fleeing famine and persecution, were disparaged as [poor, illiterate and superstitious](https://chrc-phila.org/thomas-nast-anti-irish-cartoons/).

Yet despite alarmism and periodic violence, including [ethnic riots in 1855](https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-new-york-times-cincinnati-riots-1855/33454076/), Cincinnati’s [sectarian relations were surprisingly pragmatic](https://www.exhibit.xavier.edu/hab/4/), shaped by a sense of shared civic endeavor. Protestants welcomed [the city’s first Catholic church](https://www.google.com/books/edition/Dialogue_on_the_Frontier/4jPfbCh_qYUC?hl=en&gbpv=1&bsq=1819), for example, and often sent their children to the Catholic parochial schools. [Many converted to Catholicism](https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Spires_Still_Point_to_Heaven/lTGYEAAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=%22the+spires+still+point%22+converts+protestant&pg=PA101&printsec=frontcover), including wealthy philanthropists.

In 1837, Cincinnati’s Catholic Bishop, John Baptist Purcell [debated Protestant preacher Alexander Campbell](https://www.google.com/books/edition/A_Debate_on_the_Roman_Catholic_Religion/J5hdAAAAcAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=purcell+debates+cincinnati+infallible&printsec=frontcover) on the merits of Catholic religion for several days before a crowded audience. Both debaters claimed victory, and proceeds from the published debates were evenly split between Catholic and Protestant charities in Cincinnati.

## Changing country

By the mid-19th century, the city’s Catholics, while still a minority, were larger than any single Protestant denomination and [central to the cultural landscape](https://www.google.com/books/edition/Religion_Race_and_Reconstruction/Mtz3GLA4iO8C?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=catholic+immigration+cincinnati&pg=PA27&printsec=frontcover).

[![Image 6: A black and white photo of a large crowd standing along a road with a large white building in the background.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739879/original/file-20260603-57-h07n02.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739879/original/file-20260603-57-h07n02.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

People observe the National Eucharistic Congress, a gathering for Catholics, in Cincinnati in 1911.[Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1911_National_Eucharistic_Congress_Cincinnati.jpg)

At the time, Catholics represented only 5% of the U.S. population. That percentage would [triple by the turn of the century](https://nationalhumanitiescenter.org/tserve/nineteen/nkeyinfo/nromcath.htm), due to immigration from southern and eastern Europe.

Anti-Catholic backlash [continued into the 20th century](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/A/bo5970092.html), along with other forms of religious prejudice. For example, the U.S. [Immigration Act of 1924](https://theconversation.com/a-century-ago-anti-immigrant-backlash-almost-closed-americas-doors-228589) restricted immigration from parts of Europe heavily populated by Jews and Catholics. Animosity once focused on immigrants from Germany and Ireland shifted to those from Italy and Russia.

Bias against Catholics remained a robust force in Appalachian politics, too. Leading up to the 1960 Democratic primary, John F. Kennedy campaigned tirelessly in West Virginia, considered a tough arena for a Harvard-educated Catholic but critical to his electoral strategy. [His success in the Mountain State](https://www.jfklibrary.org/visit-museum/exhibits/special-exhibits/winning-west-virginia-jfks-primary-campaign) defied the myth that a Catholic candidate could never win the White House.

[![Image 7: A black and white photo of a man in a suit above a crowd, standing on a stage on a downtown street.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739878/original/file-20260603-69-wvr58k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739878/original/file-20260603-69-wvr58k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

John F. Kennedy campaigns in West Virginia on May 10, 1960.[Corbis/Corbis Historial via Getty Images](https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/john-f-kennedy-standing-on-stage-during-a-campaign-stop-in-news-photo/615298326?adppopup=true)

## Turn toward ‘Communion’

Southern Ohio, where Vance grew up and converted to Catholicism, is deeply Midwestern. But its heritage has been influenced by [the wave of workers who left Appalachia](https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691191119/hillbilly-highway) in the mid-20th century looking for jobs, including Vance’s family.

As Vance wrote in [a 2020 essay](https://thelampmagazine.com/blog/how-i-joined-the-resistance) for Lamp magazine, which addresses Catholic issues, his early ideas of Catholicism were negative ones – assuming, for example, that the church “rejected the legitimacy of Scripture.”

#### About the site

 Amish Studies is an academic website developed by the [Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies](http://www.etown.edu/centers/young-center/) at [Elizabethtown College](http://www.etown.edu/) to provide reliable information on Amish life and culture. Designed to assist scholars, students and the general public, the site was developed with support from the National Endowment for the Humanities. 
The Amish population statistics are updated annually in the summer. Other information is updated periodically.

For an in-depth discussion of the Amish:  
[![Image 3: The Amish book cover](http://groups.etown.edu/amishstudies/files/2015/08/The_Amish_thumb.jpg)](https://www.press.jhu.edu/books/title/10458/amish)  
 Authors: Donald Kraybill, Karen Johnson-Weiner, Steven Nolt (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2013; paperback, 2018)

#### Recent books

 In partnership with the Johns Hopkins University Press, the Young Center Books in Anabaptist and Pietist Studies publishes innovative and creative scholarship. A [recent book in the series](https://press.jhu.edu/books/title/53874/dancing-devils-playground) discusses the balance the Amish strike between tradition and the demands of the modern world: 

[![Image 4: Dancing on the Devil's Playground book cover](https://groups.etown.edu/amishstudies/files/2025/04/Dancing_thumb.jpg)](https://press.jhu.edu/books/title/53874/dancing-devils-playground)  
 Author: James A. Cates (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2024)

Ohio’s Amish Country, located in the northeastern part of the state, [draws over 4 million visitors](https://www.visitamishcountry.com/media-information#:%7E:text=The%20topography%20consists%20of%20low,4%20million%20tourists%20per%20year.) every year – second only to Cedar Point amusement park as the Buckeye State’s most popular tourist attraction.

October, with its cooler temperatures and spectacular colors, is the region’s peak month for tourist traffic. Hundreds of thousands of tourists descend on the area in the fall to shop for Amish-made furniture, enjoy buggy rides and visit small towns that many Americans romanticize as bucolic escapes from the world.

And what will they find in the shops that line the main streets of towns like Berlin, Sugarcreek and Walnut Creek? Among other things, a plethora of items that feature [Christian nationalist](https://theconversation.com/talk-of-christian-nationalism-is-getting-a-lot-louder-but-what-does-the-term-really-mean-192378) motifs, intense patriotism and ominous suggestions of violence – all antithetical to the core values of the Amish.

The reality is that Amish Country tourism has long been at odds with the plain and simple life of the Amish – a discrepancy at the heart of [my 2012 book](https://www.press.jhu.edu/books/title/10517/selling-amish) “Selling the Amish: The Tourism of Nostalgia.”

## A life apart

Descended from Anabaptist immigrants who fled religious persecution in Europe, the Amish typically live in rural areas where they seek to [live a different sort of life](https://groups.etown.edu/amishstudies/), resisting aspects of contemporary American culture that undermine their commitments to church, family and community.

[![Image 4: A simple, open-top horse-drawn carriage with a man and woman inside, going down a paved road.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/554115/original/file-20231016-29-wgyabw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/554115/original/file-20231016-29-wgyabw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

An Old Order Amish couple drive their buggy through an intersection in Berlin, Ohio.Susan Trollinger

To live at a slower pace, they drive horse-drawn buggies instead of cars. To pursue their calling to follow Jesus rather than chase personal ambitions, they [stop school after eighth grade](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/406/205/). To avoid the distractions of consumer culture, they prohibit TVs and internet connections in their homes. And to keep themselves humble, they yield to communal rules about dressing plainly, living in modest homes and keeping their businesses small.

Seeking to follow Jesus, they embrace nonviolence and find inspiration in the story of [a 16th-century Anabaptist](https://amnetwork.uk/resource/why-did-dirk-willems-turn-back/), Dirk Willems, who was imprisoned for his faith. He escaped, but because of his commitments to love his enemy, he turned back when he saw that his captor had fallen through the ice. His captor survived to witness Willems being burned at the stake.

Out of their deep commitment to [separation between church and state](https://groups.etown.edu/amishstudies/social-organization/government/), the Amish refuse to swear oaths, receive Social Security benefits or join the military. That’s why you won’t see an American flag in an Amish school or hear Amish students recite the Pledge of Allegiance.

## The ‘Amish brand’

Yet tourist towns capitalizing on what has become the “[Amish brand](https://ideaexchange.uakron.edu/amishstudies/vol2/iss1/3/)” are full of gift shops selling merchandise you would not expect to find in an Amish home – Uncle Sam cutouts, Mickey Mouse yard flags, ornate lace curtains and Elvis Presley figurines.

As [a scholar of rhetoric and religion](https://udayton.edu/directory/artssciences/english/trollinger_susan.php), I’ve long been curious about Amish Country tourism, since it seemed – at least on the face of it – to have so little to do with the Amish themselves. “[Selling the Amish](https://www.press.jhu.edu/books/title/10517/selling-amish)” was my attempt to explain why many Americans found Amish Country so compelling.

My answer was that Amish Country tourism afforded visitors a nostalgic experience of a “simpler time” when Americans could imagine that they were in control of technology; that men were “men” and women were “women”; and that families sat down to Mom’s home-cooked meal every evening.

The region’s tourist towns play into this nostalgic desire that visitors have for a future that resembles an imagined past. In that imagined future, they would, like the Amish, escape cultural forces that they think have compromised America’s ability to be the [Christian nation](https://www.prri.org/research/a-christian-nation-understanding-the-threat-of-christian-nationalism-to-american-democracy-and-culture/) it supposedly once was.

## A glimpse of real life

Since 2008, I’ve taken students from the University of Dayton to the Amish settlement located in Holmes and Wayne counties in northeastern Ohio.

[![Image 5: A simple sign advertising homemade goods and candy outside a white farmhouse.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/554114/original/file-20231016-15-fgokj4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/554114/original/file-20231016-15-fgokj4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

A Swartzentruber Amish farm in Wayne County, Ohio, where tourists can purchase homemade treats and handwoven baskets.Susan Trollinger

In the course of the day, we visit a two-room school run by New Order Amish, whose rules for daily life [are among the least strict among the Amish](https://go.gale.com/ps/i.do?p=LitRC&u=googlescholar&id=GALE%7CA218190812&v=2.1&it=r&sid=LitRC&asid=9a6896ba). Then we’re off to a candle shop owned and operated by five Old Order Amish sisters, followed by a visit to a Swartzentruber Amish farm. The Swartzentruber are among the strictest Amish groups. In the small shop located between the house and a woodworking shop, a young woman sells woven baskets, homemade preserves and wood furnishings crafted by her father. We also enjoy meals and conversation at two Amish homes.

Of course, the stops we make are [part of the tourism industry](https://ecommons.udayton.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1052&context=eng_fac_pub). And many Amish make their living from that industry, whether they are crafting solid wood furniture, serving diners in Amish-style restaurants or preparing hotel rooms for guests.

Importantly, the Amish don’t own the big Amish-style restaurants or gift shops or hotels. And because I want my students to have conversations with the people they have been studying, we spend very little time in these tourist towns.

When I was invited to present a paper last summer on Amish Country tourism – an update of “Selling the Amish,” as it were – I was obliged to spend some time in those tourist towns.

## Guns and crosses

What I saw blew me away. There I was in the heart of [the biggest Amish settlement in the world](https://groups.etown.edu/amishstudies/statistics/population-2023/), when measured by the number of congregations. This area is home to nearly [40,000 Amish](https://groups.etown.edu/amishstudies/) people deeply committed to pacifism: people who would rather [suffer solitary confinement and reduced rations](https://www.press.jhu.edu/books/title/2476/amish-and-state) – as some did during World War I – than participate in “the war machine,” and who would never sing the national anthem.

[![Image 6: Store shelves show pointy, bullet-shaped silver and gold items next to novelty mugs.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/549796/original/file-20230922-15-21mkfk.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/549796/original/file-20230922-15-21mkfk.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

Beverage containers and coffee mugs for sale in Berlin, Ohio, on May 30, 2023.Susan Trollinger

Yet, I saw the Stars and Stripes everywhere: on T-shirts, ball caps, decorative wreaths, candles and, perhaps most strikingly, wooden crosses. There were concrete statues of soldiers kneeling at crosses, patriotic bunting and images of the Founding Fathers, with facsimiles of the Declaration of Independence, the Ten Commandments and the Pledge of Allegiance nearby.

A large display in one Berlin shop featured merchandise from “[Hold Fast](https://weholdfast.com/),” a company whose website says its merchandise is designed “for freedom loving Americans who want to see Biblical values preserved and are taking a stand and letting their voices be heard.” Flags figure prominently across the merchandise, along with messages like: “One nation under God. Psalm 33:12. Hold Fast.”

I was even more taken aback by home decor items announcing that the “2nd Amendment is my gun permit,” along with thermoses challenging government authorities to “come and take it” – “it” being a gun – and coffee mugs that listed gun calibers (.22, .380, 9 mm, .40, .45) and proclaiming, “All faster than dialing 911.”

Amish Country tourism has never simply been about the plain and simple life of the Amish. But these days, sites that fuse Christian symbols and sacred texts with a brand of nationalism that celebrates masculine bravado, guns and the military marks a further and dramatic remove from the character of Amish life.

Still, if one ventures down a back road and ends up behind a slow-moving buggy, or ducks into an Amish-owned shop selling bulk foods, handmade brooms or half-moon pies, they can still encounter a people whose life is wildly at odds with so much that characterizes mainstream America today.

**General**  
 Kraybill, Donald B., Karen M. Johnson-Weiner, and Steven M. Nolt. _The Amish_. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 2013. [Comprehensive study of the Amish of North America in the 21st century.]

Ten years after “Hillbilly Elegy” catapulted its author into public view, [JD Vance is publishing a new memoir](https://www.harpercollins.com/products/communion-j-d-vance?variant=45116963192866), “Communion: Finding My Way Back to Faith.” The vice president explains the book as a sort of [self-help guide for the spiritually lost](https://www.harpercollins.com/blogs/press-releases/harper-to-publish-communion-finding-my-way-back-to-faith-a-new-book-by-vice-president-jd-vance): “… by sharing my journey I might be helpful to others – Catholic, Protestant, or otherwise – who are seeking reconciliation with God.”

Scheduled for publication in June 2026, “Communion” promises “an intimate account” of its author’s religious journey. But the Catholicism to which Vance converted in Cincinnati in 2019 is quite unlike the evangelism he encountered in his childhood, famously described in “[Hillbilly Elegy](https://www.harpercollins.com/products/hillbilly-elegy-j-d-vance?variant=32207704424482).”

As a [historian of religion](https://miamioh.edu/regionals/profiles/matthew-smith.html)[in Appalachia and the Midwest](https://tupress.temple.edu/books/the-spires-still-point-to-heaven), I find America’s religious mosaic endlessly fascinating. Vance’s journey from Protestantism, to atheism, to Catholicism, not to mention his [marriage to a Hindu woman](https://religionnews.com/2025/11/03/why-i-hope-she-converts-is-bad-for-usha-vance-for-love-and-for-america/), reflects the diversity of the United States.

My [own experiences](https://theconversation.com/revisiting-middletown-ohio-the-midwestern-town-at-the-heart-of-jd-vances-hillbilly-elegy-234975) teaching in Vance’s hometown of Middletown, Ohio, suggest that America’s Midwestern communities, tarnished by “Rust Belt” stereotypes, are as dynamic and as changing as everywhere else – including in matters of faith.

Nearby Cincinnati, where [Vance was confirmed](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/25/us/jd-vance-catholic-church-conversion.html) at a Dominican priory, is a case in point and a window into Catholicism’s history in the American heartland. For more than a century, anti-Catholicism was a powerful force in culture and politics – yet, time and again, religious pluralism triumphed.

[![Image 4: A brown-haired man looks ahead of him, hands clasped, as he leans his elbows on a padded railing.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739871/original/file-20260603-57-2215m8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739871/original/file-20260603-57-2215m8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

U.S. Vice President JD Vance and his wife, Usha Vance, attend services at St. Peter’s Basilica in the Vatican on Good Friday, April 18, 2025.[Andreas Solaro/AFP via Getty Images](https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/vice-president-jd-vance-and-his-wife-usha-vance-attend-the-news-photo/2210188780?adppopup=true)

## Scots-Irish settlers

“To understand me, you must understand that I am a Scots-Irish hillbilly at heart,” [Vance declared in his first memoir](https://www.harpercollins.com/products/hillbilly-elegy-j-d-vance?variant=32207704424482).

The Scots-Irish played [an outsized role in history](https://search.worldcat.org/title/778618998). Initially, these Protestants were from Scotland, but they moved to Ireland in the 17th century. “[Planted” by the British Crown](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/articles/z2bgsrd) as a form of colonization, these immigrants riled the Catholic majority whose lands they occupied.

Later, many crossed the Atlantic and settled the Colonial American backcountry. Their distinctive influence [shaped the “hillbilly” culture of Appalachia](https://www.lmc.edu/about/news-center/articles/2022/in-the-mountains-the-scots-irish-heritage-in-appalachia.htm).

The faith of these settlers kindled a fervent Protestant piety, found in the [Great Revival](https://npshistory.com/series/symposia/george_rogers_clark/1991-1992/sec5.htm) of the Ohio Valley frontier. In this early 19th-century rebirth of backcountry religion, traveling ministers preached a fiery gospel of grace, stirring large crowds with their open-air sermons.

## Queen City

Boundaries between urban and rural America were always porous. [By 1830](https://ohiostatepress.org/books/titles/9780814208991.html) a quarter of Ohio’s 1 million inhabitants clustered in the state’s southwestern corner. Cincinnati was the heart of this region: the “[Queen City](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/7879298aac6c47c28ab3f75e59b22c6d)” of the United States’ [expanding Western frontier](https://www.cincinnati.com/story/news/2020/12/22/why-cincinnati-called-queen-city/4007103001/).

It had become a hub of Catholic immigrants [from Germany](http://www.cincinnati-cityofimmigrants.com/german/)[and Ireland](http://www.cincinnati-cityofimmigrants.com/irish/) – and a center for anti-Catholic preaching and anti-immigrant politics. In 1835, leading Protestant evangelist [Lyman Beecher infamously denounced immigrants](https://teachingamericanhistory.org/document/a-plea-for-the-west/) “rushing in like the waters of the flood” and argued the Vatican and Catholic schools posed dangers for America.

[![Image 5: A sepia illustration of a wooden building with a small cross on the top.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739875/original/file-20260603-57-sxxl17.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739875/original/file-20260603-57-sxxl17.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

The first Catholic parish in Cincinnati originally met in a small building just outside city lines.[Cincinnati Public Library via Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Christ_Church,_First_Catholic_Church_built_in_Cincinnati--Erected_1821.jpg)

Amid such prejudice, Protestant Irish Americans embraced the [term Scots-Irish](https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/irish-americans-9781608192403/) to distinguish their more established population from recent Catholic arrivals. Many of these Catholic newcomers, fleeing famine and persecution, were disparaged as [poor, illiterate and superstitious](https://chrc-phila.org/thomas-nast-anti-irish-cartoons/).

Yet despite alarmism and periodic violence, including [ethnic riots in 1855](https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-new-york-times-cincinnati-riots-1855/33454076/), Cincinnati’s [sectarian relations were surprisingly pragmatic](https://www.exhibit.xavier.edu/hab/4/), shaped by a sense of shared civic endeavor. Protestants welcomed [the city’s first Catholic church](https://www.google.com/books/edition/Dialogue_on_the_Frontier/4jPfbCh_qYUC?hl=en&gbpv=1&bsq=1819), for example, and often sent their children to the Catholic parochial schools. [Many converted to Catholicism](https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Spires_Still_Point_to_Heaven/lTGYEAAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=%22the+spires+still+point%22+converts+protestant&pg=PA101&printsec=frontcover), including wealthy philanthropists.

In 1837, Cincinnati’s Catholic Bishop, John Baptist Purcell [debated Protestant preacher Alexander Campbell](https://www.google.com/books/edition/A_Debate_on_the_Roman_Catholic_Religion/J5hdAAAAcAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=purcell+debates+cincinnati+infallible&printsec=frontcover) on the merits of Catholic religion for several days before a crowded audience. Both debaters claimed victory, and proceeds from the published debates were evenly split between Catholic and Protestant charities in Cincinnati.

## Changing country

By the mid-19th century, the city’s Catholics, while still a minority, were larger than any single Protestant denomination and [central to the cultural landscape](https://www.google.com/books/edition/Religion_Race_and_Reconstruction/Mtz3GLA4iO8C?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=catholic+immigration+cincinnati&pg=PA27&printsec=frontcover).

[![Image 6: A black and white photo of a large crowd standing along a road with a large white building in the background.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739879/original/file-20260603-57-h07n02.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739879/original/file-20260603-57-h07n02.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

People observe the National Eucharistic Congress, a gathering for Catholics, in Cincinnati in 1911.[Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1911_National_Eucharistic_Congress_Cincinnati.jpg)

At the time, Catholics represented only 5% of the U.S. population. That percentage would [triple by the turn of the century](https://nationalhumanitiescenter.org/tserve/nineteen/nkeyinfo/nromcath.htm), due to immigration from southern and eastern Europe.

Anti-Catholic backlash [continued into the 20th century](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/A/bo5970092.html), along with other forms of religious prejudice. For example, the U.S. [Immigration Act of 1924](https://theconversation.com/a-century-ago-anti-immigrant-backlash-almost-closed-americas-doors-228589) restricted immigration from parts of Europe heavily populated by Jews and Catholics. Animosity once focused on immigrants from Germany and Ireland shifted to those from Italy and Russia.

Bias against Catholics remained a robust force in Appalachian politics, too. Leading up to the 1960 Democratic primary, John F. Kennedy campaigned tirelessly in West Virginia, considered a tough arena for a Harvard-educated Catholic but critical to his electoral strategy. [His success in the Mountain State](https://www.jfklibrary.org/visit-museum/exhibits/special-exhibits/winning-west-virginia-jfks-primary-campaign) defied the myth that a Catholic candidate could never win the White House.

[![Image 7: A black and white photo of a man in a suit above a crowd, standing on a stage on a downtown street.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739878/original/file-20260603-69-wvr58k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/739878/original/file-20260603-69-wvr58k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

John F. Kennedy campaigns in West Virginia on May 10, 1960.[Corbis/Corbis Historial via Getty Images](https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/john-f-kennedy-standing-on-stage-during-a-campaign-stop-in-news-photo/615298326?adppopup=true)

## Turn toward ‘Communion’

Southern Ohio, where Vance grew up and converted to Catholicism, is deeply Midwestern. But its heritage has been influenced by [the wave of workers who left Appalachia](https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691191119/hillbilly-highway) in the mid-20th century looking for jobs, including Vance’s family.

As Vance wrote in [a 2020 essay](https://thelampmagazine.com/blog/how-i-joined-the-resistance) for Lamp magazine, which addresses Catholic issues, his early ideas of Catholicism were negative ones – assuming, for example, that the church “rejected the legitimacy of Scripture.”

As a young man, he drifted away from faith altogether. During his days at Yale Law School, however, Vance discovered a curiosity that drew him toward Catholicism, inspired by thinkers from Silicon Valley mogul Peter Thiel and French philosopher René Girard to [the fourth-century theologian St. Augustine](https://theconversation.com/st-augustine-was-no-stranger-to-culture-wars-and-has-something-to-say-about-todays-242372).

[Vance wrote in his essay](https://thelampmagazine.com/blog/how-i-joined-the-resistance), “I often wonder what my grandmother” – a woman with Christian beliefs, but skepticism of institutional religion – “would have thought about her grandson becoming a Catholic.”

Today, [1 in 5 U.S. adults is Catholic](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/06/16/47-of-us-adults-have-a-personal-or-family-connection-to-catholicism/), and another 9% consider themselves “cultural Catholics.” America’s prejudice toward their tradition has eroded. [Six out of nine Supreme Court justices](https://news.gallup.com/opinion/polling-matters/391649/religion-supreme-court-justices.aspx) are Catholic, along with [28% of Congress](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/01/02/faith-on-the-hill-2025).

In fact, Vance’s new faith highlights a growing alliance between culturally conservative elements of American Catholicism and [America’s religious right](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=46), dominated by conservative Protestants since its emergence in the 1970s.

Lately, this alignment has come under strain, in part reflecting American-born Pope Leo XIV’s wariness toward U.S. policies, [such as the war in Iran](https://www.npr.org/2026/04/13/nx-s1-5783008/trump-pope-leo). Nowhere have such spats been more ironic than in [Vance’s rebuke](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/trump-administration/vance-warns-pope-careful-talking-theology-rcna331881) of the pope. After Leo remarked that Jesus’ followers are “never on the side of those who once wielded the sword [and today drop bombs](https://x.com/Pontifex/status/2042588417578668338),” the vice president warned, “If you’re going to opine on matters of theology, you’ve got to be careful.”

It will be interesting to see how such tensions play out in years to come.
