Hundreds of thousands of Haitians in the U.S. are living in uncertain times. On June 25, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the Trump administration could proceed with a plan [to end Temporary Protected Status](https://www.scotusblog.com/cases/noem-v-doe-3/) – a federal program that allows people to stay in the United States when the government considers their own country unsafe – [for around 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/25/us/politics/supreme-court-temporary-protected-status.html). Their work permits are [scheduled to end July 24](https://www.uscis.gov/save/current-user-agencies/news-alerts/update-on-termination-of-temporary-protected-status-for-haiti-release-july-10-2026), leaving TPS holders at risk of deportation.

This uncertainty is not new. In 2010, President Barack Obama [granted TPS to Haitians living in the U.S.](https://www.nytimes.com/2010/01/16/world/americas/16immig.html?eafs_enabled=false)[after an earthquake killed approximately 200,000 people](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/03/10/science/haiti-earthquake-seismometer.html?eafs_enabled=false) in Haiti. The original period was 18 months, but [TPS has been renewed](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/07/01/2024-14247/extension-and-redesignation-of-haiti-for-temporary-protected-status) multiple times because of humanitarian concerns, gang violence and political unrest.

Haitian communities in Ohio, [where I study immigration](https://www.oberlin.edu/gina-perez), have been particularly on edge since 2024, when, during the presidential campaign, Trump and JD Vance [repeated false claims](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/15/us/politics/jd-vance-springfield-pets.html) that Haitians living in Springfield were eating pets. Many of the city’s [estimated 12,000 Haitian residents](https://www.ablelaw.org/areas-of-impact/serving-springfields-haitian-community/) endured harassment, and the city experienced [more than 30 bomb threats](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/30-bomb-threats-made-springfield-ohio-false-pets-claims-rcna171392).

[![Image 4: A woman in a blue uniform stands at the side of a sanctuary, in front of wooden pews with a few people seated in them.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/748988/original/file-20260721-71-26igjt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/748988/original/file-20260721-71-26igjt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

A police officer stands watch to protect churchgoers during a service in support of the Haitian community at St. Raphael Catholic Church in Springfield, Ohio, on Sept. 15, 2024.[AP Photo/Jessie Wardarski](https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/HaitianImmigrantsSpringfield/fa2ec920da9c43a895324ef9a9b796b6/photo?vs=false&displayquery=ohio%20haiti&currentItemNo=27&startingItemNo=50&sourceLocation=Search)

Yet Haitians have built lives here, often with the support of neighbors, nonprofits and churches – groups speaking up as the community prepares for the end of TPS. Days before the Supreme Court decision, Ohio’s Catholic bishops [issued a statement](https://www.ohiocathconf.org/) expressing deep concern for “our Haitian neighbors.” Echoing [a November 2025 statement about immigration](https://www.usccb.org/news/2025/us-bishops-issue-special-message-immigration-plenary-assembly-baltimore) from the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, they told Haitians, “We stand with you in your suffering, since, when one member suffers, all suffer.”

Meanwhile, residents in Springfield have [organized prayer vigils](https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/06/tps-we-want-you-here-springfield-ralliesand-grievesafter-scotus-clears-path-to-deport-haitians/), [rallies](https://www.springfieldnewssun.com/local/forever-interwoven-within-our-springfield-story-hundreds-rally-in-support-of-haitians-after-tps-decision/article_370f8754-52b0-57e0-bc70-00bef3f2b06f.html), food drives and donations for Haitian families. Many groups that have supported immigrants for years are faith-based, [such as G92](https://springfieldg92.org/get-involved/). Another, [Springfield Neighbors United](https://www.wyso.org/news/2025-01-30/springfield-neighbors-united-rally-around-citys-haitians-other-immigrants) describes its work as [centering “love your neighbor values](https://springfieldg92.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Clark-County-Community-Immigrant-Resources.pdf).”

These responses reflect themes in [my research on faith communities supporting immigrants](https://nyupress.org/9781479823932/sanctuary-people/) and how they become “sanctuary people.” In the 1980s, [churches in the sanctuary movement](https://theconversation.com/sanctuary-cities-in-the-us-were-born-in-the-1980s-as-central-american-refugees-fled-civil-wars-257718) prioritized offering physical protection to Central American asylum-seekers. In recent years, however, I have seen faith-based advocates’ sense of sanctuary expand. The idea now encompasses efforts to assist people most affected by immigration policy, as well as other vulnerable groups, and to assure them that they are not alone.

## Catholic roots

This broader understanding of sanctuary is [rooted in Catholic social teaching](https://theconversation.com/why-standing-in-solidarity-with-immigrants-is-an-act-of-accompaniment-in-catholic-philosophy-275224) – especially [the idea of accompaniment](https://orbisbooks.com/products/in-the-company-of-the-poor?srsltid=AfmBOoqRSm0zKG67IKTUBWwDEHJTBj2dz23HRO1nIS6oC2lYlyUm0EvQ), which prioritizes closeness to people who are suffering.

Accompaniment has a long history in faith-based social justice movements in the U.S. and Latin America. One of the most famous examples comes from Archbishop [Óscar Romero](https://kellogg.nd.edu/archbishop-oscar-romero), who was assassinated in 1980 and [declared a saint by Pope Francis in 2018](https://faith.nd.edu/saint/st-oscar-romero/). Romero challenged people to accompany the rural poor amid the violence and persecution of El Salvador’s civil war.

Pope Leo XIV affirmed the importance of accompaniment in meeting migrants’ needs during [his visit to the Italian island of Lampedusa](https://www.ncronline.org/vatican/pope-leo-visits-lampedusa-migrant-hotspot-july-4) on July 4, 2026. “Before any intellectual consideration or ideological conviction,” he said, “the encounter with those who lie before us, stripped of everything, calls us to be close to them.”

[![Image 5: Four women stand outside with signs and shirts that say things like, 'Love your neighbor as yourself.'](https://images.theconversation.com/files/748990/original/file-20260721-57-v1c2i2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/748990/original/file-20260721-57-v1c2i2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

People attend a rally in support of Haitians on June 25, 2026, in Springfield, Ohio.[AP Photo/Patrick Aftoora-Orsagos](https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/SupremeCourtImmigrationRallyOhio/45a08053b7d6435a8efdab1954a9e61d/photo?vs=false&displayquery=ohio%20haiti&currentItemNo=0&startingItemNo=0&sourceLocation=Search)

Accompaniment is [a defining feature of today’s immigrant advocacy](https://jewishcurrents.org/on-accompaniment), embraced by faith-based and secular activists alike. It is also a central value for “sanctuary people” – a term I learned from [Ruben Castilla Herrera](https://cfs.osu.edu/archives/collections/ONLO/ruben-castilla-herrera), an activist in Columbus.

Herrera, [who died in 2019](https://www.dispatch.com/story/news/local/2019/04/08/local-latino-activist-herrera-dies/5495946007), helped create coalitions of support for immigrants. After the 2016 presidential election, he called on secular and faith-based activists to see all of their efforts – including to work to end police violence that disproportionately affects the poor and people of color, and to protect LGBTQ+ rights – as interconnected struggles to create places of safety: to be sanctuary for one another.

“Sanctuary comes from the people,” Herrera somberly observed on Sept. 5, 2017, as a woman named Edith Espinal [entered into sanctuary](https://www.columbusmennonite.org/sanctuary-for-edith/) at the Columbus Mennonite Church. Faced with a deportation order that would separate her from her family, Espinal lived there for more than three years. In February 2021, during President Joe Biden’s administration, she was [granted an order of supervision](https://www.wosu.org/news/2021-02-18/edith-espinal-returning-home-after-three-years-in-sanctuary-at-columbus-church), which allowed her to return to live with her family in Columbus, Ohio.

## Wider sense of ‘sanctuary’

Throughout my research, I have observed how groups across Ohio expanded the idea of sanctuary beyond physical protection for migrants and asylum-seekers, reflecting a national shift.

Organizations like [El Centro de Servicios Sociales](https://www.lorainelcentro.com/) in Lorain, Ohio, for example, worked closely with Sacred Heart Chapel, a Catholic parish, when more than 200 Puerto Rican families [arrived in the city after Hurricane María](https://www.cleveland.com/metro/2018/03/lorain_responds_to_needs_of_pu.html) in September 2017. In the weeks and months that followed, sanctuary people helped secure housing, jobs, language instruction, translation services, health care and guidance enrolling children into local schools.

“Sanctuary people” also supported families left behind following an Immigration and Customs Enforcement [raid at Corso’s Flower & Garden Center](https://www.wosu.org/news/2018-06-12/advocates-helping-families-and-children-impacted-by-ohio-immigration-raid) in northern Ohio on June 5, 2018 – one of the largest ICE actions in the U.S. at the time. The raid prompted the creation of [Los Niños de Corsos](https://www.thenews-messenger.com/story/news/local/2018/06/07/alonso-gathering-donations-los-ninos-de-corsos/683261002/), a grassroots organization led by young people who tried to educate the public about detention’s impact on families and communities and respond to their needs.

[![Image 6: Several people with their hands cuffed behind their backs walk single-file toward a large greenhouse.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/748991/original/file-20260721-57-9qofrg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/748991/original/file-20260721-57-9qofrg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

Workers are led away during an immigration sting at Corso’s Flower and Garden Center in Castalia, Ohio, on June 5, 2018.[AP Photo/John Minchillo](https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=ohio%20raid%20garden&mediaType=photo)

The following year, when 680 workers were [detained in a Mississippi poultry plant](https://www.npr.org/2019/08/07/749243985/mississippi-immigration-raids-net-hundreds-of-workers), Los Niños de Corsos [collected food](https://www.instagram.com/p/B11gEXXHNYW/), diapers, money and clothes to help their families. Members of the organization drove to Mississippi to deliver the items, and accompany people during some of the most challenging moments of their lives.

## Here and now

In recent weeks, sanctuary people in Ohio have accompanied Haitians as they face the uncertainty of what is to come.

With some people afraid to leave their homes, advocates and volunteers are [raising money](https://www.springfieldnewssun.com/local/as-haitians-wait-for-tps-decision-springfield-g92-gives-50k-to-nonprofits-supporting-them/article_8f5148e8-2131-575c-a62f-c16d2081be90.html), collecting food and toiletries, and doing shopping for Haitian families. They also encourage neighbors to eat at immigrant-owned restaurants, shop in immigrants’ businesses, and participate in book clubs to learn more about immigration, Haiti and U.S. foreign policy.

The [sanctuary people who do this work](https://nyupress.org/9781479823932/sanctuary-people/) believe that closeness, preparing and sharing meals, and simply showing up for mundane tasks can reassure people in need that they are not alone.

Viles Dorsainvil, executive director of the Haitian Community Help and Support Center, captured this sentiment at [a rally in front of Springfield’s City Hall](https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/2026/06/26/ohioans-rally-to-support-haitians-living-with-temporary-protected-status-after-supreme-court-ruling/) the day the Supreme Court decision was announced. After assuring fellow Haitians that their resilience would guide them this moment, he told other residents, “You have welcomed your neighbors, spoken out against injustice, defended vulnerable families, and refused to let hate and division have the final word.”

**General**  
 Kraybill, Donald B., Karen M. Johnson-Weiner, and Steven M. Nolt. _The Amish_. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 2013. [Comprehensive study of the Amish of North America in the 21st century.]

# Cleo Redd Fisher Museum welcomes Trollinger for women’s suffrage lecture

Susan Trollinger will present ‘Rebels in Corsets’ during a Feb. 9 program at the museum

Published January 25, 2026 - 5:00 a.m.

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.yourohionews.com%2Fholmes-county%2Fcleo-redd-fisher-museum-welcomes-trollinger-for-womens-suffrage-lecture%2F1007244)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.yourohionews.com%2Fholmes-county%2Fcleo-redd-fisher-museum-welcomes-trollinger-for-womens-suffrage-lecture%2F1007244)[](mailto:?subject=Cleo%20Redd%20Fisher%20Museum%20welcomes%20Trollinger%20for%20women%E2%80%99s%20suffrage%20lecture&body=Susan%20Trollinger%20will%20present%20%E2%80%98Rebels%20in%20Corsets%E2%80%99%20during%20a%20Feb.%209%20program%20at%20the%20museum%0Dhttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.yourohionews.com%2Fholmes-county%2Fcleo-redd-fisher-museum-welcomes-trollinger-for-womens-suffrage-lecture%2F1007244)

AD

![Image 4](https://image.yourohionews.com/1007252.jpg?imageId=1007252&x=0.00&y=0.00&cropw=100.00&croph=100.00&width=960&height=1288&format=jpg)

Susan Trollinger

Submitted

The Cleo Redd Fisher Museum’s speaker series returns with Rebels in Corsets: The Embodied Rhetoric of the Women’s Suffrage Movement, presented by Susan Trollinger Monday, Feb. 9, in the museum’s lecture hall. Doors open at 6:30 p.m., with the program beginning at 7 p.m.

The program challenges the common perception that women’s suffrage was achieved through a quiet and orderly political process. Instead, Trollinger explores the movement as a 72-year struggle that required persistence, sacrifice and strategic creativity. It will consider what life was like for women in the 19th century, how reformers in the 1840s came to believe it was time to demand the vote and the rhetorical strategies they used to persuade a resistant public. Trollinger says that though many of these arguments appear unremarkable today, they were once viewed as shocking and even “disgusting.” The fight for suffrage reshaped not only the law but American political culture itself.

AD

Trollinger is a professor of English at the University of Dayton. She holds a bachelor’s degree in communication arts from the University of Wisconsin–Madison and a master’s degree and Ph.D. in rhetoric and communication from the University of Pittsburgh. Trollinger is the author of "Selling the Amish: The Tourism of Nostalgia" (2012), which examines Amish Country tourism in eastern Ohio, and co-author of "Righting America at the Creation Museum" (2016). She has been interviewed by national media outlets, including C-SPAN2’s BookTV, RadioWest, The Washington Post and GQ.

Admission to the lecture is free. For more information, visit www.crfmuseum.com or call 419-994-4050.

## [Make Much Ado About Will This Year](link_4)

Posted on[March 21, 2016](link_4)by[Betsy](link_5)

Sir Walter Scott, John Keats, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Charles Dickens, Thomas Hardy, Mark Twain, Harriet Beecher Stowe and I have something in common. We’ve all made the pilgrimage to Warwickshire, England to honor William Shakespeare.

Some pilgrims take the “Sacred Way of English Literature,” wandering along a footpath to the hamlet of Shottery, finding inspiration as the young Shakespeare did when he was on his way to court Anne Hathaway. In the famous half-timbered Tudor cottage with a thatched roof rests the high-backed wooden settle which Will and Anne are said to have sat upon before the fire, under the watchful eyes of her parents.

[![Image 2: Anne Hathaway's Cottage, September 2010](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/2010-09-14-england-2010-074.jpg?w=300&h=251)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/2010-09-14-england-2010-074.jpg)

But the greatest feelings of anticipation and excitement are reserved for the star attraction —the home on Henley Street in nearby Stratford-upon-Avon where the playwright was born in April 1564. To commemorate their visit to this hallowed shrine, many of those Victorian-era authors scratched their names on a window in the room where Shakespeare was born; I bought a sterling silver flower pin in the gift shop. But as we walked where he did and saw things that he had seen in the home where his father, John, also made and sold gloves, we all felt his presence pervade these legendary surroundings.

[![Image 3: Shakespeare Birthplace, September 2010](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/2010-09-14-england-2010-091.jpg?w=300&h=225)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/2010-09-14-england-2010-091.jpg)

Shakespeare’s influence is being felt even more strongly this year. Many commemorative events are under way to mark the 400 th anniversary of the playwright’s death on April 23, 1616.

_[Young Will](link_6)_, a new statue of Shakespeare was unveiled in Stratford-upon-Avon in February. The First Folio, the first printed collection of Shakespeare’s plays that was published in 1623, is visiting all 50 states in a [traveling exhibition](link_7) organized by the Folger Shakespeare Library. And over 100 Shakespeare-related titles are being published this year, including the [Hogarth Shakespeare series](link_8),in which bestselling authors like Margaret Atwood, Anne Tyler and Tracy Chevalier retell some of Shakespeare’s plays as modern-day novels.

But not all q uadricentennial pilgrimages lead to Warwickshire. Closer to home, visit Kenyon College to see “Shakespeare 400,” a special exhibition at Greenslade Special Collections & Archives exploring Shakespeare’s accomplishments and his place within literature.

One display case focuses on sources that inspired Shakespeare, such as the Latin texts of Ovid, the Greek dramas of Aeschylus, and _The Reports,_ written by Shakespeare’s contemporary, Sir Edward Coke. Another celebrates the world to which Shakespeare was responding. A 1635 edition of Gerardus Mercator’s _Atlas_ and Johannes Kepler’s _Tabulae Rudolphinae_ from 1627 illustrate this age of global exploration that popularized maps of the earth and skies, travel logs and navigational treatises.

[![Image 4: Shakespeare 400, Kenyon College](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2226.jpg?w=225&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2226.jpg)

During Shakespeare’s lifetime, stage plays were not considered serious literature. However, seven years after his death, two actors in his company published the text of 36 of his plays in a folio-sized volume, arranging them into comedies, histories and tragedies. The Second Folio was a corrected page-for-page reprint of the First Folio, followed by the publication of the Third Folio in 1663 and the Fourth Folio in 1685.

[![Image 5: Shakespeare 400, Kenyon College](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2214.jpg?w=209&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2214.jpg)

Other Shakespeare-themed texts in the exhibition include _Tales from Shakespeare_, a children’s edition of Shakespeare plays by Mary Lamb that was first printed in 1807; a facsimile of Shakespeare’s signature, part of a collection of Shakespearean papers and letters that were forged by William Ireland and published in 1796; and pressed flowers that were collected from Shakespeare’s garden in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1907.

[![Image 6: Shakespeare 400, Kenyon College](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2209.jpg?w=300&h=290)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2209.jpg)

A Federal-style secretary and bookcase, produced around 1820 for Kenyon’s founder, Philander Chase, contains Shakespeare-themed merchandise like rubber ducks, bears, action figures and pop-up versions of the Globe Theatre.

[![Image 7: Shakespeare 400, Kenyon College](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2218.jpg?w=225&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2218.jpg)

Shakespearean insults from a kit called “Dress-Up Shakespeare Says!” cover one of the area’s windows.[![Image 8: Shakespeare 400, Kenyon College](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2228.jpg?w=195&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2228.jpg)

A Shakespearean magnetic poetry kit, a poseable Shakespeare action figure, a Shakespeare punching puppet, and other Shakespeare-themed merchandise like bandages, sticky notes, lip balms and air fresheners are available for purchase in the Kenyon College Bookstore.

“Shakespeare 400” is on view through August 12 at Kenyon’s Olin and Chalmers Libraries during Greenslade Special Collections & Archives’ open hours, Monday-Friday 9 am–12 pm and 1–4pm. Related events taking place at Kenyon this semester include a sonnet-writing competition, film screenings and discussions of Shakespeare-based movies, a cooking event featuring early-modern recipes, and lectures discussing the global elements of Shakespeare’s works.

Even closer to home, the Westerville Public Library is also offering some special programming to mark the Shakespeare q uadricentennial. On Thursday, April 7 from 6:30 to 8:00 pm, join others at the library to watch _In Search of Shakespeare_, a documentary series with a companion book by Michael Wood, that follows Shakespeare’s life and explores how he created his work that was shaped by his times. Otterbein English Professor Norman Chaney will lead a discussion and lecture titled “Shakespeare’s Life, Language and Legacy” at the library on Monday, April 25 from 7:00 to 8:30 p.m.

“[The Coming Shakespeare Extravaganza](link_9),” from the December 16, 2015 edition of the _Wall Street Journal_, provides more information about the Shakespeare quadricentennial.

You can imagine how much is planned in Great Britain to commemorate this event. What I’d like to see most is “Shakespeare in the Royal Library,” on view at Windsor Castle until January 1, 2017. The exhibition draws on material in the Royal Library, including works of Shakespeare collected by the royal family, such as a copy of Shakespeare’s Second Folio with annotations by Charles I and George III; accounts of performances at Windsor Castle; and art by members of the royal family inspired by Shakespeare’s plays. Click [here](link_10) for digital representations of the items included in the exhibition.

For more on Shakespeare, check out _The Genius of Shakespeare_ and _Soul of the Age: The Life, Mind and World of William Shakespeare_, both by Jonathan Bate; _1599: Contested Will: Who Wrote Shakespeare; A Year in the Life of William_ Shakespeare and _The Year of Lear: Shakespeare in 1606,_ all by James Shapiro; _Shakespeare: The World As Stage_, by Bill Bryson; and _Shakespeare: The Biography_, by Peter Ackroyd.

Mi[![Image 9: Shakespeare 400, Kenyon College](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2234.jpg?w=300&h=205)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2234.jpg)ami University Libraries, my previous employer, made its copies of all four folios digitally available; you can see them [here](link_11).

_The Great Courses: How to Read and Understand Shakespeare_ is a series of 24 30-minute lectures given by my friend Marc Conner, interim provost and the Jo M. and James Ballengee Professor of English at Washington and Lee University. Watch and listen to Marc give you a set of tools that will help you reach your own comprehension of the plays, comprehend Shakespeare’s poetic language, discover his characters and stories, and learn about his world, including how theater and stagecraft were practiced during his day. It’s available for borrowing through the Columbus Metropolitan Library, after a certain “power patron” requested its purchase. Click [here](link_12) to reserve it.

“Approaching Shakespeare’s Kings: Understanding Shakespeare’s Stage,” a lecture Marc gave as part of Washington and Lee University’s July 2015 Alumni College on Shakespeare’s kings, discusses how the conventions of the stage allowed Shakespeare to express his political beliefs, using the historical tragedy _Richard II_ to show how Shakespeare explores kingship in his plays. You can watch it [here](link_13).[![Image 10: Shakespeare 400, Kenyon College](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2219.jpg?w=225&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2219.jpg)

If you’d like to discover more about the Shakespeare homes in the Stratford-on-Avon area, see _Anne Hathaway’s Cottage: Its History, Contents and Traditions_, by F.W. Bennett; _Anne Hathaway’s Cottage_, by Wilfrid J. Osborne _;_ _In Honour of Shakespeare: The History and Collections of the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust_, by Levi Fox; _On the Trail of William Shakespeare_, by J. Keith Cheetham; _Shakespeare’s Shrine: The Bard’s Birthplace and the Invention of Stratford-upon-Avon_, by Julia Thomas; _Walking with William Shakespeare_, by Anne-Marie Edwards; and _Shakespeare’s Gardens_, by Jackie Bennett, Andrew Lawson and the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust.

The Shakespeare Birthplace is one of the literary pilgrimage sites described in _Freud’s Couch, Scott’s Buttocks, Brontë’s Grave_, by Simon Goldhill. “Women Re-Read Shakespeare Country” is a chapter in _Literary Tourism and Nineteenth-Century Culture_, edited by Nicola J. Watson.

Two new books about Shakespeare’s First Folio have been published, just in time for the anniversary: _Shakespeare’s First Folio: Four Centuries of an Iconic Boo k_ and _The Making of Shakespeare’s First Folio_, both by Emma Smith.

## [Buy Your Postage Stamps In Gambier And Discover Kenyon’s Historic Mural](link_22)

Posted on[March 18, 2016](link_22)by[Betsy](link_5)

Sure, I thrill at the ring of my telephone and the ding when a new e-mail arrives on my iPad, but I much prefer the refined sound my engraved pewter letter-opener makes when it opens the envelope of a handwritten note that’s been mailed to me. As Alexandra Stoddard observed in her 1990 book, _Gift of a Letter_, a thoughtful letter that takes minutes to write can become a treasured source of joy for its recipient that lasts for years.

My fondness for handwritten notes derives from a gift my uncle Steve and aunt Shelley gave me back in the early 1980s — a box of pale blue, white-bordered Crane & Co. folded notecards and a matching Paper Mate retractable ballpoint pen. Ever since, I’ve been splurging on fountain pens, collecting stationery, and selecting just the right commemorative stamps to share with my pen pals.

Devoted correspondents may be dwindling, but if you’re a throwback like me who is willing to go out of your way in search of a stamp beyond the Forever flag, consider making the trip to a small-town post office like the one I discovered on the campus of Kenyon College in Gambier, Ohio.

[![Image 11: Gambier post office](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2245.jpg?w=300&h=225)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2245.jpg)There, beside the College Relations Center where I interviewed for a position with the Office of Public Affairs, across from the bookstore where I stocked up on Caspari greeting cards, and steps away from the Middle Path I’ve walked while attending [three Kenyon presidential inaugurations](link_23), you’ll find a Colonial Revival structure built of stone, topped with a wooden cupola. Just as college and village officials requested when it was designed in 1940, the post office is in perfect architectural harmony with the character of its neighboring buildings.

Open the front door, enter the lobby, and step up to the service windows to conduct your postal business. But before you leave, look to your right and admire something that caught me by surprise. A one-paneled painted mural situated over the postmaster’s door and bulletin boards depicts two men on horseback taking in a picturesque view framed by lush trees.

“Bishop Chase Selects the Location for Old Kenyon” is the title that the late Norris Rahming, professor and director of Kenyon’s art department, gave to the mural he created for the post office.[![Image 12: Bishop Chase Selects the Location for Old Kenyon, Gambier Post Office](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2242.jpg?w=300&h=124)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2242.jpg)It depicts Bishop Philander Chase, Kenyon’s founder, with his friend, a Mount Vernon, Ohio lawyer named Henry B. Curtis, at the top of Gambier Hill. In his hands, Chase holds the blueprints for Old Kenyon Residence Hall.

Chase originally established the college on his Worthington, Ohio farm that once was located just a few blocks southeast of my home. Increasing student enrollment and development of Worthington convinced Chase that he needed to find a new home for Kenyon. Curtis helped Chase discover 8,000 acres of land in Knox County along the Kokosing River’s Owl Creek.

Legend has it that on July 24, 1826, Chase and Curtis led their horses through a thick tangle of oak bushes and grape vines up Gambier Hill. When they reached the top, they surveyed the beautiful panorama before them. “Well, this will do!,” Chase exclaimed.

While a Celtic-style cross now marks the spot of this historic happening,college historians point out that how the mural depicts the event isn’t exactly accurate. The climb up the hill was so slow and difficult that Chase and Curtis left their horses behind and completed their journey on foot. That’s how Rahming had originally portrayed the scene, but those responsible for approving his design in 1942 decided that placing the legendary pair on horseback made the painting more dramatic and picturesque. The mural was installed in the post office in 1943.

The mural does more than introduce people to Kenyon’s history. It is also typical of other murals created as part of Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal programs designed to help the country recover from the Great Depression.

From 1934 to 1943, the Section of Fine Arts of the Public Building Administration supported thousands of struggling artists by commissioning them to create around 1,400 murals for 1,100 post offices throughout the country. The murals also helped to enrich people’s lives by incorporating beautiful art into an important community meeting place where citizens habitually gathered every day.

Significant local historical events — especially those that showed the activities central to founding the community — were popular subjects for post office murals. The depictions conveyed p ride in a community’s past accomplishments and hope in its plans for the future, a perfect cure for the feelings of uncertainty caused by the Depression.

Other New Deal-era post office murals can be found around the state. My next post office mural stop is going to be to see the one in the Granville post office. “The First Pulpit in Granville” depicts the first settlers in Granville who cut down a tree near the center of the village to serve as an altar and pulpit and offered a service in thanksgiving for their safe arrival after a difficult trip crossing the Appalachians. The mural was painted by a Woodstock, New York artist named Wendell Jones around 1936, and was restored for Granville’s bicentennial celebrations in 2005.

The Gambier post office is on the northwest corner of Chase Avenue and Scott Alley. For more on Depression-era post office murals, read _Wall-To-Wall America: A Cultural History of Post-Office Murals in the Great Depression_, by Karal Ann Marling; “Not By Bread Alone: Post Office Art of the New Deal,” an article by Gerald Markowitz and Marlene Park in the June-July 1989 issue of the Ohio Historical Society’s _TIMELINE;_ and “Colonial Design Chosen for Gambier Post Office,” from the July 22, 1940 issue of the _Mount Vernon News_, on display in the post office’s lobby. Color transparencies, color negatives and black-and-white negatives of photographs of the New Deal artworks in 25 Ohio post offices comprise the Ohio Post Office Artwork Collection (AV 48) at the Ohio History Connection’s Archives/Library and can be requested for study in its reading room. Click [here](link_24) to see the finding aid for the collection.

By[Erik Wesner](link_21)August 17, 2026

[2 Comments](https://amishamerica.com/amish-volleyball-4-things-to-know/#comments)

The Philadelphia Inquirer ran a long piece over the weekend on **competitive Amish volleyball**, reported from a tournament at Intercourse Community Park in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania back in June. I spoke to reporter Jason Nark on the Amish sports topic; his [full report is here](link_27).

A few things stood out to me – here are four.

## 1. Volleyball Holds A Special Function In Amish Culture

Volleyball is the game you’ll most often see at **Amish youth gatherings**, at least in Lancaster County and communities like it.

Part of the reason is simple: girls can easily play volleyball too. It makes it a sport for easy socializing and interaction between the sexes. More on why that’s important in a minute. As to the growth of competitive volleyball as seen most obviously in these tournaments, Nark got different answers:

> The Amish in Pennsylvania, for reasons few could fully explain, love competitive volleyball. Some simply shrugged their shoulders when asked why.
> 
> 
> Others said they play volleyball because previous generations played too, a skill they learned just by watching, much the same as shoeing buggy horses or baking whoopie pies.
> 
> 
> “I guess it’s just part of our culture,” said Ray Beiler, the tournament’s organizer. ”Competition-wise, though, it’s slow-pitch and volleyball, but volleyball is probably the biggest.”

But traditionally, a big part of the function of youth group gatherings is as a venue to find a special someone who eventually becomes a marriage partner.

![Image 4](https://amishamerica.com/images/lancaster-amish-youth-volleyball-match.jpg)

Amish youth play volleyball at a Sunday gathering in Lancaster County, PA. Photo: Don Shenk

Volleyball is a game that provides for that interaction. Guys get a chance to show off in front of the girls. Good-natured ribbing comes from all sides. Everyone shakes hands and congratulates on a good game afterwards. To give you the flavor, here’s an excerpt from my [post on watching Amish youth play volleyball](link_28) at a Sunday gathering:

> Teams are mixed, with boys and girls on both sides. Some were at or near age 16, and you had others ranging into their 20s. Volleyball may begin in the afternoon and carry on after the supper meal, which takes place around 5.
> 
> 
> This isn’t just your everyday tame volleyball game—there is an intensity to make big plays with dives and flying spikes common.
> 
> 
> Shortly after arriving, I witnessed a young man leap, sail towards the net and bring his arm down like a mallet on the ball—spiking it directly into the face of a girl on the other team and sending the ball careening off into the out-of-bounds area.
> 
> 
> She was surprisingly unfazed by the force of the impact and continued on with a laugh.
> 
> 
> There is a bit of a competitive spirit, with some minor “trash talk” happening, though mild compared to non-Amish standards, and done all in fun. What you hear a lot more often are encouraging words—“Good effort”, “shake it off”.

In essence it’s a sport well-rooted and widely accepted in many communities – so to see it grow to this level in arguably the most progressive large Amish settlement is not really a surprise.

## 2. It’s Bigger Than You Might Think

When it comes to the tournaments, this isn’t a few kids batting a ball around a backyard. The tournament drew **hundreds of players**, some from the state next-door, and a few thousand spectators for the Saturday night final:

> On this beautiful afternoon in late June, the coed competitors were among the hundreds of young Amish players from Pennsylvania, Ohio, and other states who converged on Intercourse Community Park, about 60 miles west of Philadelphia, in Lancaster County, for the annual volleyball tournament.
> 
> 
> Hundreds gathered around the courts in lawn chairs to watch, including Amish men with long beards beside “English” children in sneakers and sports jerseys.

There are real trophies to be won, described as “tall trophies housed in an exhibition room, with silver and gold volleyballs fastened to the tops,” along with – maybe – bragging rights. It might strike you as odd to hear about “bragging” in an Amish context, but it’s done in fun, and not all Amish are as outwardly humble as others.

[Video 4](link_29)

## 3. Some Players Are Good Enough To Go Further – And Choose Not To

Some of these kids can really play. And in another culture, that might have them thinking along different lines.

Organizer Ray Beiler told the Inquirer that a college coach attended a tournament and remarked that a number of the players could compete beyond it.

Steven Nolt of the Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies at Elizabethtown College addressed what pursuing that would involve:

> …Nolt said it’s unlikely that even the most talented volleyball players would pursue the sport more competitively.
> 
> 
> “It would be hard to imagine,” Nolt said. “They’d be making a choice not to join the Amish.”

There might be the occasional person that is drawn away from an Amish life because of sports. We’ve seen some examples of former Amish people who have done just that – a man named Melvin Byler, mentioned in the Inquirer piece, left to pursue rodeo. But it’s pretty rare. Rare enough that it’s not really a community concern, from what I can tell.

## 4. Pickleball Has Arrived On The Scene

One of the newer games showing up in Amish Country is **pickleball**. The Inquirer notes it’s caught on fast. It appeared at the volleyball event, and has made inroads in the community:

> Chris Haley oversaw the pickleball tournament at the Intercourse Heritage Days, where there are new courts.
> 
> 
> He said the Amish quickly took up that sport, too, and some have makeshift courts at their house.
> 
> 
> “They are talented and determined,” Haley said.

Pickleball’s just one of many [sports seen among the Amish](link_30), though. The Amish play a wide range of sports, and what you’ll see depends a lot on the community.

![Image 5](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-boy-recess-sliding-safe-softball.jpg)

A softball game at an Amish school recess. Photo: Don Burke

Basketball turns up in communities in Indiana, or in Geauga County, Ohio – where there’s even an [annual Amish-vs-Yankee charity game](link_31). Soccer has become popular at some Amish schools as a cold-weather game (I had a chance to join in a game with Lancaster schoolchildren some time ago).

Softball is a classic which remains common in a lot of places (even [among some Amish adults](link_32)). Add those to other newer sports like [spikeball](link_33) and can jam, on top of traditional pastimes like [cornerball](link_34).

This Inquirer piece is really about Lancaster County and communities like it. That’s where these big tournaments happen. You’ll see far less of this in smaller conservative settlements, for obvious reasons of scale, and tradition. Sports in general tend to be more common in progressive communities.

# The Amish: A to Z (Featured Articles)

By[Erik Wesner](link_21)Updated January 3, 2025

What do the Amish believe? Why do they live the way they do? Below you’ll find **over 70 articles** in 14 categories on Amish beliefs, rules, culture, customs and more.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/amish-online-encyclopedia/)1. Amish Lifestyle

![Image 3: An Amish couple dressed in black walking down a country road](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-marriage-1.jpg)

1.   **[Amish Language](link_26)**– Which languages do the Amish speak? Amish know (to varying degrees) three languages, including Pennsylvania Dutch.
2.   **[Amish Clothing](link_27)** – Why do Amish people dress “Plain”? A look at 6 reasons for this characteristic Amish custom.
3.   **[Amish Food](link_28)** – A look at the typical “Amish diet” – including home-grown and store-bought foods, Amish home cooking, baked goods, the Sunday church meal, and eating in restaurants.
4.   [**Amish Jobs**](link_29) – How do the Amish make a living? A closer look at 6 typical Amish occupations, including farming, small businesses and factory work.
5.   [**Amish Homes**](link_30) – What are Amish homes like inside? How do they heat, light, cook, keep food cool, and wash clothes?
6.   **[Amish Recreation](link_31)** – What do Amish people do for fun? Amish leisure time activities, including hunting, fishing, games, sports, visiting, and more.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/amish-online-encyclopedia/)2. Amish Population & Communities

![Image 4: Amish boy pushing a wagon load down the road](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-child.jpg)

1.   [**Amish Population: Where do the Amish live?**](link_32) – How many Amish are there? A look at the main areas where Amish live in the USA and Canada.
2.   [**The 10 Largest Amish Communities (2024)**](link_9) – Key data and interesting facts on the ten largest Amish settlements.
3.   [**How are Amish communities organized?**](link_33) – The differences between Amish “communities”, “church districts”, and “affiliations”.
4.   [**Amish State Guide (32 States)**](link_7) – State-by-state guide to Amish communities across the nation.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/amish-online-encyclopedia/)3. Amish Beliefs & Customs

![Image 5: Amish children playing in a schoolyard](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-school-children.jpg)

1.   [**Amish Education**](link_34) – Why do Amish children not go to high school? What is learning like for Amish people after 8th grade? What are Amish schools like? What do Amish children learn?
2.   [**Do the Amish Vote?**](link_35) – What do Amish believe about voting and politics? How many actually vote? How have campaigns targeted the Amish in the past? Are Amish more “Republican” or “Democrat”?
3.   **[The Amish & Photos](link_36)** – What do Amish people believe about photography? What are the differences and exceptions?
4.   **[Amish & the Law](link_37)** – Amish beliefs on the law. Do the Amish report crimes? Why don’t they file lawsuits?
5.   [**Nonresistance**](link_38) – Why don’t Amish believe in military service? Do Amish use guns?
6.   [**The Amish Barn-raising**](link_39) – The barn-raising as an example of Amish mutual aid. How a barn-raising is organized, and other communal work projects (frolics) among Amish.
7.   [**What Do The Amish Believe? 20 Faith Statements**](link_40) – The Amish are a Christian group. This list of 20 beliefs covers the fundamentals of Amish Christian faith.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/amish-online-encyclopedia/)4. Amish Rules

## ![Image 6: Two Amish women in white aprons walking down a road](https://amishamerica.com/images/two-amish-women-walking.jpg)

1.   [**Amish Church Rules**](link_41)– What is the Amish _Ordnung_? How do Amish church rules work? What happens when Amish people violate church rules?
2.   **[The Amish & Shunning](link_42)** – Why do Amish practice shunning? How long does it last? What happens to a person in the _Bann_? Is there a Biblical basis for shunning? Differences across Amish groups.
3.   **[Rumspringa](link_14)**– What is _Rumspringa_? Why do Amish youth have _Rumspringa?_ Do Amish youth behave wildly when running around? Myths and media portrayals of _Rumspringa._
4.   **[The Amish & Alcohol](link_43)** – Amish beliefs on alcohol. Which Amish drink alcohol and which groups are against it?
5.   [**Do Amish People Smoke?**](link_44) – On the practice of smoking in some Amish groups, and raising tobacco by some Amish, for example in Lancaster County, PA.
6.   [**The Amish & Sex**](link_45) – On Amish sex education, premarital sex, homosexuality, and other topics.
7.   **[10 “Exceptions” To Amish Rules](link_46)** – A look at Amish groups and individuals who act outside “the norm”.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/amish-online-encyclopedia/)5. The Amish Church

![Image 7: An open German-language Bible](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-german-bible-open.jpg)

1.   **[The Amish Church: How it Works](link_47)** – A top-to-bottom look at Amish church structure and practices. Church leaders, the church service, Amish religious customs and special services.
2.   [**Amish Church Leaders**](link_48) – Description of the roles and duties of the Amish bishop, minister, and deacon. How Amish ministers are chosen.
3.   [**Baptism in the Amish Church**](link_49) – At what age are Amish typically baptized? What is the Amish baptism process like? What commitments are made when baptized into an Amish church?
4.   **[Can You Join The Amish?](link_50)** – Can outsiders become Amish? Do Amish try to gain converts? A look at the reality of joining the Amish, and examples of outsiders who’ve become Amish converts.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/amish-online-encyclopedia/)6. Types of Amish

![Image 8: Row of parked open and white-topped Amish buggies](https://amishamerica.com/images/nebraska-amish.jpg)

1.   [**How many types of Amish are there?**](link_51) – A look at differences between various Amish groups.
2.   [**Mennonite vs Amish**](link_11) – What’s the difference between Amish and Mennonites? Diversity in the Amish and Mennonite world; Amish similarities with Old Order Mennonites.
3.   [**The Swartzentruber Amish**](link_52) – Who are the Swartzentruber Amish? The origin, customs, beliefs, technology, occupations, and more on the most traditional and conservative Amish group.
4.   **[The New Order Amish](link_53)** – The New Order Amish are a unique and often misunderstood group which originated in the 1960s in Ohio. How are they different from the Old Order Amish?
5.   **[Beachy Amish vs. Old Order Amish](link_54)** – A look at the differences and similarities between Beachy and Old Order Amish. The origin of the Beachy Amish, Beachy Amish beliefs, and use of technology.
6.   [**Are There Black Amish People?**](link_55) – Can you be Amish as a non-white person? Some sources claim that there are “Black Amish communities”. What is the real story?

## [](https://amishamerica.com/amish-online-encyclopedia/)7. Amish History

![Image 9: Old style parchment map showing Germany, France, Switzerland, and nearby countries](https://amishamerica.com/images/europe-map.jpg)

1.   **[Where do the Amish come from?](link_56)** – On the historical Anabaptist roots of the Amish in Europe. Who was Jakob Amman? The 1693 schism resulting in the Amish. Migration of the Amish to America.
2.   [**Who were the Anabaptists?**](link_57) – A brief look at the history of the early Anabaptists, European predecessors to Amish, Mennonites and related groups.
3.   [**Do Amish live in Europe?**](link_58) – On the last Old Order Amish settlement in Europe and its end. Beachy Amish in Europe.
4.   [**The 10 Oldest Amish Communities**](link_59) – Amish began arriving in North America in the early-to-mid 1700s. These are their ten oldest surviving communities.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/amish-online-encyclopedia/)8. The Amish Family

![Image 10: Silhouette of a windmill and Amish barn as sun sets](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-farm-windmill-dusk.jpg)

1.   [**Amish Family Size**](link_60) – How many children do Amish typically have? How family sizes differ across Amish groups.
2.   [**Amish Marriage: Beliefs & Customs**](link_61) – At what age do Amish typically marry? Do Amish condone divorce or remarriage? Amish wedding traditions. What about unmarried Amish?
3.   [**Amish Women**](link_62) – A look at typical roles of Amish women. The position of Amish women compared to Amish men. Do Amish women work outside the home? Are Amish women “happy”?
4.   **[Amish Children & Discipline](link_63)** – How do Amish discipline their children? On spanking and corporal punishment in Amish homes and schools.
5.   **[Common Amish Surnames](link_64)** – What are the most common Amish family names? A look at different Amish last names in different communities.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/amish-online-encyclopedia/)9. The Amish & Technology

![Image 11: Calendar in Amish buggy shop beneath buggy lights and hanging wires](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-technology.jpg)

1.   [**The Amish & Technology**](link_65) – Do Amish think tech is “evil”? How and why do Amish use technology selectively? What kinds of technologies do Amish use? How do church rules affect Amish use of technology? The pace of change in the Amish church.
2.   **[Do Amish use electricity?](link_66)** – Why Amish (generally) don’t use the public electric grid. How do Amish generate power? How Amish light homes and keep food cold. Use of power in homes, businesses, and Amish buggies.
3.   [**Amish & the Internet**](link_67) – Do Amish use computers? How and when do Amish people go online? What is the “Amish computer”? On smartphone use by some Amish.
4.   **[The Amish & Phones](link_68)** – Why do (most) Amish forbid telephones in the home? What is an Amish phone “shanty”? Use of phones in businesses and other alternatives including the smartphone.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/amish-online-encyclopedia/)10. The Amish & Money

![Image 12: White wooden handmade sign advertising vegetables, pies, and other goods](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-food-signs.jpg)

1.   **[The Amish & Money](link_69)**– How the Amish spend and use money. Amish “consumer culture”.
2.   [**Are the Amish rich?**](link_70) – A look at wealth among the Amish. How some Amish (business owners in particular) have become quite wealthy. Amish “land wealth”.
3.   [**Do Amish pay taxes?**](link_15) – Explaining which taxes Amish pay, and two limited religious-based exemptions (Social Security & worker’s comp). Debunking the idea that “Amish don’t pay taxes”.
4.   [**Amish Businesses: 8 Common Types**](link_71) – A look at the various types of Amish enterprises, Amish women in business, unusual Amish businesses, and the number and typical size of Amish companies.
5.   **[Amish Auctions](link_72)** – What are the different types of Amish auctions? A look at “mud sales”, school auctions, benefit fundraisers, and others. Information on where auctions take place.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/amish-online-encyclopedia/)11. The Amish & Health Care

![Image 13: Amish girls blocking volleyball spike at the net](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-girls-playing-volleyball.jpg)

1.   [**Do Amish visit doctors?**](link_73) – On the various Amish approaches to medical care. Reasons why Amish are often more reluctant to use conventional medical care. How do Amish pay for health care?
2.   **[Unconventional Amish Health Practices](link_74)** – A look at five atypical health practices found among the Amish.
3.   **[Amish Natural Remedies](link_75)** – Many Amish rely on natural and home remedies to treat ailments and illnesses. A look at five such remedies.

# Illinois Is America’s #10 Amish State — Here Are Its 10 Biggest Communities

By[Erik Wesner](link_21)September 25, 2026

![Image 3: Rear view of a black Amish buggy with an orange slow-moving vehicle triangle, traveling a gravel road between fields of dry grass in the Opdyke, IL community](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-buggy-rear-view-opdyke-illinois.jpg)

As of 2026, the Amish are found in 20 locations across Illinois. Photo: Don Burke

Illinois is home to America’s **tenth-largest Amish population**. Over 9,000 Amish live in around 20 settlements across the state, though more than six in ten of them live in just one community.

These ten communities are the largest in Illinois, based on the most current Amish population estimates.

_Population numbers via Young Center for Anabaptist & Pietist Studies at Elizabethtown College (source link at bottom)._

## 1. Arthur

![Image 4](https://amishamerica.com/images/arthur-illinois-amish-carriage-reflectors.jpg)

An Amish buggy travels through the Arthur, Illinois community. Photo: S.I.

**Arthur/Arcola (Moultrie, Douglas & Coles Counties)**  
**Community founded:** 1864  
**Total Amish population:** 5,790

The state’s largest Amish settlement is also by far its oldest. Founded in 1864, the Arthur community spreads across three counties in east-central Illinois. At around 5,800 people and 33 church districts (congregations), it’s the eighth-largest Amish settlement in North America.

Many Amish here work in furniture and other wood businesses, and the community has a fairly developed tourism scene, including the Illinois Amish Heritage Center at Arcola.

* * *

## 2. Ava

![Image 5](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-produce-sign-ava-illinois-community.jpg)

Sign for an Amish-run produce business in the Ava settlement. Photo: Don Burke

**Ava (Jackson County)**  
**Community founded:** 1991  
**Total Amish population:** 470

After Arthur, there’s a steep drop-off. Ava, in Jackson County in southern Illinois, is the state’s second-largest community at around 470 people, less than a tenth the size of Arthur. Founded in 1991, it’s also the second-oldest, and now numbers four church districts.

Ava is a [New Order Amish community](link_27), and one of the few horse-and-buggy Amish settlements that permit public electricity.

* * *

## 3. Opdyke

![Image 6](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-buggy-approaching-opdyke-belle-rive-illinois.jpg)

An Amish buggy makes its way down a Jefferson County backroad. Photo: Don Burke

**Opdyke (Jefferson County)**  
**Community founded:** 1995  
**Total Amish population:** 460

Just behind Ava is [Opdyke](link_28), also known by the name of nearby Belle Rive, in Jefferson County in southern Illinois. It has grown to three church districts since its founding in 1995. The settlement traces its origins to the [Amish in Delaware](link_29). Some tractor use is permitted here as well as implements with rubber tires, two signs of a more progressive group.

* * *

## 4. Macomb/Colchester

![Image 7](https://amishamerica.com/images/macomb-illinois-amish-buggy-snowfall-christmas-eve-2010.jpg)

A buggy on the road in the Macomb Amish settlement during a Christmas Eve snowfall. Photo: [Macomb Paynes/flickr](link_30)

**Macomb/Colchester (McDonough County)**  
**Community founded:** 1993  
**Total Amish population:** 350

The Macomb/Colchester settlement lies in McDonough County in western Illinois. Founded in 1993, this community is more conservative than the Arthur Amish, visible in the homes and other material signs in the community.

* * *

## 5. Oblong

![Image 8](https://amishamerica.com/images/inside-amish-country-store-oblong-illinois.jpg)

Inside Girod’s Country Market in the Oblong community. Photo: [Eli Swartzentruber/Google](link_31)

**Oblong (Crawford County)**  
**Community founded:** 2006  
**Total Amish population:** 340

The Oblong community is one of several in Crawford County. Founded in 2006, it numbers two church districts. Crawford County is home to two more small settlements, at Flat Rock and Sumner.

* * *

## 6. Johnsonville

![Image 9](https://amishamerica.com/images/johnsonville-illinois-map.jpg)

**Johnsonville (Wayne County)**  
**Community founded:** 2008  
**Total Amish population:** 335

At nearly the same size as Oblong is the community at Johnsonville, in Wayne County in southeastern Illinois. Founded in 2008, it’s the youngest community in the state’s top ten, and numbers two church districts. Wayne County has proven attractive to Amish settling in the state, as it turns up twice more on this list.

* * *

## 7. Galatia/Thompsonville

![Image 10](https://amishamerica.com/images/parked-buggy-galatia-illinois-amish-settlement.jpg)

A parked buggy in the Galatia community displays an SMV triangle with an atypical placement. Photo: Don Burke

**Galatia/Thompsonville (Saline & Franklin Counties)**  
**Community founded:** 2007  
**Total Amish population:** 185

With another steep drop in size we come to the Galatia/Thompsonville community, found in both Saline and Franklin Counties in southern Illinois. Its roots are in a [Wisconsin Amish](link_32) settlement. Founded in 2007, it has grown to two church districts in size.

* * *

## 8. Orchardville

![Image 11](https://amishamerica.com/images/lumber-business-orchardville-illinois-amish-community.jpg)

An Amish-run lumber business in the Orchardville community displays the characteristic “No Sunday Sales” notice on its sign.

**Orchardville (Clay & Wayne Counties)**  
**Community founded:** 2007  
**Total Amish population:** 180

Orchardville is located in Wayne County, with some Amish living in neighboring Clay County. It’s one of the few communities on this list that has gotten smaller in recent years. In 2021 the Young Center counted two districts and around 240 people here; it has since contracted to one district.

* * *

## 9. Roseville

![Image 12](https://amishamerica.com/images/lees-bakery-sign-roseville-illinois.jpg)

Sign for an Amish bakery in the Roseville community. Photo: [Christina D/Google](link_33)

**Roseville (Warren County)**  
**Community founded:** 2007  
**Total Amish population:** 165

Roseville, in Warren County, is the second western Illinois settlement on the list, a short drive north of #4 Macomb. Founded in 2007, it numbers two church districts.

* * *

## 10. Cisne/Fairfield

![Image 13](https://amishamerica.com/images/cisne-illinois-map.jpg)

**Cisne/Fairfield (Wayne County)**  
**Community founded:** 2002  
**Total Amish population:** 160

Rounding out the top ten is Cisne/Fairfield, the third Wayne County entry on this list. Founded in 2002, it numbers two church districts. Though it’s a top ten community for the state, at under 200 people it would be considered a “small” settlement otherwise.

For more on Amish communities in the Prairie State, check out our [Illinois Amish state guide](link_34).

## [Buy Your Postage Stamps In Gambier And Discover Kenyon’s Historic Mural](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/2016/03/18/mural/)

Posted on[March 18, 2016](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/2016/03/18/mural/ "6:58 pm")by[Betsy](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/author/beesfirstappearance/ "View all posts by Betsy")

Sure, I thrill at the ring of my telephone and the ding when a new e-mail arrives on my iPad, but I much prefer the refined sound my engraved pewter letter-opener makes when it opens the envelope of a handwritten note that’s been mailed to me. As Alexandra Stoddard observed in her 1990 book, _Gift of a Letter_, a thoughtful letter that takes minutes to write can become a treasured source of joy for its recipient that lasts for years.

My fondness for handwritten notes derives from a gift my uncle Steve and aunt Shelley gave me back in the early 1980s — a box of pale blue, white-bordered Crane & Co. folded notecards and a matching Paper Mate retractable ballpoint pen. Ever since, I’ve been splurging on fountain pens, collecting stationery, and selecting just the right commemorative stamps to share with my pen pals.

Devoted correspondents may be dwindling, but if you’re a throwback like me who is willing to go out of your way in search of a stamp beyond the Forever flag, consider making the trip to a small-town post office like the one I discovered on the campus of Kenyon College in Gambier, Ohio.

[![Image 2: Gambier post office](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2245.jpg?w=300&h=225)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2245.jpg)There, beside the College Relations Center where I interviewed for a position with the Office of Public Affairs, across from the bookstore where I stocked up on Caspari greeting cards, and steps away from the Middle Path I’ve walked while attending [three Kenyon presidential inaugurations](link_3), you’ll find a Colonial Revival structure built of stone, topped with a wooden cupola. Just as college and village officials requested when it was designed in 1940, the post office is in perfect architectural harmony with the character of its neighboring buildings.

Open the front door, enter the lobby, and step up to the service windows to conduct your postal business. But before you leave, look to your right and admire something that caught me by surprise. A one-paneled painted mural situated over the postmaster’s door and bulletin boards depicts two men on horseback taking in a picturesque view framed by lush trees.

“Bishop Chase Selects the Location for Old Kenyon” is the title that the late Norris Rahming, professor and director of Kenyon’s art department, gave to the mural he created for the post office.[![Image 3: Bishop Chase Selects the Location for Old Kenyon, Gambier Post Office](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2242.jpg?w=300&h=124)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2242.jpg)It depicts Bishop Philander Chase, Kenyon’s founder, with his friend, a Mount Vernon, Ohio lawyer named Henry B. Curtis, at the top of Gambier Hill. In his hands, Chase holds the blueprints for Old Kenyon Residence Hall.

Chase originally established the college on his Worthington, Ohio farm that once was located just a few blocks southeast of my home. Increasing student enrollment and development of Worthington convinced Chase that he needed to find a new home for Kenyon. Curtis helped Chase discover 8,000 acres of land in Knox County along the Kokosing River’s Owl Creek.

Legend has it that on July 24, 1826, Chase and Curtis led their horses through a thick tangle of oak bushes and grape vines up Gambier Hill. When they reached the top, they surveyed the beautiful panorama before them. “Well, this will do!,” Chase exclaimed.

While a Celtic-style cross now marks the spot of this historic happening,college historians point out that how the mural depicts the event isn’t exactly accurate. The climb up the hill was so slow and difficult that Chase and Curtis left their horses behind and completed their journey on foot. That’s how Rahming had originally portrayed the scene, but those responsible for approving his design in 1942 decided that placing the legendary pair on horseback made the painting more dramatic and picturesque. The mural was installed in the post office in 1943.

The mural does more than introduce people to Kenyon’s history. It is also typical of other murals created as part of Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal programs designed to help the country recover from the Great Depression.

Advertisement

From 1934 to 1943, the Section of Fine Arts of the Public Building Administration supported thousands of struggling artists by commissioning them to create around 1,400 murals for 1,100 post offices throughout the country. The murals also helped to enrich people’s lives by incorporating beautiful art into an important community meeting place where citizens habitually gathered every day.

Significant local historical events — especially those that showed the activities central to founding the community — were popular subjects for post office murals. The depictions conveyed p ride in a community’s past accomplishments and hope in its plans for the future, a perfect cure for the feelings of uncertainty caused by the Depression.

Other New Deal-era post office murals can be found around the state. My next post office mural stop is going to be to see the one in the Granville post office. “The First Pulpit in Granville” depicts the first settlers in Granville who cut down a tree near the center of the village to serve as an altar and pulpit and offered a service in thanksgiving for their safe arrival after a difficult trip crossing the Appalachians. The mural was painted by a Woodstock, New York artist named Wendell Jones around 1936, and was restored for Granville’s bicentennial celebrations in 2005.

The Gambier post office is on the northwest corner of Chase Avenue and Scott Alley. For more on Depression-era post office murals, read _Wall-To-Wall America: A Cultural History of Post-Office Murals in the Great Depression_, by Karal Ann Marling; “Not By Bread Alone: Post Office Art of the New Deal,” an article by Gerald Markowitz and Marlene Park in the June-July 1989 issue of the Ohio Historical Society’s _TIMELINE;_ and “Colonial Design Chosen for Gambier Post Office,” from the July 22, 1940 issue of the _Mount Vernon News_, on display in the post office’s lobby. Color transparencies, color negatives and black-and-white negatives of photographs of the New Deal artworks in 25 Ohio post offices comprise the Ohio Post Office Artwork Collection (AV 48) at the Ohio History Connection’s Archives/Library and can be requested for study in its reading room. Click [here](link_4) to see the finding aid for the collection.

# The Amish in Illinois: 2026 Guide (20 Communities)

By[Erik Wesner](https://amishamerica.com/author/erik-wesner/)Updated September 12, 2026

[91 Comments](https://amishamerica.com/illinois-amish/#comments)

The Illinois Amish population was approximately **9,395 people** as of 2026, spread across 20 communities. The Amish community at **Arthur** is by far the largest in Illinois, with well over half the state’s Amish. Other Amish settlements are found across the state, particularly in the south and west regions.

1.   [The Arthur Amish Community](https://amishamerica.com/illinois-amish/#arthur)
2.   [Arthur Amish Stores](https://amishamerica.com/illinois-amish/#arthur-stores)
3.   [Visit Arthur Amish Country](https://amishamerica.com/illinois-amish/#visit-arthur)
4.   [Other Illinois Amish Communities](https://amishamerica.com/illinois-amish/#other-il-communities)
5.   [Historical Illinois Amish Settlements](https://amishamerica.com/illinois-amish/#past-settlements)

![Image 3: Silhouette of an Amish buggy backlit by the rising sun](https://amishamerica.com/images/illinois-amish.jpg)

An Amish buggy races across the sun outside Arthur, Illinois. Photo: Walter Blackledge

## [](https://amishamerica.com/illinois-amish/)The Arthur Amish

The Arthur Amish community is the largest and by far the oldest Amish settlement in Illinois. Founded over 160 years ago, today the community has population of around **5,800 Amish people**. The settlement is centered around Arthur, a small town of around 2,000 souls.

Amish homes are located in both **Moultrie and Douglas Counties** (the county line bisects the town) as well as in Coles County to the south. Amish homes and farms extend in all directions, as far east as Arcola, towards Sullivan, the seat of Moultrie County in the southwest, and highway 36 to the north.

![Image 4: An Amish couple with children on bicycles](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-bicycling-arthur-illinois-community.jpg)

Bicycling is popular among Amish on the flat roads in the Arthur community area

The Arthur community was founded in 1864, by Amish from communities in Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, and Iowa (see _A History of the Amish_, Steven Nolt p 232-3).

The Arthur Amish were not the first Amish community in the Prairie State, however, with two settlements having been founded in the central part of Illinois in the 1830s. But the Arthur community was destined to grow and ultimately survive, while the others eventually disappeared.

The Arthur Amish community has grown to **33 church districts** (congregations) as of 2026.

While the Arthur Amish do not face quite the same external population pressures as Amish settlements in the east, farmland is still quite expensive. This has affected occupational choices – with small business and factory work popular. Nonetheless, many Amish at Arthur continue in the dairy farm tradition.

![Image 5: Views of the backs of Amish women's heads with a quilt hanging in the background](https://amishamerica.com/images/illinois-amish-quilt-auction-crowd.jpg)

View from the seats an Amish quilt benefit auction in Arthur, Illinois.

The terrain of the Arthur community is buggy-friendly, generally very flat and with paved roads. Common names in the Arthur community are Miller, Kauffman, Gingerich, and Schrock. Less-common names seen here include Jess, Otto, Diener, and Rocke.

While agriculture remains fairly common, Amish at Arthur work in a number of other trades. Some work for large overhead door manufacturer C.H.I. and can be seen bicycling to and from work at the local plant. Other Amish in the Arthur community are known for their small business activity, in particular furniture and wood-related enterprises.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/illinois-amish/)Amish Stores & Businesses at Arthur

Arthur is home to a thriving **Amish business community**, with many Amish operating businesses in wood-related industries.

Lower-end wood businesses are found at Arthur, such as pallet makers. More frequently seen are higher-end operations producing cabinets and furniture.

![Image 6: Beachy's Bulk Foods store sign with pie and other simple food images](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-bulk-foods-store-sign-illinois.jpg)

Beachy’s Bulk Foods is one of many Amish stores & businesses in the Arthur community

These number in the dozens and employ hundreds of Amish males throughout the community. Arthur furniture businesses attract consumer attention from urban areas such as Chicago, St. Louis, and Indianapolis, all within a three-hour drive. Find an [Illinois Amish furniture](https://amishamerica.com/amish-furniture-illinois/) business.

In addition to furniture, a number of other Amish-operated businesses can be found. One Amish family operates a jelly-making and canning business. Another runs a small bookstore catering to the Plain community. Machine, metal, and engine shops are also found throughout the Arthur settlement, as are construction businesses.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/illinois-amish/)Visit the Arthur Amish

As one of the largest Amish communities in the Midwest, Arthur has a fairly developed tourist industry, welcoming visitors from across the region.

The area is also home to the [Illinois Amish Heritage Center](https://www.illinoisamish.org/) found at Arcola, which specializes in educating the public about the Amish and Anabaptist peoples. The Center features buildings important to Illinois Amish history, including **two of the oldest historic Amish homes** in the state, restored and preserved at the Center.

![Image 7: An Amish man and two sons ride in a pony cart past a field of brown corn stalks](https://amishamerica.com/images/illinois-amish-pony-cart.jpg)

An Illinois Amish family traveling by pony cart. Photo: Walter Blackledge

At least one Amish family in the Arthur community hosts non-Amish visitors for meals and [overnight stays](https://amishamerica.com/amish-country-where-to-stay/).

There are many **small shops and stores** run by the Amish throughout the community, including food and grocery, crafts, dry goods, and even an [Amish-run coffee shop](https://amishamerica.com/roselens-amish-coffee-shop-at-arthur-illinois/). Stopping in to patronize an Amish store is one of the best ways to meet and talk to the Amish.

The Arthur area is pretty easy to get around, and with its rural grid road system, hard to get lost. It can be fun to simply drive through the Amish areas (extending for miles in each direction around the town) and see what stores you come across. They are typically marked by simple signs at the end of Amish lanes.

Rockome Gardens was once a longstanding tourist destination located in the community. Rockome featured “rock gardens” comprised of numerous rock formations and stone fences, as well as a number of other attractions. However, Rockome **closed operations** in the 2010s.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/illinois-amish/)Other Illinois Amish settlements

While Arthur is by far the largest Amish community in Illinois, there are numerous other small Amish settlements found throughout the Land of Lincoln.

After Arthur, the next oldest Illinois Amish community is Ava in southern Illinois, founded in 1991 – over 125 years after Arthur. Ava is also the site of the state’s second-largest Amish community. But at roughly 470 people, it is still less than 10% the size of the Arthur community.

![Image 8: Amish jams and jellies business sign](https://amishamerica.com/images/millers-country-crafts.jpg)

Millers Country Crafts is an Amish-owned business in the Ava settlement in southern Illinois. Photo: Don Burke

Another notable community is found at **Macomb** in **McDonough County** in western Illinois. This community is more conservative than the Arthur Amish. With an estimated Amish population of 350 people, it is the state’s fourth-largest settlement, behind the [Opdyke community](https://amishamerica.com/amish-belle-rive-opdyke-illinois/) in Jefferson County (around 460 people).

Most other Amish communities in Illinois can be found in the western and southern portions of the state. Amish are found in Crawford County, home to three settlements, Jackson and Wayne Counties (home to two settlements each), and a number of others.

For a full list of Illinois Amish communities, see “Amish Population in the United States by State and County, 2026” linked at bottom.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/illinois-amish/)Historical Amish settlements in Illinois

A number of Amish settlements which once existed in Illinois no longer do today. A few were of significant size.

The community in **Tazewell and Woodford Counties** was formed in 1831, in large part by direct immigrants from Lorraine in France. Over the next 20 years, around 130 Amish families moved to the area, and by the early 1850s, five congregations had been formed.

Amish historian David Luthy tells us that at by this time, the Tazewell/Woodford settlement was larger than the Lancaster County settlement. It was also equal to, or larger in size than the community at Holmes County, which had been founded over 20 years before the Tazewell/Woodford community (_Settlements that Failed_, Luthy pp 75-80).

Eventually Amish in this community were influenced by progressive religious movements which were in the ascendant in America at the time. Amish in the area began to build meetinghouses, typically a key step in the journey from a traditional to progressive alignment.

[![Image 9: Silhouette of an Amish farmer in field working with a horse team in winter](https://amishamerica.com/images/arthur-illinois-amish.jpg)](https://amishamerica.com/illinois-amish/arthur-illinois-amish-2/)

An Illinois Amish farmer hard at work. Photo: Walter Blackledge

Many Amish at Tazewell and Woodford Counties eventually formed the “Western District Amish Mennonite Conference” in 1884. Some congregants in this community also joined other movements, including the “Egly Amish” and the “Stuckey Amish” groups.

At the time, many other Amish settlements which were affected by progressive change (such as the Kalona, Iowa Amish, or Elkhart/Lagrange County community in Indiana) formed an Old Order element as well, which kept to traditional practices and beliefs.

Such was not the case with the Tazewell and Woodford County settlement – which is why no Old Order Amish are found today at what was once one of the largest Amish communities in North America.

As a result, Luthy notes that many Amish surnames once found in this community are unseen anywhere among Amish today, such as Yordy, Roggy, Litwiller, and Klopfenstein (_Settlements that Failed_, Luthy, p. 80-81).

Another Amish community was founded in 1835 in **Bureau and Putnam Counties**, also in north-central Illinois. In a sense, this community followed a similar progressive path as that of the settlement at Tazewell and Woodford Counties, with member eventually joining the Western District Amish Mennonite Conference mentioned above.

Further failed settlements were found at **Prairie Bird in Shelby County** (lasting from 1871 to 1884), and **Vandalia in Fayette County** (1893-1906) (_Settlements that Failed_, Luthy, pp. 81-91)

## Illinois: Not an Amish “Hot Spot”

Illinois is a state with a long history of Amish settlement – and well-established Amish population, seen most obviously in the sizeable Arthur community.

Through the first decade of the 2000s, Illinois consistently saw new Amish communities founded across the state. At least **11 communities** were started by Amish, either from in-state or by out-of-state arrivals, in the 2000s.

The community in Saline County, for instance, originates from a [Wisconsin Amish](https://amishamerica.com/wisconsin-amish/) settlement. On moving to this area, one of the Amishmen commented to a local newspaper that he hoped they can “blend in here without being too much of a nuisance to anybody”, and expected to enjoy the warmer weather.

![Image 10: Rear view of Amish buggy on flat asphalt road among summer cornfields](https://amishamerica.com/images/illinois-amish-buggy-asphalt-road.jpg)

Buggies have been increasingly common on the road in some parts of Illinois, though new Amish settlement has slowed

However, in recent years, new Amish settlement has **nearly stopped**. In the past 15 years, **only two new Amish communities** have been added to the state’s current tally.

The total Illinois Amish population has grown, but it has done so at a slower rate than typical for the Amish. This is likely due to out-migration to other states, with some Illinois communities having ceased to exist since 2010.

This is in contrast to the prior 20-year period, when Illinois was listed as a “High Growth State” by the Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies for the time span 1991-2010. In that period, the Amish population increased by 133% due in part to in-migration from communities outside the state.

In contrast, over the 10-year period from 2015 to 2024, the Illinois Amish population has grown at a slow pace for Amish – only about a 20% increase in that time span.
