# The Amish in Delaware: 2026 Guide (Dover Community)

By[Erik Wesner](https://amishamerica.com/author/erik-wesner/)Updated September 12, 2026

[15 Comments](https://amishamerica.com/delaware-amish/#comments)

Tiny Delaware is home to a single sizable, long-lived Amish settlement. Founded over 100 years ago, the community just outside state capital **Dover** continues to grow, despite land pressure. Today (2026), over **2,100 Amish** live in the Dover Amish community.

1.   [The Dover Amish Community](https://amishamerica.com/delaware-amish/#dover-community)
2.   [Delaware Amish Businesses](https://amishamerica.com/delaware-amish/#businesses)
3.   [Unique Delaware Amish Buggies](https://amishamerica.com/delaware-amish/#buggies)
4.   [Future of the Delaware Amish](https://amishamerica.com/delaware-amish/#future)

![Image 3: A black buggy parked under a roof overhang of a white garage](https://amishamerica.com/images/delaware-amish-dover.jpg)

Only one Amish community is found in Delaware, outside of state capital Dover

## [](https://amishamerica.com/delaware-amish/)Amish in Delaware: The Dover Community

Amish first settled in the middle of **Kent County**, the central county of the state’s three, in 1915. Settlers arrived here from states as diverse as Wisconsin, Montana, Alabama, and Ohio.

Today, the community numbers 15 church districts (congregations), with approximately 2,155 people, according to the latest figures from the Young Center at Elizabethtown College (PA).

![Image 4: Kitchen table in an old-fashioned, cozy kitchen](https://amishamerica.com/images/delaware-amish-home-dover.jpg)

Inside the kitchen of an Amish home in the Dover, DE community

The Dover community is one of a few truly “East Coast” communities, along with Lancaster County, the [St. Mary’s County, Maryland Amish community](https://amishamerica.com/the-amish-of-mechanicsville-maryland/), and a few others.

In fact – leaving out the atypical Pinecraft, Florida Amish community – the Dover group may be the most “coastal” of all, in the sense that they are within feasible buggying distance of the ocean.

At the Dover settlement, traditional plain white shutterless homes mix with suburban and rural English dwellings. Numerous buggy signs alert drivers to the presence of the Amish, cautioning vehicles to maintain low speeds when passing buggies.

### Land pressure – from the state capital

The Amish at Dover are also close to another landmark of importance – the **state capital**. With suburban growth, the Amish community has found itself interspersed with large neighborhoods.

Fields of McMansions stand where corn once did, and a number of golf courses are found in the area. With the rise of settlement by non-Amish, road traffic inevitably increases as well.

![Image 5: A white barn of an Amish farm among bare winter trees](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-farm-delaware.jpg)

In Delaware, Amish farms have given way…

Years ago, the Dover Amish began leaving the settlement in significant numbers due to these pressures – with some no doubt enticed by the high land prices.

An Amish family here can sell its farmland and comfortably purchase one, two or even more farms in less-densely populated regions of the country.

Numerous Amish from Dover have migrated and started daughter settlements. One example of such community is the [Halifax County, Virginia Amish](https://amishamerica.com/halifax-county-virginia-amish/) group, or that at [Burke’s Garden, Virginia](https://amishamerica.com/images-burkes-garden-virginia-40-photos/).

![Image 6: Large homes in a suburb against a blue winter sky](https://amishamerica.com/images/dover-delaware-suburb.jpg)

…to suburbs and golf courses

Realtor’s signs in some Amish yards as well as formerly Amish homes now wired for electricity are signs of such changes in the settlement.

As a result of the land situation, **few Amish** at Dover remain in full-time agriculture. The price of land in the area generally prohibits young men starting up in full-fledged dairy farming.

![Image 7: Amish buggy traveling on a city road with busy traffic](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-delaware-dover.jpg)

An Amish buggy on a busy road in the Dover community

High land prices may make some question why they continue to farm themselves. In fact, a number of those still owning large farms rent the land to be farmed by English farmers. In the early 2010s, a local Amish person estimated that only around 20 full-time Amish farmers remained.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/delaware-amish/)Delaware Amish Businesses

While farming has dwindled, Amish have opened numerous **businesses**, consistent with the general trend in Amish society.

At the Dover settlement, Amish are involved in a number of trades typical among Amish people. They include furniture, buggy-making, blacksmithing, greenhouses, sawmills, and a number of shops, including dry goods, quilts, and appliance stores.

![Image 8: Simple signs advertising Amish furniture makers on a white pole](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-furniture-delaware.jpg)

Amish furniture company signs in the Dover, Delaware settlement

Shops are typically located on-site at Amish homes, with roadside signs advertising their presence. As with all Amish, Dover businesses are closed on Sundays. Read more about [Delaware Amish furniture](https://amishamerica.com/amish-furniture-delaware/) businesses.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/delaware-amish/)Unique Delaware Amish Buggies

The buggies driven by the Amish in Delaware are of particular interest due to their unique style. Dover buggies feature rounded sides, fully-opening back doors, and a generally bulky size. Other communities’ Amish buggies are more boxy in shape, or have angled, not curved sides.

![Image 9: Two black buggies with curved sides parked in a parking lot among cars](https://amishamerica.com/images/de-amish-buggies.jpg)

Characteristic Amish buggies parked in a lot in the Dover settlement

Some have likened the appearance of Delaware buggies (perhaps a bit tongue-in-cheek) to that of hearses. The distinctive look is seen only in the Dover community, and other Delaware Amish spin-off settlements.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/delaware-amish/)Future of the Amish in Delaware

Amish settlements – even sizable ones – have gone “extinct” in the past, for a host of reasons. Despite land pressures, the Dover community remains sizeable.

The current estimated Amish population of just over 2,100 has Delaware ranking at **#15 out of 33 states** with Amish. The community has even continued to grow over the past decade, adding several church districts to the community.

This growth has gone again the trend seen in the early 2010s, when the first edition of this Delaware state guide was published on this website – a time when out-migration from the Dover community appeared to be going strong.

As for the state itself, given its small size and relatively high land prices, Delaware is not very likely to attract much additional Amish settlement. Besides the Dover community, there have been few if any other settlement attempts by Amish in the state.

![Image 10: Yellow Amish buggy speed warning sign on a road with white Amish home in background](https://amishamerica.com/images/dover-delaware-amish-buggy-sign.jpg)

A yellow warning sign alerts drivers to the presence of horse-drawn transport in Delaware’s sole Amish community

The general trend of Amish migration has been northward and westward. This is unlike in the early 1900s – when more of the country was up for agricultural development – and the first Amish settlers arrived in Delaware from diverse states in the West.

The Dover community has a long history, and though its proximity to the capital may continue to hamper its growth, it is not going anywhere. The trend of Amish from Dover **starting new communities** and/or settling in existing Dover daughter settlements is likely to continue, however.

Amish in the community are likely to find the best opportunities for growth by focusing future settlement westward, opposite from the expanding capital.

Occupations which don’t require large amounts of land – such as home businesses like furniture making or carpentry crews – also provide ways for Amish to make a living. These alternative occupations allow them to remain in the community without the large capital outlay that purchasing a dairy farm would require.

# “Yankees vs. Amish”: Charity Basketball Game Raises Money For A Good Cause

By[Erik Wesner](https://amishamerica.com/author/erik-wesner/)March 15, 2024 May 5, 2024

Amish vs. non-Amish in a competitive basketball game? In **Geauga County, Ohio**, home to the [world’s fourth-largest Amish settlement](https://amishamerica.com/ohio-amish/#geauga%20county), it happens every year in a charity event, pitting Amish against non-Amish teams. The purpose is to raise money for the local **DDC Clinic**, which helps children with rare genetic disorders.

![Image 3](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-man-shooting-basketball.jpg)

Photo: Bill Fugate/Geauga Maple Leaf

This is something I’d heard about, but hadn’t ever had a chance to share here on the site. And they’ve actually been holding this event for decades now. So I was happy to see this report in the [Geauga Maple Leaf](https://www.geaugamapleleaf.com/sports/yankees-clip-amish-in-charity-basketball-game/). Here’s more on the game:

Patti Gallagher, the clinic’s operations director, shared the purpose of providing the community with this fun and exciting game.

“We see children with rare genetic disorders, and now adults with rare genetic disorders since we now have an adult physician (on staff) as well,” Gallagher said. “The basketball game, believe it or not, has been going on for over 25 years. My son (Bryan Kuch) is in charge of the Yankee basketball team, and also gets the Amish team to come (to participate).”

After holding the event at other locations for many years, Gallagher said her son saw and embraced an excellent opportunity last year to hold the event at the new gymnasium of Berkshire High School.

One of the things she loves most about the event is seeing the special needs clients enjoying it.

“It just warms my heart to see that,” Gallagher said.

In this year’s game, the “Yankee” team defeated the Amish squad by a hair, coming back to win 63-60 in a contest that came down to the very end.

![Image 4](https://amishamerica.com/images/spectators-amish-basketball-game.jpg)

“Yankees” in this case would be the local term for non-Amish people – what most other Amish would call “English”. There is an interesting backstory to why the Geauga Amish use “Yankee” for the rest of us – explained at the video [here](https://amishamerica.com/why-do-amish-call-us-english/).

There are a ton of photos from the game by Bill Fugate, which you can view [here](https://geaugamapleleaf.smugmug.com/Sports/Basketball/Yankee-vs-Amish-Charity-Basketball). It looks like mostly younger Amish guys take part, but I did spot one or two beards in the game – and there were certainly some among the spectators.

![Image 5](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-jump-shot.jpg)

DDC Executive Director Eli Miller had this to say about the event:

“Both teams, the Amish and Yankee teams, came out after working all day and just played their hearts out,” Miller said. “Competitive, but at the same time it’s more about raising money for DDC Clinic. So we certainly appreciate them, all the sweat and everything that went into the game. It was a great game (and) both sides had close scores, so it was great to see.”

You don’t too often see Amish adults involved in public sporting events (see here for more on [Amish and sports](https://amishamerica.com/do-amish-play-sports/)), though it sometimes [happens](https://amishamerica.com/amish-english-softball-game/), both as participants and spectators. This is another nice example of that. Here’s more on [supporting the DDC Clinic](https://www.ddcclinic.org/why-support-us/).

# Inside the world of competitive Amish volleyball

![Image 1](https://www.inquirer.com/resizer/v2/BLK5RAUZWZEOBHPLJO5G6UA45U.jpg?auth=b2cb1adc9a56c33c99db3e89a7b1880f3fc01f59e4945c4fcf2b292281983780&width=1920&height=1080&smart=true)

A woman serves the ball during a volleyball match on day one of the Heritage Days Volleyball Tournament at Intercourse Community Park in Gordonville, Pa., on June 19.[Read more](https://www.inquirer.com/news/pennsylvania/a/amish-volleyball-intercourse-tournament-20260815.html)Elizabeth Robertson / Staff Photographer

by [Jason Nark](https://www.inquirer.com/author/nark_jason/)

Published Aug. 15, 2026, 5:02 a.m. ET

Listen to article •0:00 min

[Audio 1](https://media.inquirer.com/audio-articles/QREN7FUUSZHVPIJ2OCLMDTOQTQ/ElevenLabs/elevenlabs/article_277de6be-10ec-4de4-8052-396ff8922ea1_EXAVITQu4vr4xnSDxMaL_rate1.0_pitch0.0.m3u8)

INTERCOURSE, Pa. — A young Amish woman stood barefoot in the back right corner of a grassy volleyball court, spinning a ball in her hands.

She wore a simple green dress with a black apron, and when she leapt and hammered a serve over the net with a grunt, her prayer covering looked as white as the passing clouds.

On this beautiful afternoon in late June, the coed competitors were among the hundreds of young Amish players from Pennsylvania, Ohio, and other states who converged on Intercourse Community Park, about 60 miles west of Philadelphia, in Lancaster County, for the annual volleyball tournament. Hundreds gathered around the courts in lawn chairs to watch, including Amish men with long beards alongside “English” children in sneakers and sports jerseys.

The Amish in Pennsylvania, for reasons few could fully explain, love competitive volleyball. Some simply shrugged their shoulders when asked why. Others said they play volleyball because previous generations played too, a skill they learned just by watching, much the same as shoeing buggy horses or baking whoopie pies.

“I guess it’s just part of our culture,” said Ray Beiler, the tournament’s organizer. ”Competition-wise, though, it’s slow-pitch and volleyball, but volleyball is probably the biggest.”

The Amish also dabble in ice hockey when ponds freeze, Beiler said, and, in Indiana, they play basketball, of course. In Intercourse, the sharp pop of pickleball paddles on this Friday afternoon revealed another growing sport among the Amish.

Volleyball, it seems, has always been there, some said.

“I grew up with it,” said competitor Irv Beiler, 18, of Christiana, Lancaster County. “It’s a team game.”

One older Amish man said he grew up playing softball, but reckoned volleyball was a new phenomenon. When asked his name, the man spoke to his wife in Pennsylvania Dutch, and declined to answer.

The Amish do have a traditional game called cornerball, or “eck balle” in Pennsylvania Dutch, that looks like a cross between baseball and dodgeball, but is played in a cow pen. According to AmishAmerica.com, the sport was originally played with homemade balls made by “wrapping a quarter-sized steel nut in twine and covering it with black tire tape.”

According to the website, eck balle is a disappearing sport.

Erik Wesner, founder of AmishAmerica.com, said the purpose of volleyball and other sports in Amish communities is mostly about socialization, not competition.

“This is a game that’s played commonly at the Sunday youth group gatherings or meetings at church members’ houses for dinner,” he said. “It’s a way for teens and young adults to interact.”

Older Amish in Intercourse didn’t know much about the rise in popularity, but, ever efficient and resourceful, said volleyball takes up little room, compared to say, soccer, and can keep a lot of children busy at a gathering.

John Lapp, 51, of Gap, Lancaster County, said there are “volleyball barns” in the area where the more serious players gather in the winter.

“I played softball,” he said. “Volleyball was just a sport that took hold, I suppose.”

There doesn’t appear to be much trash talk in the competitive world of Amish volleyball, unless you understand Pennsylvania Dutch, but the talent is plain as day. That makes sense, locals said, if you consider the day-to-day life of Amish youth. They’re wrangling calves, riding kick scooters, and lifting hay, building muscle and balance the whole time.

“I used to play too,” said Simon Stoltzfus. “I just can’t jump as high as I could or stay up there as long.”

Wesner said sports tend to be more prevalent in progressive Amish communities, like in Lancaster County, and less so in more conservative areas, like Mifflin and Clearfield Counties.

Last year, The [Inquirer spoke to Melvin Byler,](https://www.inquirer.com/news/pennsylvania/grayson-cole-bull-riders-velocity-tour-20250302.html "https://www.inquirer.com/news/pennsylvania/grayson-cole-bull-riders-velocity-tour-20250302.html") who grew up Amish in Western Pennsylvania, after he won the Professional Bull Riding event in Reading. Byler had to leave his Amish community to pursue bull riding as a profession.

“I didn’t even see bull riding until I was 14, and when I told my parents I wanted to do it, they said it was a phase,” Byler said.

Steven Nolt, an Elizabethtown College professor who has researched and written about the Amish extensively, said situations like Byler’s are rare. Ray Beiler said a college coach came to one of the Intercourse tournaments and said many of the competitors could play at higher levels, but Nolt said it’s unlikely that even the most talented volleyball players would pursue the sport more competitively.

“It would be hard to imagine,” Nolt said. “They’d be making a choice not to join the Amish.”

Chris Haley oversaw the pickleball tournament at the Intercourse Heritage Days, where there are new courts. He said the Amish quickly took up that sport, too, and some have makeshift courts at their house.

“They are talented and determined,” Haley said.

They compete in sports for the fun of it, not for the prospects of future scholarships, and, at a tournament as big as Intercourse, the socializing was front and center. Young Amish slipped off their black leather boots and Crocs for sneakers or went barefoot, dozens chatting up one another in both English and Pennsylvania Dutch.

“This tournament is most definitely for the fun of it,” said Wilmer Stoltzfus, 20.

The players took big gulps from jugs of water and walked onto one of several courts spread out over several acres in the park. Some of the men wore thick, black work pants with suspenders, but others wore shorts. When one young Amish man dove for a dig and missed, his teammates rushed to help him up.

“Good job,” they said.

By Saturday night, only one net would remain, and a few thousand spectators would be crowding the court for the finals. The winners would get tall trophies housed in an exhibition room, with silver and gold volleyballs fastened to the tops.

They’d also get bragging rights until next year, maybe.

“Not bragging, no,” said Wilmer Stoltzfus. “We don’t really brag.”

# PA Amish trip highlights

By[Erik Wesner](https://amishamerica.com/author/erik-wesner/)August 31, 2012 August 31, 2012

[23 Comments](https://amishamerica.com/pa-amish-trip-highlights/#comments)

I’ve finally put together some trip highlights from Lancaster County. Today begins a new trip, a week-long journey across Indiana and Ohio. Before we get into that, here’s what I liked from last week’s visit:

**Seven nights, four bonfires, two mountain pie feasts.** Amish people like to burn stuff in the summer time. Mostly wood from what I can tell. It makes for a nice setting to sit, talk, and eat, and roast [mountain pies](https://amishamerica.com/do-you-know-these-10-amish-terms/#comment-34778). This past week was bonfire-o-rama. Two of the fires were lit in celebration of birthdays ([mine and Eli’s](https://amishamerica.com/what-makes-a-great-birthday/), and another friend’s surprise party).

My second try at mountain pies came out tastier than the first. Part of the problem the first time is that I got to choose from the last two pie irons–both round. Nothing wrong with that, except that the bread we had was all square. If you’re hungry enough it tastes good whatever final shape it takes.

**Big Valley baby.** A quick story. My Polish girlfriend, Izabela, is visiting the USA for the first time and was along on this trip. While in Big Valley we paid a visit to a [Nebraska Amish](https://amishamerica.com/amish-nebraska/#pa%20nebraska) family I’m acquainted with. I had met them once 4 years earlier and just decided to drop in on a whim.

![Image 3: Amish Big Valley](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-big-valley.jpg)

Big Valley buggy

The man of the house vaguely remembered me, and ended up inviting us in to chat with his wife. After a few minutes of talking, the 9-year-old daughter is handing her 9-_day_-old sister to a dumbfounded Izabela–a perfect stranger 10 minutes before. Iza couldn’t imagine something similar happening in her culture. The baby quickly won her heart and I think wanted to leave with us (or so she thought). I think that says something about attitudes to children in Amish culture, where you’re comfortable sharing them–even with random Polish-English people that just show up at your door.

**Connecting friends.** Introducing two Amish families as a third (English) party is kind of weird. You feel like you are in the wrong spot, that you are the one that should be getting introduced to someone and not making the connections. When Amish people meet there is the usual search for a link of some sort–who is your dad, where do you come from, what do you do and who you work(ed) with. I was glad that it could finally happen, as I usually only talk about the Zooks and the Kings (who live on one side of Lancaster) to the Riehls (who live on the other), and vice versa.

In little Amish communities of a few church districts you generally know everyone. In the big Lancaster community (going on 200 churches), you might not have many relatives, dealings or running-around friends in a given area, which was the case here. For an Amish person strangers can include both English and other Amish. The nice thing is that there is usually an Amish connection somewhere if you poke around enough.

![Image 4: Amish Hat City](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-hat-city.jpg)

Amish hat in the City

**Day trip to Philly.** We had Amish friends along. Even in a place like Philadelphia with an Amish presence nearby, people notice Amish walking around one of America’s largest cities. I noticed some heads turn and some sheepish smiles of people we passed or interacted with.

I also think that it helps to be Amish in certain situations. One example. We visited the US Mint. You need identification to get in. Three of us had IDs, while the fourth did not–not one of our Amish companions, but Izabela. My friend’s wife explained the situation and asked if we could slide, which the understanding guard let happen. Once inside my friend joked that it was “the hat” that got us in. I think that was just a half-joke as there must be a kernel of truth there.

**Visiting Centralia.** This has nothing to do with the Amish. Centralia is a central PA mining town–or I should say _was_, because it’s been essentially abandoned for many years. Centralia lies in anthracite coal mining country. A half-century ago, a mine fire was sparked and began slowly burning, snaking its way along the massive coal veins running beneath the town. Noxious gases and ground collapses threatened the townspeople’s health and safety. Multi-million dollar efforts to extinguish the fire failed. Many residents moved away and nearly all buildings in the town were demolished beginning in the 1980s. Today only a handful, perhaps 3 or 4, homes remain in this town which once had a population over 1000 souls.

![Image 5: Centralia PA Street](https://amishamerica.com/images/centralia-pa-street.jpg)

A former homesite in Centralia, PA

Centralia is a tragic and rather eerie place. I remember stumbling across it five years ago while traveling across the state. I came to a stop at what looked like a normal country highway intersection, except for the odd, out-of-place bench placed near the crossroads. Like something you’d see in a town, and not in the middle of nowhere. Looking closer I began to notice sidewalks and the layout of a street plan. As I creeped along the cracked, overgrown asphalt streets, old retaining walls and steps hinted at a forgotten past. I slowly realized that a town once lay here. Governmental response to the town’s crisis has evoked controversy particularly among those who once lived there, and the town appears in the news from time to time. It’s a modern-day ghost town in a place you’d hardly expect to find one.

**Jokes.** Hang around with Amish folks long enough, and the jokes start flowing. This time I got to hear the one about the origins of the fictional “Stoltzfus Chinese Market” in Philly, among others. Amish like to make Polish jokes, which they hit me with from time to time knowing my origins. And with a true blooded Polish person along this time, of course some wondered what Izabela thought of them. She was good-natured about it. It helps that she can give as good as she gets.

Amish also joke about themselves. We even got a second hearing of a [friend’s favorite Amish joke](https://amishamerica.com/the-polish-amish-hybrid-joke/), about the bridge in the desert. “I’ll tell you a really good Amish joke,” he began with a smile. “But it starts with a Polish joke,” he conceded to an uproar of laughter.  Well of course it does!

# Where Do The Amish Live? (30+ States & International Locations)

By[Erik Wesner](https://amishamerica.com/author/erik-wesner/)Updated August 25, 2024

[22 Comments](https://amishamerica.com/where-do-the-amish-live/#comments)

**You’ll find Amish communities in over 30 states**

[![Image 3: where amish live](https://amishamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2010/08/where-amish-live.png)](https://amishamerica.com/where-do-the-amish-live/where-amish-live/) From a population of 5,000 at the beginning of the 20 th century, the Amish have grown to **over 400,000 strong** in North America. Amish have long been associated with Pennsylvania. But they are in fact present today in **32 states**, three Canadian provinces, and even one South American country.

The states with the largest Amish populations are **Pennsylvania** and **Ohio**. The largest individual communities are found at Lancaster County, Pennsylvania and Holmes County, Ohio. **Indiana** has the third-highest Amish population. Together these three states are home to roughly **two-thirds of all Amish**.

![Image 4: Black Amish buggy going down the road with green fields in background.](https://amishamerica.com/images/holmes-county-ohio-amish-country.jpg)

Holmes County, Ohio is home to tens of thousands of Amish people. Photo: Don Burke

These three states are also home to significant populations of Old Order or “Team” [Mennonites](https://amishamerica.com/whats-the-difference-between-amish-and-mennonites/), who share some similarities with Amish, including [plain dress](https://amishamerica.com/why-do-the-amish-wear-plain-clothing/) and use of the [horse-and-buggy](https://amishamerica.com/why-do-the-amish-drive-buggies/).

## Amish settlements across North America

Amish people can today be found in every major region of America (though no Amish live in Alaska or Hawaii). Here’s a brief look at Amish populations around the country, by **region**.

### Amish on the East Coast

Besides the Amish heartland of Pennsylvania, you can find Amish in other East Coast states, including Delaware, Maryland, and Virginia. Of course, these states would also be grouped among Amish in the South (see below).

### Amish in the Midwest

Amish are typically associated with the Midwest, though have significant populations outside of the region. Besides Ohio and Indiana, Missouri, Michigan, and Wisconsin are a few of the states with large Amish populations in the Midwest. Nearly every state in the Midwest region has at least one Amish community.

![Image 5: Yellow Amish Share the Road buggy sign](https://amishamerica.com/images/summersville-hartshorn-amish-shannon-county-missouri.jpg)

Buggy warning sign in an Amish settlement in Missouri. Image: Don Burke

### Amish in the South

Amish are also found in areas outside the corn belt. Amish communities are found in the South, including in Tennessee, North Carolina, Virginia, Mississippi, Texas, and Kentucky. The largest southern community is found an hour’s drive south of Nashville, at [Ethridge in Tennessee](https://amishamerica.com/tennessee-amish/#ethridge-community). Florida is home to a unique Amish settlement at Pinecraft, a popular vacation and retirement community in Sarasota, Florida.

### Amish in the West

Amish are also found in the West, with a number of settlements in Montana and Colorado. Small communities have also arisen in Wyoming, Idaho, and New Mexico in recent years. No Amish currently live in California, Oregon or Washington, however.

### Amish in the North

Amish have migrated into northern states such as New York and Maine in recent years. Immigrants to New York have added to the long-established Amish presence in that state, and have contributed to make it the state with the fastest-growing Amish population. The [Maine Amish](https://amishamerica.com/amish-maine/) communities at one time were the only Amish found in New England; some years ago a small community was founded in Vermont, joined by a second in 2024.

## Amish Communities outside the US

A small percentage of the overall Amish population lies outside America’s borders, most notably in Canada. There is also a small community in South America (Bolivia).

### **Amish in Canada**

Amish are found in Ontario, long the only Canadian province which Old Order Amish called home. Significant settlements are found at Kitchener and Aylmer. Ontario is also home to a sizable Team Mennonite population.

Recently, new settlements have arisen in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. A Manitoba settlement ceased to exist in 2024 when Amish exited the province. Canada also has large numbers of Hutterites, a related group, primarily located in the western provinces of Alberta, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan.

![Image 6: Amish boy riding white horse among a crowd of Amish people](https://amishamerica.com/images/milverton-boy-horse-school-auction.jpg)

At an Amish auction in the Milverton, Ontario community

### Amish in South America

In 2015, new Amish settlements were established in Bolivia and Argentina, after Old Colony Mennonite communities in these countries reached out to Amish in North America about affiliation. Later, the Argentina community disbanded, leaving only the Bolivia group. Read more [here](https://amishamerica.com/2016-amish-population/).

## A Long History of Amish Migration

Amish have had a long history of migration, and with a growing population (Amish families typically have six to seven children) that trend will likely continue. [Not all Amish settlements survive](https://amishamerica.com/amish-settlemen/), however.

Historically, Amish communities have been found in the **unlikely locations** of [California](https://amishamerica.com/california-amish-community/), [Mexico, and even New Orleans](https://amishamerica.com/5-surprising-places-amish-once-lived/). One group even founded a short-lived community in the Central American nation of Honduras.

Besides the Bolivia settlement, no Old Order Amish presently live outside of North America, though [Beachy Amish](https://amishamerica.com/whats-the-difference-between-beachy-amish-and-old-order-amish/) communities exist in Europe, Latin America, and Africa.

Figures](https://amishamerica.com/amish-state-guide/#state-figures)

![Image 3: Amish State Population Map By State](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-population-usa-states-map.jpg)

The most recent total Amish population estimate (2026) is **421,340****people** in 728 distinct communities (Young Center).

Old Order (horse-and-buggy) Amish currently live in **33 states, three Canadian provinces**, and the countries of **Bolivia** and **Mexico**.

Find the state-by-state population numbers [here](https://amishamerica.com/amish-state-guide/#state-figures). Scroll down or use the jump-links above to check out individual **state guides** and find an Amish community near you.

For ideas on the best Amish community to visit, check out [Amish Country: Where To Go (25-Community Guide)](https://amishamerica.com/amish-country-where-to-go/).

![Image 4](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-boys-ordering-food.jpg)

Amish live in over 700 locations throughout North America. Image: Jim Halverson

## Amish Communities by State

The Amish are typically associated with states like **Pennsylvania**, **Ohio** or **Indiana** – long home to large Amish communities. But today Amish populations can be found **throughout the US**, including in the South, West, and Northeast regions.

Each article linked below outlines the main communities and other details for the Amish populations of each state.

* * *

**[Alabama Amish](https://amishamerica.com/amish-new-southern-state-settlement/)** – Alabama became the newest Amish state in 2026, when Amish families connected to a Tennessee community settled there. It is the first Amish presence in the state in roughly a century.

* * *

**[Arkansas Amish](https://amishamerica.com/arkansas-amish/)** – Relatively few Amish live in Arkansas today, despite attempts at settling the state dating to the 1920s.

* * *

**[Colorado Amish](https://amishamerica.com/colorado-amish/)**– Amish communities in the West are uncommon. But over the past two decades, Colorado has attracted a fair share of Amish pioneers. Today the Centennial State is home to eight small Amish communities.

* * *

**[Delaware Amish](https://amishamerica.com/delaware-amish/)**– A single Amish settlement is found outside state capital Dover. This sizable community has faced land and development pressures in the 21st century, but continues to grow.

* * *

**[Florida Amish](https://amishamerica.com/florida-amish/)**– Part vacation destination, part southern Amish outpost, the unique Pinecraft community attracts a wide range of Plain people from across the country.

* * *

[](https://amishamerica.com/amish-state-guide/)[**Idaho Amish**](https://amishamerica.com/the-amish-in-idaho/) – The solitary Gem State Amish community dates to 2012. This small settlement lies near the town of Salmon (Lemhi County). Idaho was also home to a previous Amish settlement at Bonners Ferry in the early 2000s.

* * *

**[Illinois Amish](https://amishamerica.com/illinois-amish/)**– The sizeable Amish community near the town of Arthur is by far the largest in Illinois. The rest of the approximately 20 Illinois Amish communities number from a handful of households to several hundred Amish. The Illinois Amish population was the 10th-largest in North America as of 2026.

* * *

**[Indiana Amish](https://amishamerica.com/indiana-amish/)**– The Hoosier State is home to America’s third-largest Amish population, at over 68,000 people as of 2026. The Elkhart-LaGrange County community is by far the largest in the state. Other sizable Indiana Amish communities are found at Adams County, Nappanee, Allen County, and Daviess County. Over two dozen Amish settlements can be found across Indiana.

![Image 5](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-buggy-row-topeka-indiana.jpg)

A row of neatly-parked Amish buggies. Topeka, Indiana. Photo: Jim Halverson

* * *

**[Iowa Amish](https://amishamerica.com/iowa-amish/)**– Amish have lived in Iowa for nearly 180 years. Today, the largest communities are found at Kalona, Bloomfield, and in Buchanan County. A number of smaller Amish settlements are found across the Hawkeye State as well.

* * *

[Kansas Amish](https://amishamerica.com/kansas-amish/) – Despite its 150-year history of Amish settlement, today just over 3,000 Amish call the Sunflower State home. Kansas is home to three communities over 100 years old (in Reno County and Anderson County). It has lately been attracting more Amish settlement, with eight communities founded since 2017.

* * *

**[Kentucky Amish](https://amishamerica.com/amish-kentucky/)**– The Amish are found in nearly five dozen communities in the Bluegrass State. Over 17,000 Amish live in Kentucky, making it the state with the eighth-largest Amish population.

* * *

**[Maine Amish](https://amishamerica.com/amish-maine/)**– Maine continues to steadily attract Amish settlements, with eight of its present 11 communities founded since 2011. Together with Vermont, the state boasts the only Amish presence in New England. Four communities are found in massive Aroostook County, with another notable presence in Waldo County at Unity.

* * *

[Maryland Amish](https://amishamerica.com/maryland-amish/) – Maryland’s five Amish communities are spread to the corners of the state. The St. Mary’s County settlement in southern Maryland is the largest, with a population of about 1,600 Amish as of 2025.

* * *

**[Michigan Amish](https://amishamerica.com/michigan-amish/)**– Michigan is home to North America’s sixth-largest Amish population. Sizeable communities are found in St. Joseph’s and Branch Counties, among others. Michigan is home to over four dozen Amish settlements.

![Image 6](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-farm-quilts-michigan.jpg)

An Amish farm near Clare, Michigan. Photo: Jim Halverson

* * *

**[Minnesota Amish](https://amishamerica.com/minnesota-amish/)**– Minnesota’s two dozen-plus Amish settlements are concentrated in the southeast and central/northwest regions of the state. Amish first settled in the North Star State around the turn of the 20th century. The community near Harmony in Fillmore County is Minnesota’s largest, while Todd County in central MN hosts five separate Amish communities.

* * *

[Mississippi Amish](https://amishamerica.com/mississippi-amish/) – Amish have only rarely settled the Deep South. Mississippi is home to a small but longstanding Amish presence in Pontotoc County. A second settlement reportedly began putting down roots in the state in 2026.

* * *

**[Missouri Amish](https://amishamerica.com/missouri-amish/)– The Missouri Amish population has grown rapidly thanks to migration from other states. As of 2026 there are over 19,000 Amish in Missouri, giving it the seventh-highest Amish population. Sizeable Amish communities are found at Seymour, Jamesport, and Clark, among other locations.**

* * *

**[Montana Amish](https://amishamerica.com/montana-amish/)**– Montana has more than doubled its number of Amish communities since 2010, with 16 communities found across the state as of 2026. The oldest Montana Amish settlement is at Rexford in the northwest corner of the state, with the largest in Fergus County. Communities including Rexford and St. Ignatius hold annual school auctions.

* * *

**[Nebraska Amish](https://amishamerica.com/amish-nebraska/)**– The current Cornhusker State Amish population is the result of two mini “waves” of settlement – one in the mid-2000s, and another in the early 2020s. However, only around 700 Amish live in the state, in seven small settlements. _The term “Nebraska Amish” more commonly refers to the conservative “white-top buggy” group found mainly in Pennsylvania, who take their name from an early leader and community (read more about [PA Nebraska Amish](https://amishamerica.com/amish-nebraska/#pa%20nebraska))._

* * *

[](https://amishamerica.com/amish-state-guide/)[**New Mexico Amish**](https://amishamerica.com/amish-population-2022-new-mexico/) – In 2020, Amish founded a settlement in New Mexico, on the border with Colorado. A handful of Amish live in this remote community today.

* * *

**[New York Amish](https://amishamerica.com/new-york-amish/)**– New York has been a popular destination for Amish in recent years, attracting much in-migration from other states. The Empire State is home to over 26,000 Amish as of 2026, making it the state with the fifth-largest Amish population.

* * *

**[North Carolina Amish](https://amishamerica.com/north-carolina-amish/)**– North Carolina was long home to just a single Amish community, at Union Grove. In 2015, an ultraconservative group migrated into the state, settling near the town of Ellenboro. Besides its current Amish presence, the state has a colorful history of Amish settlement.

* * *

**[Ohio Amish](https://amishamerica.com/ohio-amish/)**– Along with Pennsylvania, Ohio has the largest concentration of Amish anywhere in North America – over 87,000 strong. The Holmes County Amish community is among the most diverse, with around a dozen distinct affiliations found in the settlement. Significant communities are also found at Geauga County, Ashland and Medina Counties, and in Knox County.

* * *

**[Oklahoma Amish](https://amishamerica.com/oklahoma-amish/)**– The Sooner State is home to four, mostly small Amish communities. The Chouteau Amish settlement is well over a century old. The settlement at Clarita in Coal County hosts a well-attended annual school auction.

* * *

**[Pennsylvania Amish](https://amishamerica.com/pennsylvania-amish/)**– The well-known Lancaster County community is the oldest in North America, and one of the nation’s two largest Amish settlements. Besides Lancaster County, large communities can be found at Big Valley, New Wilmington, and Smicksburg in Indiana County. Pennsylvania is home to over 60 Amish communities and boasts the nation’s largest Amish population, at over 96,000.

* * *

**[South Dakota Amish](https://amishamerica.com/south-dakota-amish/)**– South Dakota was added to the Amish map in 2010, when a group of Amish from Wisconsin settled in Hutchinson County (Tripp). That community ceased to exist in the early 2020s, but was replaced by two more at around the same time.

* * *

**[Tennessee Amish](https://amishamerica.com/tennessee-amish/)**– The Tennessee Amish population numbers over 4,600, spread over sixteen settlements. The community at Ethridge is by far the biggest in the state, and one of the largest in the South.

* * *

**[Texas Amish](https://amishamerica.com/texas-amish/)**– Texas’ lone Amish community is found near Beeville in Bee County, in the southern part of the state. A number of Amish also lived in Texas beginning in the early 1900s. More recently, a community existed near Stephenville in Central Texas.

* * *

[](https://amishamerica.com/amish-state-guide/)[**Vermont Amish**](https://amishamerica.com/vermont-amish-doing-well-3-years-later/) – Vermont saw its second Amish community founded in the Northeast Kingdom region in 2024, joining a settlement established in the same region (Brownington) nearly a decade earlier.

* * *

**[Virginia Amish](https://amishamerica.com/amish-virginia/)**– Amish first settled the state in the late 1800s. Virginia’s Amish population has steadily grown, as Amish from nearby states have found it an attractive place to live. In the past decade-plus, the number of Amish communities in the Old Dominion state has tripled, though its overall Amish population remains relatively low at around 2,600 people.

* * *

**[West Virginia Amish](https://amishamerica.com/west-virginia-amish/)**– The Mountain State has seen increasing interest from Amish people in recent years. The state has added over a dozen communities since the year 2017, though its overall Amish population remains low.

* * *

[Wisconsin Amish](https://amishamerica.com/wisconsin-amish/) – Wisconsin is America’s #4 Amish state, with a population of nearly 29,000. Significant settlements are found at Cashton, Wilton/Tomah, Hillsboro, and the Kingston/Dalton area, among others. Notable counties include Grant County with five settlements, and Clark County, home to four Amish communities.

* * *

[](https://amishamerica.com/amish-state-guide/)**Wyoming Amish** – Another fairly recent addition to the list, Wyoming saw Amish settle its northeast corner (the Hulett area of Crook County) in 2011. In recent years the Equality State has seen an uptick in Amish interest, with five more communities being settled since 2019.

* * *

[](https://amishamerica.com/amish-state-guide/)[**Canada Amish**](https://amishamerica.com/canada-amish/) – Amish have lived in Canada since the 1800s. Today the country is home to an over 6,000-strong Amish community, mainly in **Ontario**. Small populations are also found in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.

![Image 7](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-bales-field-ontario.jpg)

Canada is home to over 6,000 Amish.

* * *

[](https://amishamerica.com/amish-state-guide/)[**Amish in Latin America**](https://amishamerica.com/amish-in-mexico-2026-population-numbers/) – The remarkable case of Amish settlements in Bolivia and Argentina came about in 2015. Pre-existing communities of Old Colony Mennonites, a related Anabaptist people, affiliated with Amish in North America that year.

# Art on the Alley returns Oct. 11

Downtown New Philadelphia festival will feature 120 vendors, trick-or-treating and an expanded layout

![Image 5: Child in a witch costume writes on a chalkboard beside a pink event banner.](https://image.yourohionews.com/1083071.jpg?imageId=1083071&x=0.00&y=22.21&cropw=100.00&croph=37.98&width=960&height=548&format=jpg)

The downtown arts festival will feature more than 120 vendors, including visual artists, makers, local organizations, food trucks and live entertainment. Activities and creative experiences also will be available for visitors of all ages.

Submitted

Published October 5, 2026 - 1:56 p.m.

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.yourohionews.com%2Ftuscarawas-county%2Fart-on-the-alley-returns-oct-11%2F1083068)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.yourohionews.com%2Ftuscarawas-county%2Fart-on-the-alley-returns-oct-11%2F1083068)[](mailto:?subject=Art%20on%20the%20Alley%20returns%20Oct.%2011&body=Downtown%20New%20Philadelphia%20festival%20will%20feature%20120%20vendors%2C%20trick-or-treating%20and%20an%20expanded%20layout%0Dhttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.yourohionews.com%2Ftuscarawas-county%2Fart-on-the-alley-returns-oct-11%2F1083068)

AD

The Tuscarawas Arts Partnership will bring Art on the Alley back to downtown New Philadelphia Oct. 11 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.

The downtown arts festival will feature more than 120 vendors, including visual artists, makers, local organizations, food trucks and live entertainment. Activities and creative experiences also will be available for visitors of all ages.

AD

This fall, trick-or-treating also will be offered throughout the event, with participating vendors and organizations providing candy and activities for children. Costumes are encouraged for guests of all ages, but face coverings will not be permitted.

Art on the Alley also will feature an expanded event footprint. The festival will be set up along First Drive, Ashwood Lane and Allen Lane, with West High Avenue closed between Broadway and Second Street.

Organizers said the expanded layout is intended to improve traffic flow and create more space for vendors, activities and visitors.

New event signage also will be used to help with wayfinding, visitor flow and safety. The signage was made possible through support from the Tuscarawas County Community Foundation and the Rosenberry Foundation.

“We’re always looking for ways to make Art on the Alley easier to navigate, more connected and accessible,” Tuscarawas Arts Partnership Executive Director Wilma Mullet said. “The new layout and signage are exciting steps forward for the event, while still keeping the creativity and community atmosphere people have come to love.”

Parking will remain free throughout the day. Visitors may park in city and county lots on the east side of North and South Broadway, at the Tuscarawas County Public Library Main Library or in available street parking outside the event area.

AD

Visitors are encouraged to follow event signage when arriving downtown and allow extra time to find parking and walk to the festival.

## [Pauli May Not Have A Movie, But He Has My Highest Regard](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/2016/03/16/pauli/)

Posted on[March 16, 2016](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/2016/03/16/pauli/ "8:01 pm")by[Betsy](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/author/beesfirstappearance/ "View all posts by Betsy")

Remember Eddie the Eagle? Now that’s a name from the past.

Michael (Eddie) Edwards dreamed of competing in the Olympics. In 1988, he was the United Kingdom’s only athlete to compete in ski jumping at the Winter Olympic Games in Calgary. He finished last in his two events, but his popularity soared because of his perseverance. Eddie’s most loyal supporter was his mother, who wore a sweater Eddie’s grandmother made that read “I’m Eddie’s Mum.”

Eddie’s story returns in “[Eddie the Eagle](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hyzQjVUmIxk),” a new film starring Taron Egerton as Eddie, with Hugh Jackman portraying Eddie’s coach, Bronson Peary, and Christopher Walken playing Peary’s mentor, Warren Sharp.

When Laura Zander, owner of [Jimmy Beans Wool](https://jimmybeanswool.com/) and author of _[Stitch Mountain: 30 Warm Knits for Conquering the Cold](http://www.stitchmountain.com/)_, saw that sweater in the movie, she decided to knit an Eddie-themed hat for her son. She offered the [pattern](https://jimmybeanswool.com/details/images/eddie/EddieTheEagleHatKnitV3.pdf) at n o charge, and created a [website](http://www.iknitforeddie.com/) where knitters can submit photos of their own Eddie hats and watch a [video](https://jimmybeanswool.com/details/eddie/default.asp) in which Egerton and Jackman supervise a knitting contest.

When I learned about the movie, I didn’t think about sweaters and hats. I thought about another athlete who competed in the 1988 Winter Olympics — and how a profile of him that aired on CBS during the 1992 Winter Olympics transformed me into the first American member of the “Pauli Fan-Club.”

Growing up on a farm in Davos, Switzerland, Paul Accola learned to ski on his stunning hometown slopes at age 4 and had begun racing by age 7.

[![Image 2: Paul Accola in Aspen, Colorado, March 1993](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/scan0013.jpg?w=201&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/scan0013.jpg)
_Paul Accola in Aspen, Colorado, March 1993_

In 1988, he emerged as a promising skier. He made the team for the Calgary Olympics at the last minute and took home a bronze medal in the combined event. He joined the World Cup competitive circuit as a member of the Swiss National Ski Team, and his career as a professional ski racer took off. 
Skiing smoothly and deceptively fast, Accola started winning World Cup races. He became known as a good all-around skier, racing downhill in addition to competing in slalom, giant slalom and super-giant slalom races. He won the 1991-1992 overall World Cup title in men’s Alpine skiing, but left the 1992 Albertville Olympics without a medal.

While Accola was winning races, I was studying journalism in graduate school at Ohio State. I had just taken a class on writing for magazines, so I decided to make him the subject of my first freelance magazine article. I successfully pitched the story, and it was published in February 1993.

I interviewed Accola a few times during the summer and early fall of 1992, sometimes relying on the skills I learned in my college German classes to ask him questions. His thorough, thoughtful responses gave him the chance to practice his English. Accommodating and helpful, he sent me copies of interviews he gave for some Swiss newspapers, hoping that they might also improve my German.

[![Image 3: Paul Accola on his way to the next World Cup race in Sierra Nevada, Spain, March 1993](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/scan0011.jpg?w=199&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/scan0011.jpg)
_Paul Accola on his way to the next World Cup race in Sierra Nevada, Spain, March 1993_

Life isn’t always glamorous for a professional athlete, Accola revealed. He described how he and his teammates trained on the glaciers in Switzerland, Austria and Chile during the summertime. When they weren’t skiing, they did a lot of running, biking, weightlifting, and playing soccer and volleyball to get faster. He admitted that skiing was very hard on his body, and how tiring it got to be always traveling.
Known to his fans as “Pauli,” Accola told me that he enjoyed spending time off the slopes by driving his tractor and operating construction machinery on his family’s farm. A carpenter by trade, he helped fellow teammates build additions to their houses and landscape their gardens. He shared that he was working on his collection of Swatch watches, that his favorite music was Alpine folk music, and that his favorite meal was _Bündner Z’vieri_, a hearty local dish made with dried beef, ham, homemade bread, butter and cheese that is usually eaten by hungry Swiss in the late afternoon.

Advertisement

“I’m just myself and I am how I am,” he told me. “I’m just a regular guy from the Swiss Alps who is a bit faster on skis than almost everybody else. Other than that, I try to be as normal and natural as I can.”

I tried to be as normal and natural I could when my friend Elkin invited me to visit her in Aspen, Colorado and watch the World Cup ski races that would be held there in March 1993. Accola suffered a torn meniscus earlier that season, so we wondered if he’d be able to compete in Aspen, but he healed well enough to join the rest of the Swiss national ski team and put on his distinctive racing suit that resembled Swiss cheese — the result of the Switzerland Cheese Association’s sponsorship of the team.

We stood in the finish area and cheered Accola on as he and his competitors raced down the mountain.[![Image 4: Paul Accola, Downhill, 3/6/93](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/scan0005.jpg?w=200&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/scan0005.jpg)

Since the skiers had to stay there between runs, we stood alongside legendary racers like Marc Girardelli of Luxembourg…

[![Image 5: Marc Girardelli, Luxembourg, Downhill, 3/6/93](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/scan0008.jpg?w=195&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/scan0008.jpg)

Lasse Kjus, Lasse Arnesen, Kjetil Andre Aamodt and Ole Christian Furuseth of Norway; Frederik Nyberg of Sweden; Bruno Kernen and Urs Lehmann of Switzerland; and Patrick Ortlieb of Austria.

[![Image 6: Patrick Ortlieb, Austria, Downhill, 3/6/93](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/scan0003.jpg?w=199&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/scan0003.jpg)They all joined Accola in signing an official World Cup sweatshirt for me. I took it home and wore it for years, until it went into holes.

[![Image 7: Bruno Kernen, Switzerland, 3/6/93](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/scan0006.jpg?w=300&h=265)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/scan0006.jpg)In the overall results for the Aspen races, the top three spots went to Kjetil Andre Aamodt of Norway, Stephan Eberharter of Austria and Daniel Mahrer of Switzerland. Accola came in 13 th.[![Image 8: Kjetil Andre Aamodt, Stephan Eberharter (Austria), Daniel Mahrer (Switzerland), 3/7/93](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/scan0010.jpg?w=192&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/scan0010.jpg)

Advertisement

After the races, we ran into the skiers all over town. When we were shopping at Gorsuch, a shop specializing in ski resort wear, a couple of Norwegian racers helped me pick out a pair of socks for my dad. He, too, wore them until they went into holes.

Accola retired from professional skiing in February 2005, on his 38th birthday. He still drives his tractor around the family farm in Davos. Even though I’ve published almost 200 articles about other subjects since then, writing about this charming, down-to-earth Swiss skier is something I’ll never forget.

Susan Orlean said it best in _The Bullfighter Checks Her Makeup._

“Readers often ask me if I stay in touch with anyone I’ve written about. It’s an understandable question; after all, when you profile people, you spend a lot of time with them, and you do come to know them very well – sometimes even better than people you think of as your friends.[![Image 9: With Paul Accola, March 1993](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/scan0012.jpg?w=222&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/scan0012.jpg)But writing a profile is a process that has a beginning, a middle, and an end. Usually when it has ended, the writer and the subject have very little in common except for the fact that they were for a while a writer and a subject.”

“Inevitably, I lose track of many of the people I’ve written about. It’s the one part of the job that makes me melancholy. I know it is unrealistic and impractical to think I could stay close to everyone I’ve profiled, and even if I could, we would never be as close as we were when I was writing about them; still, it’s hard not to feel attached to people once you’ve been allowed into their lives. So what I have of them, and always will have, is just that moment we spent together – now preserved on paper, bound between covers, cast out into the world – and they will never get any older, their faces will never fade, their dreams will still be within reach, and I will forever still be listening as hard as I can.”

## [Make Much Ado About Will This Year](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/2016/03/21/will/)

Posted on[March 21, 2016](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/2016/03/21/will/ "6:05 pm")by[Betsy](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/author/beesfirstappearance/ "View all posts by Betsy")

Sir Walter Scott, John Keats, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Charles Dickens, Thomas Hardy, Mark Twain, Harriet Beecher Stowe and I have something in common. We’ve all made the pilgrimage to Warwickshire, England to honor William Shakespeare.

Some pilgrims take the “Sacred Way of English Literature,” wandering along a footpath to the hamlet of Shottery, finding inspiration as the young Shakespeare did when he was on his way to court Anne Hathaway. In the famous half-timbered Tudor cottage with a thatched roof rests the high-backed wooden settle which Will and Anne are said to have sat upon before the fire, under the watchful eyes of her parents.

[![Image 2: Anne Hathaway's Cottage, September 2010](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/2010-09-14-england-2010-074.jpg?w=300&h=251)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/2010-09-14-england-2010-074.jpg)

But the greatest feelings of anticipation and excitement are reserved for the star attraction —the home on Henley Street in nearby Stratford-upon-Avon where the playwright was born in April 1564. To commemorate their visit to this hallowed shrine, many of those Victorian-era authors scratched their names on a window in the room where Shakespeare was born; I bought a sterling silver flower pin in the gift shop. But as we walked where he did and saw things that he had seen in the home where his father, John, also made and sold gloves, we all felt his presence pervade these legendary surroundings.

[![Image 3: Shakespeare Birthplace, September 2010](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/2010-09-14-england-2010-091.jpg?w=300&h=225)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/2010-09-14-england-2010-091.jpg)

Shakespeare’s influence is being felt even more strongly this year. Many commemorative events are under way to mark the 400 th anniversary of the playwright’s death on April 23, 1616.

_[Young Will](http://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-coventry-warwickshire-35640717)_, a new statue of Shakespeare was unveiled in Stratford-upon-Avon in February. The First Folio, the first printed collection of Shakespeare’s plays that was published in 1623, is visiting all 50 states in a [traveling exhibition](http://www.folger.edu/about-the-first-folio-tour) organized by the Folger Shakespeare Library. And over 100 Shakespeare-related titles are being published this year, including the [Hogarth Shakespeare series](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ERpZTHYB3kA),in which bestselling authors like Margaret Atwood, Anne Tyler and Tracy Chevalier retell some of Shakespeare’s plays as modern-day novels.

But not all q uadricentennial pilgrimages lead to Warwickshire. Closer to home, visit Kenyon College to see “Shakespeare 400,” a special exhibition at Greenslade Special Collections & Archives exploring Shakespeare’s accomplishments and his place within literature.

One display case focuses on sources that inspired Shakespeare, such as the Latin texts of Ovid, the Greek dramas of Aeschylus, and _The Reports,_ written by Shakespeare’s contemporary, Sir Edward Coke. Another celebrates the world to which Shakespeare was responding. A 1635 edition of Gerardus Mercator’s _Atlas_ and Johannes Kepler’s _Tabulae Rudolphinae_ from 1627 illustrate this age of global exploration that popularized maps of the earth and skies, travel logs and navigational treatises.

Advertisement

[![Image 4: Shakespeare 400, Kenyon College](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2226.jpg?w=225&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2226.jpg)

During Shakespeare’s lifetime, stage plays were not considered serious literature. However, seven years after his death, two actors in his company published the text of 36 of his plays in a folio-sized volume, arranging them into comedies, histories and tragedies. The Second Folio was a corrected page-for-page reprint of the First Folio, followed by the publication of the Third Folio in 1663 and the Fourth Folio in 1685.

[![Image 5: Shakespeare 400, Kenyon College](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2214.jpg?w=209&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2214.jpg)

Other Shakespeare-themed texts in the exhibition include _Tales from Shakespeare_, a children’s edition of Shakespeare plays by Mary Lamb that was first printed in 1807; a facsimile of Shakespeare’s signature, part of a collection of Shakespearean papers and letters that were forged by William Ireland and published in 1796; and pressed flowers that were collected from Shakespeare’s garden in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1907.

[![Image 6: Shakespeare 400, Kenyon College](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2209.jpg?w=300&h=290)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2209.jpg)

A Federal-style secretary and bookcase, produced around 1820 for Kenyon’s founder, Philander Chase, contains Shakespeare-themed merchandise like rubber ducks, bears, action figures and pop-up versions of the Globe Theatre.

[![Image 7: Shakespeare 400, Kenyon College](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2218.jpg?w=225&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2218.jpg)

Advertisement

Shakespearean insults from a kit called “Dress-Up Shakespeare Says!” cover one of the area’s windows.[![Image 8: Shakespeare 400, Kenyon College](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2228.jpg?w=195&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2228.jpg)

A Shakespearean magnetic poetry kit, a poseable Shakespeare action figure, a Shakespeare punching puppet, and other Shakespeare-themed merchandise like bandages, sticky notes, lip balms and air fresheners are available for purchase in the Kenyon College Bookstore.

“Shakespeare 400” is on view through August 12 at Kenyon’s Olin and Chalmers Libraries during Greenslade Special Collections & Archives’ open hours, Monday-Friday 9 am–12 pm and 1–4pm. Related events taking place at Kenyon this semester include a sonnet-writing competition, film screenings and discussions of Shakespeare-based movies, a cooking event featuring early-modern recipes, and lectures discussing the global elements of Shakespeare’s works.

Even closer to home, the Westerville Public Library is also offering some special programming to mark the Shakespeare q uadricentennial. On Thursday, April 7 from 6:30 to 8:00 pm, join others at the library to watch _In Search of Shakespeare_, a documentary series with a companion book by Michael Wood, that follows Shakespeare’s life and explores how he created his work that was shaped by his times. Otterbein English Professor Norman Chaney will lead a discussion and lecture titled “Shakespeare’s Life, Language and Legacy” at the library on Monday, April 25 from 7:00 to 8:30 p.m.

“[The Coming Shakespeare Extravaganza](http://www.wsj.com/articles/the-coming-shakespeare-extravaganza-1449777010),” from the December 16, 2015 edition of the _Wall Street Journal_, provides more information about the Shakespeare quadricentennial.

You can imagine how much is planned in Great Britain to commemorate this event. What I’d like to see most is “Shakespeare in the Royal Library,” on view at Windsor Castle until January 1, 2017. The exhibition draws on material in the Royal Library, including works of Shakespeare collected by the royal family, such as a copy of Shakespeare’s Second Folio with annotations by Charles I and George III; accounts of performances at Windsor Castle; and art by members of the royal family inspired by Shakespeare’s plays. Click [here](https://www.royalcollection.org.uk/exhibitions/shakespeare-in-the-royal-library/items) for digital representations of the items included in the exhibition.

For more on Shakespeare, check out _The Genius of Shakespeare_ and _Soul of the Age: The Life, Mind and World of William Shakespeare_, both by Jonathan Bate; _1599: Contested Will: Who Wrote Shakespeare; A Year in the Life of William_ Shakespeare and _The Year of Lear: Shakespeare in 1606,_ all by James Shapiro; _Shakespeare: The World As Stage_, by Bill Bryson; and _Shakespeare: The Biography_, by Peter Ackroyd.

Mi[![Image 9: Shakespeare 400, Kenyon College](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2234.jpg?w=300&h=205)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2234.jpg)ami University Libraries, my previous employer, made its copies of all four folios digitally available; you can see them [here](http://contentdm.lib.miamioh.edu/cdm/landingpage/collection/wshakespeare).

_The Great Courses: How to Read and Understand Shakespeare_ is a series of 24 30-minute lectures given by my friend Marc Conner, interim provost and the Jo M. and James Ballengee Professor of English at Washington and Lee University. Watch and listen to Marc give you a set of tools that will help you reach your own comprehension of the plays, comprehend Shakespeare’s poetic language, discover his characters and stories, and learn about his world, including how theater and stagecraft were practiced during his day. It’s available for borrowing through the Columbus Metropolitan Library, after a certain “power patron” requested its purchase. Click [here](https://cml.bibliocommons.com/item/show/2039968105_how_to_read_and_understand_shakespeare) to reserve it.

“Approaching Shakespeare’s Kings: Understanding Shakespeare’s Stage,” a lecture Marc gave as part of Washington and Lee University’s July 2015 Alumni College on Shakespeare’s kings, discusses how the conventions of the stage allowed Shakespeare to express his political beliefs, using the historical tragedy _Richard II_ to show how Shakespeare explores kingship in his plays. You can watch it [here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6-Cxe47ITm4).[![Image 10: Shakespeare 400, Kenyon College](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2219.jpg?w=225&h=300)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/dscn2219.jpg)

If you’d like to discover more about the Shakespeare homes in the Stratford-on-Avon area, see _Anne Hathaway’s Cottage: Its History, Contents and Traditions_, by F.W. Bennett; _Anne Hathaway’s Cottage_, by Wilfrid J. Osborne _;_ _In Honour of Shakespeare: The History and Collections of the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust_, by Levi Fox; _On the Trail of William Shakespeare_, by J. Keith Cheetham; _Shakespeare’s Shrine: The Bard’s Birthplace and the Invention of Stratford-upon-Avon_, by Julia Thomas; _Walking with William Shakespeare_, by Anne-Marie Edwards; and _Shakespeare’s Gardens_, by Jackie Bennett, Andrew Lawson and the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust.

Advertisement

The Shakespeare Birthplace is one of the literary pilgrimage sites described in _Freud’s Couch, Scott’s Buttocks, Brontë’s Grave_, by Simon Goldhill. “Women Re-Read Shakespeare Country” is a chapter in _Literary Tourism and Nineteenth-Century Culture_, edited by Nicola J. Watson.

Two new books about Shakespeare’s First Folio have been published, just in time for the anniversary: _Shakespeare’s First Folio: Four Centuries of an Iconic Boo k_ and _The Making of Shakespeare’s First Folio_, both by Emma Smith.

## [“The foremost woodcarver in the United States.”](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/2025/09/06/robinson/)

Posted on[September 6, 2025](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/2025/09/06/robinson/ "4:24 pm")by[Betsy](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/author/beesfirstappearance/ "View all posts by Betsy")

[![Image 2](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/img_6241.jpg?w=662)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/img_6241.jpg)

An example of someone who overcame challenges to pursue his passion and accomplish great things can be found in a regular guy who had a talent for woodcarving. And then to have the results of that creative outlet turn into a research project and an exhibition – how inspiring! Imagine what my prolific output of creations could turn into!

I discovered many interesting facts about John Edwin Robinson, thanks to the Delaware County Historical Society, which recently displayed in its Nash House a collection of his creations donated by his descendants.

Tables, cabinets, chairs, a washstand, mirrors, wall brackets, portraits, even a botanical painting on black velvet attest to this craftsman’s versatility and creativity. Most expressive were sculptures of a lion and a girl with a lyre, both thought to be part of a Greek mythology series.

Born in London, England in 1802, John Edwin Robinson grew up in a family of woodcarvers so talented that they were asked to contribute to the remodeling of Windsor Castle that took place between 1826 and 1831. He and his brother worked at their father’s wooden picture and mirror frame factory until it was torched by a disgruntled worker in 1832.

[![Image 3](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/img_6239.jpg?w=909)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/img_6239.jpg)

While his brother determined to stay in London and restart the family business, Robinson decided to start again in the United States, emigrating with his wife, Elizabeth, and another brother in 1833. Instead of settling in New York City, he searched for farmland, first on Long Island, then through New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Maryland, and eventually to Ohio in 1834, where he bought 400 acres of wooded land to clear and farm in Delaware County, near modern-day Ostrander.

Three years after moving to Ohio, Robinson was decked with a severe case of malaria. Recovered, but too weak to continue farming, he returned to his artistic talents, carving butter molds and picture frames from native hardwoods and painting $1.00 watercolor portraits of his neighbors. Soon, he became well-known, expanding his client base and his income potential by becoming an itinerant portrait artist as he traveled though Kentucky, Tennessee and Alabama.

By 1845, Robinson had also earned a name for himself as a skilled woodcarver, creating furniture and decorative pieces for homes in Columbus, as well as in the old State Library, Senate chamber and other areas in the Ohio Statehouse until they were removed during subsequent renovations.

[![Image 4](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/img_6222.jpg?w=768)](https://beesfirstappearance.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/img_6222.jpg)

More adversity came that year, when Robinson’s house burned to the ground. During a trip to Columbus to buy supplies, he encountered William Starling Sullivant, the well-known botanist who just happened to have sold him his Delaware acreage. Hearing Robinson’s sad tale, Sullivant handed him two things: a $500 check and a new interest in cryptogamia, the study of spores, ferns, algae and fungus.

After collecting specimens along the wooded banks of the Scioto River, Robinson would draw and paint them as part of his studies. In fact, he sent his collection of specimens to Germany to be published in a book, but they were lost when the boat on which they were traveling sank. He continued his studies, eventually giving his cryptogam collection to the Smithsonian Institute. His most memorable creation was his black walnut coffin, in which he was placed after his death at age 91 on November 27, 1893.

# Hiland volleyball outlasts Garaway in five sets

Hawks earn IVC victory after back-and-forth match

![Image 5: Volleyball players jump and reach at the net during an indoor match.](https://image.yourohionews.com/1081693.jpg?imageId=1081693&width=960&height=548&format=jpg)

Julia Overholt and Claire Detweiler helped Hiland defeat Garaway in Inter-Valley Conference volleyball action Sept. 29.

Dave Mast

Published September 30, 2026 - 1:46 p.m.

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.yourohionews.com%2Fholmes-county%2Fhiland-volleyball-outlasts-garaway-in-five-sets%2F1081462)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.yourohionews.com%2Fholmes-county%2Fhiland-volleyball-outlasts-garaway-in-five-sets%2F1081462)[](mailto:?subject=Hiland%20volleyball%20outlasts%20Garaway%20in%20five%20sets&body=Hawks%20earn%20IVC%20victory%20after%20back-and-forth%20match%0Dhttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.yourohionews.com%2Fholmes-county%2Fhiland-volleyball-outlasts-garaway-in-five-sets%2F1081462)

AD

![Image 6](https://image.yourohionews.com/935193.jpg?imageId=935193&x=0.00&y=0.00&cropw=100.00&croph=100.00&width=960&height=960&format=jpg)

Hiland defeated Garaway 25-21, 18-25, 25-19, 16-25, 15-10 in Inter-Valley Conference volleyball action Sept. 29.

Addisyn Mast led Hiland with 28 kills and 25 digs. Samantha Coblentz had 30 assists, 13 digs and aces. Claire Detweiler added seven kills, nine digs and two aces, while Karli Schrock finished with seven kills, four blocks and eight digs. Sophia Hamsher recorded 15 assists, five kills, two aces and four blocks. Julia Overholt had seven kills and three blocks, and Sienna Immel added nine digs.

AD

Hiland swept Ridgewood 25-12, 25-15, 25-16 in IVC play Sept. 24.

Schrock had 19 points, nine kills and six aces, Mast recorded 15 kills, Overholt had eight kills, Coblentz finished with 18 assists, nine points and two aces, Hamsher had 17 assists and Olivia Miller recorded 18 digs.

### Varsity boys golf

Hiland won the Division III sectional tournament Sept. 23 at Cambridge Country Club with a team score of 305, advancing to districts as one of the top six qualifying teams.

Andrew Beun led Hiland and all golfers with a 71, followed by Marcus Beun with a 77, Joshua Raber with a 78 and Austin Miller with a 79.

**H.S. FOOTBALL WEEK 7 — THE GAMES**

**WAYNE-HOLMES EDITION**

AD

**Oct. 2**

**All games 7 p.m.**

**Ohio Cardinal Conference**

**Wooster (2-4, 2-1) at Dover (4-2, 3-0)**

**Last week:**Wooster 17, New Philadelphia 10; Dover 56, West Holmes 35

**Last year**: Dover 42, Wooster 14

AD

![Image 7: West Holmes sophomore Coi Beachy (right) had a school-record 19 receptions in the Sept. 24 loss to Dover.](https://image.yourohionews.com/1081557.jpg?imageId=1081557&x=0.00&y=0.00&cropw=100.00&croph=100.00&width=960&height=692&format=jpg)

West Holmes sophomore Coi Beachy (right) had a school-record 19 receptions in the Sept. 24 loss to Dover. Beachy's catches were good for 182 yards and three touchdowns.

Dave Mast

**This year:**The Generals got a pair of touchdowns from Kaj Meier last week and a late field goal from Roy Melrose to give Wooster a touchdown lead that held up. Wooster has won two of its last three after an 0-3 start that stretched the Generals’ then-losing streak to 15 games. Dover took a 35-14 halftime lead and made it stand up against West Holmes. Dieter Weber threw three first-half touchdown passes. Junior speedster Dante Clark scored four times in four different ways — one rushing, one receiving, one on a punt return and one on a kickoff return. The Tornadoes won despite giving up more than 450 yards of offense.
