# Wayne, Holmes County football teams hold playoff spots in latest OHSAA ratings

Garaway, Triway, Smithville and West Holmes sit among top four in their regions

![Image 5: Football players in green uniforms run onto a field beneath banners and flags.](https://image.yourohionews.com/1073934.jpg?imageId=1073934&x=0.00&y=12.62&cropw=100.00&croph=85.59&width=960&height=548&format=jpg)

Smithville, Garaway, Triway and West Holmes hold top-four positions in their regions, while several other area teams remain among the top 12 in the OHSAA football computer ratings entering Week 7.

Joshua McWilliams

Published September 30, 2026 - 3:00 p.m.

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.yourohionews.com%2Fwayne-county%2Fwayne-holmes-county-football-teams-hold-playoff-spots-in-latest-ohsaa-ratings%2F1081867)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.yourohionews.com%2Fwayne-county%2Fwayne-holmes-county-football-teams-hold-playoff-spots-in-latest-ohsaa-ratings%2F1081867)[](mailto:?subject=Wayne%2C%20Holmes%20County%20football%20teams%20hold%20playoff%20spots%20in%20latest%20OHSAA%20ratings&body=Garaway%2C%20Triway%2C%20Smithville%20and%20West%20Holmes%20sit%20among%20top%20four%20in%20their%20regions%0Dhttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.yourohionews.com%2Fwayne-county%2Fwayne-holmes-county-football-teams-hold-playoff-spots-in-latest-ohsaa-ratings%2F1081867)

AD

Several area football teams are in playoff position in the Ohio High School Athletic Association computer ratings released Sept. 29, with Garaway, Triway, Smithville and West Holmes currently holding top-four spots in their respective regions.

The ratings enter Week 7 of the regular season. The top 12 teams in each region in the final computer ratings Oct. 25 will qualify for the playoffs, while the top four seeds will receive first-round byes.

AD

In Division IV, West Holmes (4-2) is fourth in Region 15 with a 9.596 computer average. The Knights trail Indian Valley, New Lexington and Johnstown.

Orrville (5-1) is 11th in Division IV, Region 13 with a 7.4167 average. Rocky River leads the region at 13.0.

Triway (5-1) is third in Division V, Region 18 at 10.5333. Keystone is first at 10.8, followed by Bluffton at 10.55. Norwayne (3-3) is 13th in the same region with a 5.2828 average.

Three area teams are among the top 11 in Division VI, Region 21. Smithville (6-0) is third with an 8.9167 average, Hillsdale (5-1) is eighth at 7.0167 and Chippewa (4-2) is 11th at 6.2333. South Range leads the region at 10.835, followed by Kirtland at 10.7833.

Garaway (5-1) is second in Division VI, Region 23 with a 9.3333 average. Nelsonville-York (6-0) leads the region at 10.4.

In Division VII, Region 25, Rittman (3-3) is eighth with a 3.8662 average, while Dalton (2-4) is 11th at 3.4. McDonald leads the region at 7.9.

AD

Wooster (2-4) is 16th in Division II, Region 7 with a 4.6333 average. Bishop Watterson leads the region at 16.2333.

# Amish Country: Where To Go (25-Community Guide)

By[Erik Wesner](https://amishamerica.com/author/erik-wesner/)

[2 Comments](https://amishamerica.com/amish-country-where-to-go/#comments)

So you’re thinking about a visit to **Amish Country**. There’s one thing you’ll need to figure out first: **where should you go?**

There are over 600 Amish communities, after all. Narrowing down your choices will depend on different things – like driving distance, what you want to do in Amish Country, and so on.

To make things easier, I’ve put together my **best ideas** on which Amish places to visit – in three categories: **1)****large**, tourist-oriented communities; **2)****smaller**, also tourist-friendly places, and **3)****“off-the-beaten-path”** communities. Use this guide to help make the best choice for your visit.

1.   [Option 1: Large Tourist-Friendly Communities](https://amishamerica.com/amish-country-where-to-go/#large-community)
2.   [Option 2: Smaller Tourist-Friendly Communities](https://amishamerica.com/amish-country-where-to-go/#smaller-community)
3.   [Option 3: “Off-the-Beaten-Path” Communities](https://amishamerica.com/amish-country-where-to-go/#off-the-beaten-path)
4.   [Two others worth considering](https://amishamerica.com/amish-country-where-to-go/#worth-considering)
5.   [One Amish Community I wouldn’t visit…](https://amishamerica.com/amish-country-where-to-go/#avoid)

![Image 3: A yellow Amish buggy warning sign](https://amishamerica.com/images/lancaster-county-buggy-warning.jpg)

Welcome to Amish Country. You’ll see signs like this one in over 600 places in America. Photo: Don Burke

### How to use this Amish Country Guide

In this bird’s-eye view guide, I share the attractions of each community, and give you an idea of what to expect. You’ll find over **two dozen Amish community options** listed below.

I’ve also linked to a full listing of 600+ Amish communities below. You might be surprised to find there is an Amish community in your neighborhood – or not too far away.

The **goal of this guide** is to give you a general bird-eye view of the types of Amish destinations out there – to help you choose a community, based on what you’re looking for in your Amish Country visit.

*   For example, some people find a **larger, tourist-friendly place** more appealing. Do you want to eat at an Amish-style restaurant? Are you interested in buggy rides and farm tours?
*   Others are drawn to **smaller, lesser-known communities**, which don’t offer those attractions – but do give you a slice of Amish life, out of the spotlight. With this guide, I give you an idea of what options are out there, and what to expect.

Once you’ve narrowed down your options, you can tap local resources for more information. Many of these communities have **local websites** built to help visitors find accommodation, activities, etc. (I’ve linked some of those sites below).

I hope this guide helps you make the best choice for your Amish Country trip! ~Erik

* * *

![Image 4: An Amish woman rides a bicycle on a gravel road with a buggy approaching](https://amishamerica.com/images/woman-bicycle-indiana-amish-country.jpg)

Photo: Jim Halverson

## [](https://amishamerica.com/amish-country-where-to-go/)Option 1: Large Community

A large Amish community gives you a lot of **advantages**, including:

### Pluses

*   Many **Amish stores & shops** to visit
*   Many **accommodation** options
*   Variety of PA Dutch and Amish-style **restaurant options**
*   Other **activities** like buggy rides, farm tours and more
*   No need to “hunt” for the Amish like in a smaller community – they are **everywhere**

There are also some **drawbacks**, including:

### Drawbacks

*   Can be a little too **“touristy”** in some areas
*   Can be relatively **crowded** in peak seasons
*   Generally **higher prices**
*   **Geographically restricted** to the Midwest and eastern PA

So in this section we’ll focus on the largest, and arguably most tourist-friendly Amish communities. And there are really **three that stand out** above all others.

![Image 5: Three Amish toddlers standing on the back of a simple wagon](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-country-children.png)

Photo: Jim Halverson

## The 3 largest (& most tourist-friendly) Amish communities

The **three largest Amish communities** are also the best-known of Amish communities – one each in Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Indiana.

Each of these settlements is home to**tens of thousands of Amish people**. Their Amish populations are so large, that they would form small cities of Amish – if they all lived close together.

Each of these has many options for lodging, food, activities, and Amish stores and businesses to visit. So read on for more on the three largest, and most popular, Amish Country destinations.

## [](https://amishamerica.com/amish-country-where-to-go/)1. Lancaster County, Pennsylvania

![Image 6: A young boy guides a two-horse team with an Amish farmhouse in background](https://amishamerica.com/images/lancaster-county-amish-country.jpg)

Lancaster County, Pennsylvania. Photo: Don Burke

**Lancaster County, PA** is home to the largest Amish community of them all. It is located on the East Coast within an easy drive of many major population centers. It has a highly-developed Amish tourism industry with many things to do.

There is no shortage of Amish shops to visit, buggy rides and farm tours, and other attractions here. [All-you-can-eat PA Dutch restaurants](https://amishamerica.com/a-closer-look-at-3-lancaster-county-mass-eateries/) including Shady Maple Smorgasbord, Miller’s, Bird-in-Hand Family Restaurant, and others keep visitors well-fed.

The area is home to picture-perfect Amish dairy farms with 200-year-old stone barns, many covered bridges, and other charming rural scenes. Come at the right time, and you can attend an [Amish mud sale](https://amishamerica.com/lancaster-county-amish-mud-sales/) or other auction.

![Image 7: Various fruit pies on the shelves of an Amish store](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-pies-for-sale-lancaster.jpg)

Pies for sales in a Lancaster County-area Amish store.

For all these reasons and more, it’s no surprise that Lancaster County is the most-visited Amish tourism destination in the country. I have visited Lancaster County many times, and I like much about it. I’m fond of visiting Amish stores, and there are **many of them here** – food places like [Emma’s Gourmet Popcorn](https://amishamerica.com/emmas-popcorn-new-store-lancaster-county/), [Gordonville Book Store](https://amishamerica.com/gordonville-book-store-lancaster-county-pa/), dry goods and variety stores, and many more.

The community has many beautiful and quaint **small towns**, some of which you’ve probably heard of – Intercourse (the most “tourist” town of them all), Bird-in-Hand, Strasburg (maybe the most beautiful, with its many historic homes), and Churchtown, to name a few.

There are also attractions like theatre shows at the Plain & Fancy Theatre, Amish Experience Theatre, and Sight & Sound Theatres. The area can get “busy”, however (for an Amish community at least), with a lot of traffic in certain parts of the county.

That’s because a half-million people, most of them _not_ Amish, live in Lancaster County. So while it is a rural area, it is relatively highly-populated, especially compared to other communities on this list. Add that to the tourist traffic, and it can feel a bit cramped at times.

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6r8TDa-S9Nk)

That said, this community is definitely one of the **top choices** for an Amish Country visit for all the reasons listed above. For a full guide to visiting this community, including information on places to stay, things to do, where to eat and more, check out [discoverlancaster.com](https://www.discoverlancaster.com/amish/) or a similar website.

I’ve also done a more in-depth comparison of Lancaster County and the next community on the list, Holmes County, which you’ll find here: [Which Community Should You Visit? 7 Differences Between Lancaster County & Holmes County](https://amishamerica.com/7-differences-between-lancaster-county-holmes-county/).

## [](https://amishamerica.com/amish-country-where-to-go/)2. Holmes County, Ohio

![Image 8: A black horse-drawn Amish buggy ](https://amishamerica.com/images/holmes-county-ohio-amish-country.jpg)

Holmes County, Ohio. Photo: Don Burke

The Amish settlement in **Holmes County, Ohio** is not much smaller than the one in Lancaster County, having about 40,000 Amish people. It also gets a lot of visitors, but has a less-busy “feel”. That’s because the area is more rural, and more heavily Amish, with fewer non-Amish living in the area. That is one of its main appeals, in my opinion.

Another one is the **diversity of Amish groups** you’ll find here. While Lancaster County is home to one major Amish affiliation, Holmes County has nearly a dozen different horse-and-buggy Amish groups – from the very conservative [Swartzentruber Amish](https://amishamerica.com/who-are-the-swartzentruber-amish/) to the progressive [New Order Amish](https://amishamerica.com/whats-the-difference-between-new-order-and-old-order-amish/).

After a little while you’ll start to notice differences between these groups – in clothing, hair, buggies, homes, and more. This is a special aspect of this community and, in my opinion, one of its biggest appeals.

![Image 9: An exhibit telling the story of the Ausbund Anabaptist songbook](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-mennonite-heritage-center-ausbund-exhibit.jpg)

An exhibit at the Amish & Mennonite Heritage Center on the Ausbund, a church hymnal used by the Amish. Berlin, Ohio

Like Lancaster County, there are many options for food, stores, accommodation, shopping, and so on. Popular small towns in this community include Berlin, Walnut Creek, Mount Hope, Mount Eaton, Sugarcreek, Charm, and Millersburg.

**Berlin** is the most famous tourist town here, at the center of the Amish community. **Mount Hope** holds regular auctions at its auction center, well-attended by the Amish. **Sugarcreek** is nicknamed the “Little Switzerland of Ohio” and this is reflected in the Swiss-style buildings in town.

Popular **places to eat** include **Mrs. Yoder’s** in Mount Hope, **Der Dutchman** in Walnut Creek, and [**Boyd & Wurthmann**](https://amishamerica.com/boyd-wurthmann-restaurant-berlin-ohio/) in Berlin (great local spot with a small-town feel and Amish waitresses). To learn about the history and culture of the Amish, the [Amish & Mennonite Heritage Center](https://behalt.com/) in Berlin (home to the famous “Behalt” cyclorama painting), is a great choice.

All in all, Holmes County has a very “rural” feel, and is generally very friendly towards visitors – on the whole, I’d say more so than Lancaster County. There are many Amish craftspeople in this community. You’ll come across furniture making, leather goods, quiltmaking, and other family cottage industries.

[Video 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1IWS-u7bLtI)

The Holmes County community actually spans multiple counties, including Wayne, Tuscarawas, and Coshocton, each of which have sizeable Amish populations. Holmes County is a great place to go for a drive (GPS) and just see what you’ll come across down the gravel roads and over the rolling hills.

For more details on where in Holmes County to stay, eat, and more, check out [visitamishcountry.com](https://www.visitamishcountry.com/), or a similar site. And for a more in-depth comparison of the two largest Amish communities, check out my guide to [Holmes County vs. Lancaster County](https://amishamerica.com/7-differences-between-lancaster-county-holmes-county/).

## [](https://amishamerica.com/amish-country-where-to-go/)3. Northern Indiana: Elkhart & LaGrange County (Shipshewana) + Nappanee

![Image 10: Amish woman in buggy approaching Menno-Hof Amish center sign](https://amishamerica.com/images/northern-indiana-amish-country-menno-hof.jpg)

A woman in an Amish buggy passes the Menno-Hof informational center in Shipshewana, Indiana. Photo: Jim Halverson

The third of the “Big Three” Amish communities, the Amish of **northern Indiana** (Elkhart and LaGrange County) also draws millions of visitors annually, many of whom descend on the area’s most famous town, **Shipshewana**. Besides being more-or-less the center of the Amish community, Shipshewana is home to a famous – and gigantic – **flea market**. It also has the [Menno-Hof](https://menno-hof.squarespace.com/) cultural center, which tells the Amish and Mennonite story.

Like the other communities mentioned above, the area is dotted with charming small towns, including Topeka, Millersburg, Middlebury, LaGrange, and others. Nearly 30,000 Amish people live here, so you won’t have trouble spotting a buggy going down the road.

![Image 11: Sign for "Laura's Fabrics" in front of a white Amish home](https://amishamerica.com/images/fabric-shop-indiana-amish-country.jpg)

Amish-run fabric store in northern Indiana. Photo: Jim Halverson

The area has its share of Amish farms and abundant small stores run by Amish people. You’ll notice signs for these as you drive the many grid roads of the community (side note: that makes it harder to get lost in this community, unlike the two we’ve covered above). That noted, many Amish men here work in the recreational vehicle industry, a unique feature of the region. You’ll see them traveling to and from work, often riding [bicycles](https://amishamerica.com/why-do-amish-ride-scooters-but-not-bicycles/).

This community is home to the famous **Rise’n Roll Bakery**, as well as the **Blue Gate Restaurant** in Shipshewana, which besides offering food, puts on shows in its associated theatre. There are many other food options besides those.

I find the Amish people here overall quite friendly and laid-back. You might spot an Amish buggy hauling a boat to one of the area’s numerous lakes and ponds, or see Amish youth playing softball late night at one of the local fields.

With its cornfields and down-home charm the area has a great middle America feel. The Amish folks here are among the more progressive, and easy to relate to.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qy4nk0rm_AM)

We can also include the nearby, very similar community of **Nappanee** here, home to another nearly 7,000 Amish people. The [Nappanee Amish settlement](https://amishamerica.com/indiana-amish/#nappanee) basically touches the Elkhart-LaGrange community, and the Amish in Nappanee are quite similar, as far as technology, jobs, and appearance. Nappanee is also home to **The Barns at Nappanee** attraction (formerly Amish Acres).

For more on Elkhart-LaGrange Amish Country, check out [visitshipshewana.org](https://visitshipshewana.org/), and for information on Nappanee, see [visitnappanee.com](https://visitnappanee.com/).

* * *

## [](https://amishamerica.com/amish-country-where-to-go/)Option 2: Smaller, visitor-friendly Amish community

These communities are smaller than the “Big Three”, but are all still pretty sizeable. Each of these communities has **from 1,000 to 6,000 Amish residents**. That means they’ll have a good variety of Amish stores, places to stay and eat, and other amenities.

So these are a nice choice if you want to go to a good-sized community with at least some tourist amenities, but want to avoid the larger, most heavily-visited places. I’ve chosen **ten options** for you below.

### Pluses:

*   **Large enough** to offer multiple options for stores, places to eat
*   **Less “touristy” feel** to these places, while still offering attractions
*   More **manageable** in deciding what to do and visit due to smaller size

### Drawbacks:

*   **More limited options** for lodging, food, Amish-theme tours and experiences
*   Some are in quite **remote** locations

[Video 4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDtLmpq3vFY)

## 1. Arthur, Illinois

[Illinois](https://amishamerica.com/illinois-amish/)‘ largest Amish community, and the first Amish place I ever visited. I spend three weeks here one summer and have fond memories of the place. This is a classic Amish settlement where you have a charming small town, **Arthur**, at the center, with Amish homes and farms extending for miles in every direction around it.

Many Amish woodworkers and small shops to visit here, dotted among the cornfields. In town, **Yoder’s Kitchen** provides Amish-style meals, a bakery, and gift shop.

## 2. Big Valley, Pennsylvania

I highly recommend visiting this unique Amish community if you have a chance. What makes it special? “[Big Valley](https://amishamerica.com/pennsylvania-amish/#big%20valley)” is home to **three distinct Amish groups**, each with a different-colored buggy top – the Renno Amish (black), Byler Amish (yellow!), and Nebraska Amish (white). # Visiting the Amish at Belle Rive, Illinois (19 Photos)

By[Don Burke](https://amishamerica.com/author/don-burke/)August 28, 2015 September 19, 2015

[14 Comments](https://amishamerica.com/amish-belle-rive-opdyke-illinois/#comments)

![Image 3: belle-rive-il-map](https://amishamerica.com/images/belle-rive-il-map.jpg)[Don Burke](http://www.flickr.com/photos/ozarkinspirations) today shares photos from a little visit to the Belle Rive/Opdyke, Illinois Amish community, taken last autumn.

This is a small community in southern Illinois (Jefferson County), two church districts in size.As a state, [Illinois](https://amishamerica.com/illinois-amish/) ranks #10 in its total Amish population, which is dominated by [the large Arthur settlement](https://amishamerica.com/amish-community-arthur-illinois/).

Don gives you a tour around the settlement below. You can also think of it as a little preview of fall, which I am frankly quite ready for,as I’ve been roasting these past few weeks ![Image 4: 😉](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/svg/1f609.svg)

* * *

![Image 5: buggy-in-side-view-mirror](https://amishamerica.com/images/buggy-in-side-view-mirror.jpg)

Looking Back at a Passing Visit to Belle Rive, IL

In the fall of 2014 I took about three days to visit several Amish communities in the southern Illinois and western Kentucky area. One of those passing visits was in the Belle Rive / Opdyke, IL settlement.

![Image 6: buggy-warning-il](https://amishamerica.com/images/buggy-warning-il.jpg)

Some of the Amish homes in this community had the characteristic Amish feel to them,while many of them did not stand out as particularly Amish, but looked fairly contemporary.

![Image 7: farm-lane-amish-opdyke-il](https://amishamerica.com/images/farm-lane-amish-opdyke-il.jpg)

There were [the customary phone shanties](https://amishamerica.com/amish-phone-shacks/) here and there….

![Image 8: phone-shanty-belle-rive](https://amishamerica.com/images/phone-shanty-belle-rive.jpg)

…and of course the typical Amish schoolhouses and playground activities.

![Image 9: children-playing-amish-illinois](https://amishamerica.com/images/children-playing-amish-illinois.jpg)

A closer look at the schoolhouse shows [the community’s use of scooters](https://amishamerica.com/who-makes-amish-scooters/) (I don’t recall seeing a regular bicycle anywhere while I was there)….

![Image 10: scooters-illinois-amish](https://amishamerica.com/images/scooters-illinois-amish.jpg)

…and here is another scooter I noticed at one of the homes.

![Image 11: scooter-by-house-illinois](https://amishamerica.com/images/scooter-by-house-illinois.jpg)

I’m told that the Belle Rive settlement traces its history to [Amish in Delaware](https://amishamerica.com/delaware-amish/), and that the buggies still show design characteristics from that area.

![Image 12: buggy-illinois-belle-rive](https://amishamerica.com/images/buggy-illinois-belle-rive.jpg)

![Image 13: parked-buggy-southern-illinois-amish](https://amishamerica.com/images/parked-buggy-southern-illinois-amish.jpg)

At least some of the Amish here work the fields…

![Image 14: shocks-in-field-illinois](https://amishamerica.com/images/shocks-in-field-illinois.jpg)

…but the farmers are [allowed to use tractors](https://amishamerica.com/they-dont-make/)…

![Image 15: parked-tractor-amish-belle-rive](https://amishamerica.com/images/parked-tractor-amish-belle-rive.jpg)

…farm implements with rubber/pneumatic tires…

![Image 16: equipment-farming-illinois-amish](https://amishamerica.com/images/equipment-farming-illinois-amish.jpg)

…and even heavy machinery (notice the yellow bulldozer on the right).

![Image 17: gourds-belle-rive](https://amishamerica.com/images/gourds-belle-rive.jpg)

So, this community is clearly not among the strictest of the Amish. I saw other signs of that included the occasional [solar panel](https://amishamerica.com/amish-solar-power/)…

![Image 18: solar-panel-metal-roof](https://amishamerica.com/images/solar-panel-metal-roof.jpg)

…the not so subtle wind vane on one Amish shop….

![Image 19: weathervane-illinois](https://amishamerica.com/images/weathervane-illinois.jpg)

…signs for some of the Amish businesses, which were a bit more fancy than most Amish signage….

![Image 20: j-r-supply-amish-illinois](https://amishamerica.com/images/j-r-supply-amish-illinois.jpg)

…and at least one Amish [hunter](https://amishamerica.com/do-amish-hunt/) who mounted his trophy deer and elk antlers on the barn near the road for all to see.

![Image 21: belle-rive-red-barn](https://amishamerica.com/images/belle-rive-red-barn.jpg)

As I said, my trip through Belle Rive was mostly a passing-through visit, but I did make one stop at a bakery and bulk food store for a donut and a brief-but-enjoyable visit with the Amish lady that run the shop.

![Image 22: east-view-bulk-foods-amish-illinois](https://amishamerica.com/images/east-view-bulk-foods-amish-illinois.jpg)

![Image 23: bulk-food-store-opdyke-illinois-amish](https://amishamerica.com/images/bulk-food-store-opdyke-illinois-amish.jpg)

And in case you’re wondering, yes, the donut was really good!

![Image 24](https://amishamerica.com/images/D607172-009_2-scaled.jpeg)

The Cleo Redd Fisher Museum’s speaker series returns with Rebels in Corsets: The Embodied Rhetoric of the Women’s Suffrage Movement, presented by Susan Trollinger Monday, Feb. 9, in the museum’s lecture hall. Doors open at 6:30 p.m., with the program beginning at 7 p.m.

The program challenges the common perception that women’s suffrage was achieved through a quiet and orderly political process. Instead, Trollinger explores the movement as a 72-year struggle that required persistence, sacrifice and strategic creativity. It will consider what life was like for women in the 19th century, how reformers in the 1840s came to believe it was time to demand the vote and the rhetorical strategies they used to persuade a resistant public. Trollinger says that though many of these arguments appear unremarkable today, they were once viewed as shocking and even “disgusting.” The fight for suffrage reshaped not only the law but American political culture itself.

AD

Trollinger is a professor of English at the University of Dayton. She holds a bachelor’s degree in communication arts from the University of Wisconsin–Madison and a master’s degree and Ph.D. in rhetoric and communication from the University of Pittsburgh. Trollinger is the author of "Selling the Amish: The Tourism of Nostalgia" (2012), which examines Amish Country tourism in eastern Ohio, and co-author of "Righting America at the Creation Museum" (2016). She has been interviewed by national media outlets, including C-SPAN2’s BookTV, RadioWest, The Washington Post and GQ.

Admission to the lecture is free. For more information, visit www.crfmuseum.com or call 419-994-4050.

# Hiland volleyball outlasts Garaway in five sets

Hawks earn IVC victory after back-and-forth match

![Image 5: Volleyball players jump and reach at the net during an indoor match.](https://image.yourohionews.com/1081693.jpg?imageId=1081693&width=960&height=548&format=jpg)

Julia Overholt and Claire Detweiler helped Hiland defeat Garaway in Inter-Valley Conference volleyball action Sept. 29.

Dave Mast

Published September 30, 2026 - 1:46 p.m.

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.yourohionews.com%2Fholmes-county%2Fhiland-volleyball-outlasts-garaway-in-five-sets%2F1081462)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.yourohionews.com%2Fholmes-county%2Fhiland-volleyball-outlasts-garaway-in-five-sets%2F1081462)[](mailto:?subject=Hiland%20volleyball%20outlasts%20Garaway%20in%20five%20sets&body=Hawks%20earn%20IVC%20victory%20after%20back-and-forth%20match%0Dhttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.yourohionews.com%2Fholmes-county%2Fhiland-volleyball-outlasts-garaway-in-five-sets%2F1081462)

AD

![Image 6](https://image.yourohionews.com/935193.jpg?imageId=935193&x=0.00&y=0.00&cropw=100.00&croph=100.00&width=960&height=960&format=jpg)

Hiland defeated Garaway 25-21, 18-25, 25-19, 16-25, 15-10 in Inter-Valley Conference volleyball action Sept. 29.

Addisyn Mast led Hiland with 28 kills and 25 digs. Samantha Coblentz had 30 assists, 13 digs and aces. Claire Detweiler added seven kills, nine digs and two aces, while Karli Schrock finished with seven kills, four blocks and eight digs. Sophia Hamsher recorded 15 assists, five kills, two aces and four blocks. Julia Overholt had seven kills and three blocks, and Sienna Immel added nine digs.

AD

Hiland swept Ridgewood 25-12, 25-15, 25-16 in IVC play Sept. 24.

Schrock had 19 points, nine kills and six aces, Mast recorded 15 kills, Overholt had eight kills, Coblentz finished with 18 assists, nine points and two aces, Hamsher had 17 assists and Olivia Miller recorded 18 digs.

### Varsity boys golf

Hiland won the Division III sectional tournament Sept. 23 at Cambridge Country Club with a team score of 305, advancing to districts as one of the top six qualifying teams.

Andrew Beun led Hiland and all golfers with a 71, followed by Marcus Beun with a 77, Joshua Raber with a 78 and Austin Miller with a 79.

# PA Amish trip highlights

By[Erik Wesner](https://amishamerica.com/author/erik-wesner/)August 31, 2012 August 31, 2012

[23 Comments](https://amishamerica.com/pa-amish-trip-highlights/#comments)

I’ve finally put together some trip highlights from Lancaster County. Today begins a new trip, a week-long journey across Indiana and Ohio. Before we get into that, here’s what I liked from last week’s visit:

**Seven nights, four bonfires, two mountain pie feasts.** Amish people like to burn stuff in the summer time. Mostly wood from what I can tell. It makes for a nice setting to sit, talk, and eat, and roast [mountain pies](https://amishamerica.com/do-you-know-these-10-amish-terms/#comment-34778). This past week was bonfire-o-rama. Two of the fires were lit in celebration of birthdays ([mine and Eli’s](https://amishamerica.com/what-makes-a-great-birthday/), and another friend’s surprise party).

My second try at mountain pies came out tastier than the first. Part of the problem the first time is that I got to choose from the last two pie irons–both round. Nothing wrong with that, except that the bread we had was all square. If you’re hungry enough it tastes good whatever final shape it takes.

**Big Valley baby.** A quick story. My Polish girlfriend, Izabela, is visiting the USA for the first time and was along on this trip. While in Big Valley we paid a visit to a [Nebraska Amish](https://amishamerica.com/amish-nebraska/#pa%20nebraska) family I’m acquainted with. I had met them once 4 years earlier and just decided to drop in on a whim.

![Image 3: Amish Big Valley](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-big-valley.jpg)

Big Valley buggy

The man of the house vaguely remembered me, and ended up inviting us in to chat with his wife. After a few minutes of talking, the 9-year-old daughter is handing her 9-_day_-old sister to a dumbfounded Izabela–a perfect stranger 10 minutes before. Iza couldn’t imagine something similar happening in her culture. The baby quickly won her heart and I think wanted to leave with us (or so she thought). I think that says something about attitudes to children in Amish culture, where you’re comfortable sharing them–even with random Polish-English people that just show up at your door.

**Connecting friends.** Introducing two Amish families as a third (English) party is kind of weird. You feel like you are in the wrong spot, that you are the one that should be getting introduced to someone and not making the connections. When Amish people meet there is the usual search for a link of some sort–who is your dad, where do you come from, what do you do and who you work(ed) with. I was glad that it could finally happen, as I usually only talk about the Zooks and the Kings (who live on one side of Lancaster) to the Riehls (who live on the other), and vice versa.

In little Amish communities of a few church districts you generally know everyone. In the big Lancaster community (going on 200 churches), you might not have many relatives, dealings or running-around friends in a given area, which was the case here. For an Amish person strangers can include both English and other Amish. The nice thing is that there is usually an Amish connection somewhere if you poke around enough.

![Image 4: Amish Hat City](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-hat-city.jpg)

Amish hat in the City

**Day trip to Philly.** We had Amish friends along. Even in a place like Philadelphia with an Amish presence nearby, people notice Amish walking around one of America’s largest cities. I noticed some heads turn and some sheepish smiles of people we passed or interacted with.

I also think that it helps to be Amish in certain situations. One example. We visited the US Mint. You need identification to get in. Three of us had IDs, while the fourth did not–not one of our Amish companions, but Izabela. My friend’s wife explained the situation and asked if we could slide, which the understanding guard let happen. Once inside my friend joked that it was “the hat” that got us in. I think that was just a half-joke as there must be a kernel of truth there.

**Visiting Centralia.** This has nothing to do with the Amish. Centralia is a central PA mining town–or I should say _was_, because it’s been essentially abandoned for many years. Centralia lies in anthracite coal mining country. A half-century ago, a mine fire was sparked and began slowly burning, snaking its way along the massive coal veins running beneath the town. Noxious gases and ground collapses threatened the townspeople’s health and safety. Multi-million dollar efforts to extinguish the fire failed. Many residents moved away and nearly all buildings in the town were demolished beginning in the 1980s. Today only a handful, perhaps 3 or 4, homes remain in this town which once had a population over 1000 souls.

![Image 5: Centralia PA Street](https://amishamerica.com/images/centralia-pa-street.jpg)

A former homesite in Centralia, PA

Centralia is a tragic and rather eerie place. I remember stumbling across it five years ago while traveling across the state. I came to a stop at what looked like a normal country highway intersection, except for the odd, out-of-place bench placed near the crossroads. Like something you’d see in a town, and not in the middle of nowhere. Looking closer I began to notice sidewalks and the layout of a street plan. As I creeped along the cracked, overgrown asphalt streets, old retaining walls and steps hinted at a forgotten past. I slowly realized that a town once lay here. Governmental response to the town’s crisis has evoked controversy particularly among those who once lived there, and the town appears in the news from time to time. It’s a modern-day ghost town in a place you’d hardly expect to find one.

**Jokes.** Hang around with Amish folks long enough, and the jokes start flowing. This time I got to hear the one about the origins of the fictional “Stoltzfus Chinese Market” in Philly, among others. Amish like to make Polish jokes, which they hit me with from time to time knowing my origins. And with a true blooded Polish person along this time, of course some wondered what Izabela thought of them. She was good-natured about it. It helps that she can give as good as she gets.

Amish also joke about themselves. We even got a second hearing of a [friend’s favorite Amish joke](https://amishamerica.com/the-polish-amish-hybrid-joke/), about the bridge in the desert. “I’ll tell you a really good Amish joke,” he began with a smile. “But it starts with a Polish joke,” he conceded to an uproar of laughter.  Well of course it does!

An Amish Hat Story

On Saturday the eighth of September I helped a museum I participate with at a big street festival in our community. I was doing what I was asked to do in my period appropriate clothing, which includes a straw hat much like the one in Erik’s picture.

A young man walked toward me and began to, badly, sing ‘Weird Al’ Yankovick’s “Amish Paradise” because of my choice in headgear. I quickly thought about what I should do, I thought about reciting the “You’re making a big mistake” scene from Harrison Ford’s “Witness”, or quoting “Amish Paradise” back to him with the line “Don’t be vain, don’t be whiny, or my brother I might have to get medieval your hiny”, but instead of playing along with the gag my gut reaction was to say “hello, I’m with this museum and our next event is this which will be on this date. I can give you a flyer.”

I did think the scene was funny though, and I did hear “Look they’re Amish”, but I was too far away to say “no we’re not.” I did not hear any Jane Austen quips though. My group would take that as complement, but “look they’re Amish” gives us an in to engage and educate.

True Hat Story. [Reply](https://amishamerica.com/pa-amish-trip-highlights/#comment-35359)

**H.S. FOOTBALL WEEK 7 — THE GAMES**

**WAYNE-HOLMES EDITION**

AD

**Oct. 2**

**All games 7 p.m.**

**Ohio Cardinal Conference**

**Wooster (2-4, 2-1) at Dover (4-2, 3-0)**

**Last week:**Wooster 17, New Philadelphia 10; Dover 56, West Holmes 35

**Last year**: Dover 42, Wooster 14

AD

![Image 7: West Holmes sophomore Coi Beachy (right) had a school-record 19 receptions in the Sept. 24 loss to Dover.](https://image.yourohionews.com/1081557.jpg?imageId=1081557&x=0.00&y=0.00&cropw=100.00&croph=100.00&width=960&height=692&format=jpg)

West Holmes sophomore Coi Beachy (right) had a school-record 19 receptions in the Sept. 24 loss to Dover. Beachy's catches were good for 182 yards and three touchdowns.

Dave Mast

**This year:**The Generals got a pair of touchdowns from Kaj Meier last week and a late field goal from Roy Melrose to give Wooster a touchdown lead that held up. Wooster has won two of its last three after an 0-3 start that stretched the Generals’ then-losing streak to 15 games. Dover took a 35-14 halftime lead and made it stand up against West Holmes. Dieter Weber threw three first-half touchdown passes. Junior speedster Dante Clark scored four times in four different ways — one rushing, one receiving, one on a punt return and one on a kickoff return. The Tornadoes won despite giving up more than 450 yards of offense. Dover’s final opponents head into the Week 6 slate a combined 7-16, putting the Tornadoes in very good spot heading into the stretch run.

**West Holmes (4-2, 2-1) at Lexington (1-5, 1-2)**

**Last week:** Dover 56, West Holmes 35; Mansfield Senior 32, Lexington 27  
**Last year:** Lexington 41, West Holmes 7  
**This year:** West Holmes is ranked fourth in Division IV, Region 15 and features the area’s leading passer and receiver. Brayden Parsons has thrown for 1,646 yards and an area-best 19 touchdowns, while Coi Beachy leads the area with 52 catches for 789 yards and 10 scores. Chris Williams has rushed for 559 yards and eight touchdowns. Beachy has 68 tackles, while Oliver Fleming has 64 tackles and eight sacks. Lexington has been outscored 205-98, although the Minutemen have scored 71 points over their past two games.

**Principals’ Athletic Conference**

**Northwest (6-0, 2-0) at Orrville (5-1, 3-0)**

![Image 8: Mark Lorson](https://image.yourohionews.com/1067267.jpg?imageId=1067267&x=0.00&y=0.00&cropw=100.00&croph=100.00&width=960&height=1200&format=jpg)

Mark Lorson, Orrville

yourohionews.com

**Last week:** Northwest 34, Coventry 6; Orrville 41, Canton South 14  
**Last year:** Northwest 28, Orrville 14  
**This year:** Orrville quarterback Mark Lorson has accounted for 1,500 total yards, passing for 1,037 yards and 11 touchdowns while rushing for 463 yards and eight scores. Parker Hostetler has rushed for 594 yards and eight touchdowns and added 199 receiving yards. Tyson Woodruff leads the Red Riders with 285 receiving yards and four touchdowns. Abran Perez has recored 72 tackles, while Aiden Shoup has 65. Northwest is ranked third in Division IV, Region 13. The Indians have allowed 73 points through six games and have held four opponents to 21 points or fewer.

**Triway (5-1, 2-1) at Canton South (0-6, 0-3)**

![Image 9: Football player in purple leaps over a diving defender in white and blue on a field.](https://image.yourohionews.com/1081720.jpg?imageId=1081720&x=0.00&y=0.00&cropw=100.00&croph=100.00&width=960&height=644&format=jpg)

Triway quarterback Jaxon Clippinger (right) has passed for 1,226 yards and 10 touchdowns to lead a well-rounded attack for the 5-1 Titans, who travel to Canton South Friday.

Joshua McWilliams

**Last week:** Triway 35, Fairless 7; Orrville 41, Canton South 14  
**Last year:** Triway 47, Canton South 23  
**This year:** Triway is ranked third in Division V, Region 18. Jaxon Clippinger has passed for 1,226 yards and 10 touchdowns, while Austin Houser has rushed for 517 yards and nine scores. Brandt Clippinger has 607 receiving yards and four touchdowns on 35 catches. Alex Robinson leads the Titans with 52 tackles, while Landon Harvey has 19 tackles for loss and five sacks. Canton South has scored 54 points while allowing 205 and has been held to 14 points or fewer in five of its six games.

Inter-Valley Conference South

**Garaway (5-1, 1-0) at Sandy Valley (1-5, 0-1)**

**Last week:** Garaway 49, Tusky Valley 16; Claymont 48, Sandy Valley 0  
**Last year:** Garaway 49, Sandy Valley 7  
**This year:** Garaway is ranked second in Division VI, Region 23. Matthew Frey has 837 rushing yards and 17 touchdowns, while Grady Miller has passed for 806 yards and nine touchdowns and added 197 yards and three scores on the ground. Trey Miller has 277 receiving yards and three touchdowns, Andrew Miller has 275 receiving yards and Henry Miller has five touchdown catches. Braylon Books has 26 tackles, seven tackles for loss and two sacks. Sandy Valley has scored 91 points while allowing 199.

Wayne County Athletic League

**Chippewa (4-2, 2-1) at Waynedale (1-5, 0-3)**

**Last week:** Norwayne 21, Chippewa 7; Hillsdale 62, Waynedale 7  
**Last year:** Waynedale 23, Chippewa 7  
**This year:** Chippewa’s Brayden Mihelic has rushed for 706 yards and has scored six touchdowns. Brock Bennett has passed for 231 yards and rushed for 221, while Ian Radebaugh has 107 receiving yards and two touchdown catches. Radebaugh also has 69 tackles and 12.5 tackles for loss, while Jonas Radebaugh has 54 tackles. Waynedale’s Maddox Kidd has contributed 225 rushing yards, 187 receiving yards and five total touchdowns while adding 32 tackles on defense. Reece Campbell has rushed for 211 yards, and Hezekiah Topp leads the defense with 35 tackles.

**Norwayne (3-3, 3-0) at Dalton (2-4, 2-1)**

![Image 10: Cameron Hackworth, Norwayne](https://image.yourohionews.com/1081270.jpg?imageId=1081270&x=0.00&y=0.00&cropw=100.00&croph=100.00&width=960&height=1200&format=jpg)

Cameron Hackworth, Norwayne RB/LB

Joshua McWilliams

**Last week:** Norwayne 21, Chippewa 7; Dalton 35, Rittman 0  
**Last year:** Norwayne 26, Dalton 7  
**This year:** Norwayne quarterback Bradley Lanz has passed for 1,604 yards and 15 touchdowns. Drew Wenninger has 40 catches for 559 yards and four touchdowns, while Cade Leach has 326 receiving yards and three scores and Carter Miller has 289 yards and four TDs. Cameron Hackworth has 260 rushing yards and four touchdowns and leads the defense with 58 tackles, 12 tackles for loss and three sacks. Dalton’s Gage Stitt has rushed for 366 yards and six touchdowns, and Ethan Raber has 339 rushing yards. Brady McFarren has stepped in and passed for 468 yards and four touchdowns as the Bulldogs have overcome an 0-4 start to get back in the WCAL race.

**Northwestern (2-4, 0-3) at Hillsdale (5-1, 2-1)**

**Last week:** Smithville 34, Northwestern 0; Hillsdale 62, Waynedale 7  
**Last year:** Hillsdale 49, Northwestern 7  
**This year:** Hillsdale is ranked eighth in Division VI, Region 21. Kael Lewis has passed for 1,058 yards and 13 touchdowns while rushing for a team-high 442 yards and five scores. Knox Lewis has 331 receiving yards and six touchdowns, while Ayden Salyer has 289 yards and four scores. Mason Sloan has 64 tackles and two interceptions, and Drew Daugherty has 52 tackles. Northwestern quarterback Leonardo Guidetti has passed for 738 yards and seven touchdowns without an interception. Rylie Ramsier has 366 receiving yards and three touchdowns, while Jesse Hanshaw has 264 rushing yards and three interceptions on defense. Grady Ellerbrock leads Northwestern with 55 tackles.

**Rittman (3-3, 0-3) at Smithville (6-0, 3-0)**

![Image 11: Smithville senior Brennan Piatt and the Smithies are Wayne County's only unbeaten team.](https://image.yourohionews.com/1081733.jpg?imageId=1081733&x=0.00&y=0.00&cropw=100.00&croph=100.00&width=960&height=644&format=jpg)

Smithville senior Brennan Piatt and the Smithies are Wayne County's only unbeaten team at 6-0 entering Friday's game with visiting Rittman.

Joshua McWilliams

**Last week:** Dalton 35, Rittman 0; Smithville 34, Northwestern 0  
**Last year:** Smithville 31, Rittman 0  
**This year:** Smithville is the area’s lone unbeaten team and is ranked third in Division VI, Region 21. Brady Sidle has passed for 649 yards and 12 touchdowns with one interception while rushing for 346 yards and two scores. Isaiah Lee has rushed for 399 yards and nine touchdowns and added 272 receiving yards and five scores. Ben Beichler has 230 rushing yards, 48 tackles and nine tackles for loss, while Logan Smith has four sacks and nine tackles for loss. Rittman’s Carson Smith has rushed for 816 yards and scored 12 touchdowns. Rocco Taylor has 369 rushing yards and 52 tackles, including 12 for loss and four sacks, while Jason Sears has 51 tackles.

# Talk About Clyde: Museum celebrates women's right to vote

Jeanette Ricker

Correspondent

June 2, 2021, 6:03 a.m. ET

[](link_11)[](link_12)[](mailto:?subject=Talk%20About%20Clyde%3A%20Museum%20celebrates%20women's%20right%20to%20vote%20-%20from%20The%20News-Messenger&body=Talk%20About%20Clyde%3A%20Museum%20celebrates%20women's%20right%20to%20vote%0A%0AThe%20100th%20Anniversary%20of%20the%2019th%20Amendment%20to%20be%20discussed%20by%20Dr.%20Susan%20Trollinger.%0A%0ACheck%20out%20this%20story%20on%20thenews-messenger.com%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.thenews-messenger.com%2Fstory%2Fnews%2F2021%2F06%2F02%2Ftalk-clyde-museum-celebrates-womens-right-vote%2F5290010001%2F)

![Image 1: Jeanette Liebold Ricker](https://www.thenews-messenger.com/gcdn/presto/2019/10/22/PFRE/a62be9e1-aa56-4426-990b-fb2080a72d0b-Jeanette_photo.jpg?width=300&height=317&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)
Did 1970 feminists really burn their bras in protest of the Miss America Pageant? They didn’t. In celebration of the 100th anniversary of the 19th Amendment (Women's Right to Vote) in 2020, Dr. Susan Trollinger, professor of English at the University of Dayton, will present a program on this historic landmark.

Her story of the women’s suffrage movement, “Rebels in Corsets,” is at 7 p.m.June 8, in the Clyde Museum, 124 W. Buckeye St. She will discuss myths and facts and how the rhetoric of the movement changed over time and became more radical; how Ohio women fought for the cause; the arguments and appeals that women made and about the ways in which women used their bodies and put them on the line for the vote.

More: [Talk About Clyde: City hires Garcia as rec administrator](link_14)More: [Clyde seniors graduate with pre-pandemic pomp and circumstance](link_15)
She will tell how people, especially men, responded to the increasingly radical rhetoric of this movement.

![Image 2: Dr. Susan Trollinger](https://www.thenews-messenger.com/story/news/2021/06/02/talk-clyde-museum-celebrates-womens-right-vote/5290010001/)
At the University of Dayton,Trollinger teaches courses in rhetoric (especially visual rhetoric), writing and vocation. She is the author of "Selling the Amish: The Rhetoric of Nostalgia" (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2012) and gives talks around the state on the Amish for the Ohio Humanities Council.

Her presentation is the first of Second Tuesday events scheduled at the Clyde Museum following the lifting of COVIS-19 restrictions by Gov. Mike DeWine. Masks and social distancing are not required, but masks may be worn if one feels more comfortable doing so, said Gene Smith, museum curator.

Second Tuesday programs at the museum are scheduled through summer and fall. Dates and programs may be subject to change without notice.

## St. Paul plans outdoor service

St. Paul Lutheran Church is holding an outdoor service Sunday on the Forest Street lawn, across from the library. Visitors are welcome. Dress and service is informal. Music leader is Brian Farrar.

People are encouraged to bring take own lawn chairs, but chairs will be available. No masks required. In case of rain, services will be held inside the sanctuary.

## Alumni planning September event

The Clyde Alumni Association is in the planning stages of the annual banquet/reunion on Sept. 11 at Clyde High School for those who attended or graduated CHS 50 years ago or more. Plans are subject to any COVID-19 updates or restrictions.

The class of 1971 is planning to hold its 5-year reunion in conjunction with the annual CHS Alumni reunion on Sept. 11. Class members can get more information by going to the Clyde Fliers Class of '71 Facebook page.

## One room school house

More than 100 years ago, country students attended one room schools, where all eight grades were taught by one teacher. Both of my parents attended such schools. My father, Clarence Wott, his four brothers and sister walked from their brick home near the corner or County Roads 242 and 229 to Hildewin School on County Road 223. By the time they got to school in the winter, their packed lunches were frozen.

That school was later converted to a family home. My mother, Florence Rife Wott, and her two sisters lived in the 5000 block on Ohio 101 and only had to walk west toward Clyde and around the corner to Richards School on County Road 268, which sat on a knoll. It is demolished and the area is now farmed.

In a box of mother’s memorabilia, I found her grade cards and a 1914-15 souvenir booklet from their teacher, Blanch E. May, who taught 22 children, eight boys and 14 girls.

Mother’s first grade card showed that students were graded on deportment, application to study, reading, spelling, writing, arithmetic, language, grammar, geography, history and civics, physiology, agriculture and literature. The grading system was as follows: E- Excellent, G-Good, M- Medium, F-Fair, P-Poor (below 65).

The back of the grade card stated that after 1915 students graduating from the Eighth Grade must be able to do the following: girls, prepare a simple meal, bake bread, pie and cake; churn and work butter, can or preserve produce; make jelly, dress a fowl, do plain sewing, wash and iron clothing, do neat housekeeping and keep household accounts.

Boys must be able to milk cows, do farm chores and farm work which included planting and tilling the soil, provide a true account of the produce of some field or garden, or the account of the year of any animal or animals on the farm, make a seed corn tester and test the corn to be planted.

_Jeanette Liebold Ricker writes about Clyde and Green Springs. Contact her at 419-547-8177 or by email at jeanette.ricker@gmail.com._

# New JPAC Issue Released: Amish Migration, Fertility, the Dawdyhaus & More

By[Joe Donnermeyer](link_20)July 16, 2025

_Journal of Plain Anabaptist Communities, Volume 5, Issue 2 now released_

![Image 6](https://amishamerica.com/images/jpac-issue-ten-600px.jpg)

New milestones have been reached for both the _Journal of Plain Anabaptist Communities_ (JPAC) and Anabaptist scholarship in general. JPAC is blessed with nearly 500 registrants, but there is room for many, many more, as its **tenth issue** is now released.

It is now the “go-to” journal for Anabaptist studies, particularly scholarship about the Amish, with over 124,000 views and downloads so far from its first nine issues.

The release of **Volume 5, Issue 2** comes only a week before the July 22-24 Young Center Conference at Elizabethtown College (PA) on “[Early Anabaptism in Global Perspective: Past, Present and Future at 500 Years](link_26).”

## Lead Article: “Vaccination Risk through the Lens of Faith, Family, and Community”

The lead article includes three scholars from West Virginia University (Rachel Stein, Katie Corcoran, and Corey Coyler) on **“Vaccination Risk through the Lens of Faith, Family, and Community”**.

![Image 7](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-woman-holding-head.jpg)

Image: Don Burke

This article advances the study of health and culture by using both the concept of vaccine hesitancy and how “worldviews” of various religious groups shape beliefs about health and health care options.

## Amish Migration to Wisconsin

This is followed by an analysis of **“Migration to Wisconsin’s Amish settlements”** by Professor Emeritus John Cross (University of Wisconsin-Oshkosh). Cross offers a very detailed account of “source counties” of Amish households moving to several of the larger settlements in the Badger State.

![Image 8](https://amishamerica.com/images/aerial-view-amish-farm-wisconsin.jpg)

As both the number of Amish increases, along with the number of new settlements, understanding the pattern of population movement becomes an increasingly important topic.

## Swiss Amish Birth Rates

From The Ohio State University, Joe Donnermeyer, a member and former chair of the OSU Emeritus Academy, examined both the **total fertility and birth intervals** among the four largest communities of Amish known as the “Swiss Amish.”

![Image 9](https://amishamerica.com/images/swiss-amish-families-adams-county.jpg)

Total fertility refers to the number of live births for women age 45 years and older, that is, with only a few exceptions, no longer have children. His findings confirm that Swiss Amish communities display some of the highest total fertility numbers of any Amish group.

## Amish Men’s Longevity

Henry Troyer, another retired professor who remains an active scholar and continues to examine the population dynamics of the Amish, focused in this issue of JPAC on **longevity of men**.

![Image 10](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-men-socializing.jpg)

Image: Don Burke

Specifically, he uses the 1965 Ohio Amish directory to first identify slightly over 1,500 men, most of whom were born in the 1940s, and then uses more recent Ohio Amish directories and various genealogies to determine their date of death and calculate their ages.

He compares those results with data from the Social Security Administration for Caucasian men from Ohio, and discovers that Amish men do live longer.

## The Dawdyhaus, and Amish Tourism

Beyond research articles, there are two more submissions under the JPAC section titled “fieldwork and reflections.” The first is by Claire Mensack at Lander University in South Carolina. Her focus is an account of the **_dawdyhaus_** and its place in the lives two Amish families.

![Image 11](https://amishamerica.com/images/amish-dawdihaus-minnesota.jpg)

Following this are the observations of Susan Trollinger (University of Dayton) on the **“weaponizing of Amish country tourism.”** It is subtitled an update of her monograph, “Selling the Amish” (published by Johns Hopkins University Press in 2012).

## Mennonite Life Library & Archives: An Overview

Rounding out the tenth issue of JPAC is an overview by Julia Wiker, the archivist/librarian at **Mennonite Life**, located in Ephrata, Pennsylvania. In previous issues of JPAC, a number of other libraries containing large collections of books, genealogies and historical documents about Anabaptists groups were featured.

## Book Reviews

Finally, there are two book reviews. One is by Corey Colyer (West Virginia University) of James Cates’ book, **“Dancing on the Devil’s Playground: The Amish Negotiate with Modernity”**. The subtitle refers to the a concept from the previous work of Don Kraybill, especially his classic book “The Riddle of Amish Culture.” He uses the concept to examine the diversity of ways that various Amish fellowship deal with issues from drug use to family violence.

![Image 12](https://amishamerica.com/images/dancing-on-the-devils-playground-james-cates-600px.jpg)

Rod Janzen, Professor Emeritus of History from Fresno Pacific University, examines the recently published book by Astrid von Schlachta’s titled **“Holding Fast to What is Good? Tradition and Renewal in Hutterite History.”** This book was published by the Hutterian Brethren Book Centre.

Janzen describes it as “…an impressive collection of essays on the entire experience of the first 350 years of Hutterite life in Europe, and important period when the sermons (still read today) and many organizations and theological principles were institutionalized for the benefit of future generations.”

## Subscribe and read JPAC for free

The _Journal of Plain Anabaptist Communities_ is published twice each year, and is dedicated to advancing scholarship about Amish, conservative Mennonites, Amish-Mennonites, Apostolic Christians, Brethren, Bruderhof, Hutterites and other plain Anabaptist groups.

It is co-sponsored by the [Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies](link_25), Elizabethtown College, Elizabethtown, Pennsylvania, [Behalt, the Amish & Mennonite Information Center](link_27), Berlin, Ohio, the [Amish America website](link_0), and [The Ohio State University libraries](https://plainanabaptistjournal.org/index.php/JPAC).

To **subscribe** (no charge), go to the [JPAC website](https://plainanabaptistjournal.org/index.php/JPAC) of The Ohio State University Libraries, and follow the windows found in the upper right-hand corner. Registering requires only a few minutes to complete.

_Read the latest issue of JPAC for free [**here**](https://plainanabaptistjournal.org/index.php/JPAC/issue/view/385)_

information, please contact  ecommons@udayton.edu .11/6/13 University of Dayton : News : Obama Visit Brings Media Attention to University of Dayton www.udayton.edu/news/articles/2012/03/obama_visit_brings_media_attention.php 1/2 

# University of Dayton, Ohio (url: http://w [link_0] w w .udayton.edu/index.php) 

# The Eyes of the World 

03.20.2012 | Hot Topics, Campus and Community, International, Athletics, Students The visit of President Barack Obama and British Prime Minister David Cameron to the NCAA Division I Men's Basketball Championship First Four was a slam dunk of media coverage for the University of Dayton. News outlets in the U.S. and the U.K. covered the March 13 visit from wheels up to wheels down of Air Force One, generating thousands of online stories and mentions. It was March Madness for sure, but with babies as well as basketballs and global hot dogs as well as hoops. Uncounted photos and videos were snapped of the president with a baby, the two world leaders with hot dogs and both deep in conversations with University of Dayton students. According to a University of Dayton media relations report generated by the tracking service CisionPoint March 20, in the past week, media outlets in 155 U.S. media markets other than Dayton ran stories mentioning Dayton and the University. The estimated publicity value of the media attention, excluding the Dayton market, is at least $1.1 million. Those stories made at least 2.1 billion impressions outside of the Dayton market. In addition to media outlets in the U.K., outlets in Canada, Indonesia, Argentina, Malaysia and the Philippines ran stories. The University seized the opportunity to take its unique brand worldwide, noted The Washington Post in the Campus Overload 

(url: http://w [link_0] w w .w ashingtonpost.com/blogs/campus-overload/post/university-of-dayton-uses-first-four-as-a-branding-opportunity/2012/03/13/gIQAW01EAS_blog.html) blog. "This year, the private Catholic university is using the national spotlight as a branding opportunity, sending out a flurry of press releases and buying a full-page ad (url: http://w [link_0] w w .udayton.edu/new s/images/documents/us_airw ays_ad_basketball_03132012.pdf) in U.S. Airways magazine that proclaims: “No matter who’s in the tournament, Dayton takes the lead." Dozens of high-profile publications and outlets such as The Washington Post, ESPN, Reuters, The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg News carried stories, photos and videos of the visit. Obama told CBS Sports, in the only interview of the two at the event, that he was happy to bring Cameron to the heartland of the U.S. The CBS story said the president praised Ohio, saying he was glad he had been able to bring Cameron to the state. 'I thought it was going to be wonderful for the prime minister to have a chance not only to see a basketball game for the first time, but also to come to the great state of Ohio,' said Mr. Obama. 'Because sometimes when we have foreign visitors they're only visiting the coasts. They go to New York, they go to Washington, they go to Los Angeles. But, you know, the heartland is what it's all about.'" U.K. outlets covering the visit included the BBC, The Telegraph and The Times and Reuters news service. Along with a cheeky story about Cameron's apparent unfamiliarity with basketball, U.K.'s MailOnline (url: http://w [link_0] w w .dailymail.co.uk/new s/article-2114508/Camerons-U-S-tour-Obama-lays-rules-game-w ouldnt-basketball-Eton.html#ixzz1p78EDo2Y) 

ran an extended photo gallery in which University of Dayton President Daniel Curran and a number of University students are plain to see. Reuters wrote: "President Barack Obama, America's basketball fan-in-chief, treated British Prime Minister David Cameron to courtside seats for 'March Madness' on Tuesday, taking him to an NCAA tournament game in the presidential election swing state of Ohio… Obama, an avid basketball fan, whisked Cameron out of Washington to attend the National Collegiate Athletic Association game between Western Kentucky and Mississippi Valley State at the University of Dayton sports arena." The University of Dayton was prominently featured in a photo with a story in the Jakarta Globe, Indonesia (url: http://w [link_0] w w .thejakartaglobe.com/international/cameron-obama-meeting-on-w eighty-issues/504684) , which commented: "The setting created the image of two buddies, dressed in casual clothes, eating hot dogs and enjoying the NCAA tournament, one of 11/6/13 University of Dayton : News : Obama Visit Brings Media Attention to University of Dayton www.udayton.edu/news/articles/2012/03/obama_visit_brings_media_attention.php 2/2 

America’s premier sporting events." For more information, contact Shawn Robinson, associate director of media relations, at 937-229-3391 or srobinson@udayton.edu.

# Author: Don Burke

![Image 3](https://amishamerica.com/images/don-burke-author-page-photo.jpg)

As a minister, **Don Burke** has served since 2004 as pastor for a church in a small county-seat community in the rural Ozarks. Don’s introduction to the Amish world is told in the Amish America post [here](link_22).   
  
The interest that began on that trip has since taken him to over 50 Amish communities in 11 states. His visits have mainly been to the larger communities (prompted by his wife’s familiarity from reading Amish novels), and to much-less-touristy settlements in and around Missouri, where he lives.   
  
A self-taught photography enthusiast, Don has merged these two passions into an [online library](link_23) of nearly 8,000 Amish-themed images. His Amish photos have appeared in the landmark book _The Amish_, digital and print media by The Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies, and feature regularly in Amish America articles and videos.

# Author: Joe Donnermeyer

![Image 3](https://amishamerica.com/images/joe-donnermeyer-bio-photo.jpg)

**Joseph F. Donnermeyer** is professor emeritus in the Rural Sociology program, part of the School of Environment and Natural Resources at **The Ohio State University**. His Amish research concerns examination of the demographic dimensions of the Amish, including population growth, settlement expansion, and occupational change. He has co-written two books about the Amish (_A Quiet Moment in Time_ and _Lessons for Living_) and about two dozen peer-reviewed journal articles and book chapters.   
  
Dr. Donnermeyer now supervises an online course titled “Amish Society”, and recently developed an online continuing education course of the same title. He continues as an adjunct professor at the West Virginia Center for Violence Research, West Virginia University (Morgantown), and the University of New England, Armidale, New South Wales. He is the founder/editor of the _International Journal of Rural Criminology_ and cofounder/coeditor of the **_Journal of Plain Anabaptist Communities_** ([https://plainanabaptistjournal.org](link_22)).

# How to Access Your Taboola Data

English

  

# Taboola’s Data Subject Access Request Portal

This policy outlines what personal data and behavioural information Taboola holds about you and how you can access or delete your personal data.

Your Rights — What You Can Request

You have the right to request that Taboola provide you with access to the personal data that we hold about you, correct your personal data, delete your personal data, and cease or restrict processing of your personal data. You have also the right to lodge a complaint with a data protection authority about our collection and use of your Personal Data, including the UK Information Commissioner's Office where applicable.

However, if you have any questions or concerns about our collection and use of your Personal Data, including any complaints, please first contact us at [privacy@taboola.com](mailto:privacy@taboola.com) so we can review and address them. If you are unable to obtain the information or resolution that you seek, you may also contact our Data Protection Officer at [dpo@taboola.com](mailto:dpo@taboola.com).

To learn more, please contact your local data protection authority, via the contact methods available [here](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/about-edpb/about-edpb/members_en). For more information about how we collect, use, and disclose information that we obtain through our websites and services, please see our [Privacy Policy](https://www.taboola.com/privacy-policy).

What Information Taboola Holds

Taboola maintains data about you in only pseudonymized form, which means that we do not know your identity because we do not process your name, email address, or other identifiable data. Instead, we only process digital identifiers such as cookie IDs, IP addresses (truncated in Germany), mobile advertising IDs on your device, and in some limited circumstances, your hashed email address (for a full list of pseudonymized data that we process, please see our [Privacy Policy](https://www.taboola.com/privacy-policy)). # Author: Haley Straw

![Image 3: Portrait of a woman with shoulder-length blond hair wearing a black top, seated at a desk with bookshelves in the background under purple lighting.](https://amishamerica.com/images/haley-straw-author-photo.jpg)

**Haley Straw** is a barefoot, homeschooling mom of six who possesses one of the most unique vantage points into the modern Plain world as an Amish taxi driver. Originally from the Pacific Northwest, Haley now lives with her family in rural Missouri, where they are actively restoring a historic, century-old jailhouse.   
  
Over years of driving, Haley has highlighted a personal map that spans 27 states and two different countries, safely delivering her Plain passengers to dozens of Amish communities for weddings, auctions, family gatherings, and specialized doctor appointments.   
  
Because she is allowed to see deep inside the Amish world without ever being a part of it, her books capture the raw, humorous, and awkward moments of everyday Plain life that outsiders rarely get to see. Her true stories help readers slow down, laugh a little, and remember what matters most.   
  
To explore her books, grab free Amish-inspired goodies, and connect with her online, visit [haleystraw.com](https://www.haleystraw.com/).

# 6 Things You Probably Didn’t Know About Ohio’s Largest Amish Community

By[Joe Donnermeyer](https://amishamerica.com/author/joe-donnermeyer/)July 27, 2026

![Image 3: A rolling hills landscape with a tree and fencepost visible and a windmill in the background](https://amishamerica.com/images/windmill-scenic-view-holmes-county-ohio-amish-community.jpg)

The rolling countryside of Holmes County, Ohio — home to the nation’s second-largest Amish settlement. Photo: Don Burke

_A Population Profile of the Greater Holmes County settlement of Northeast Ohio_

Out of 700-plus Amish settlements, there are four that can be considered **super-sized**. In previous editions of _The Journal of Plain Anabaptist Communities_ (JPAC), profiles for three already were published.

The first of these was by Lawrence Greksa about the Greater Geauga, Ohio settlement, published in volume 1, issue 2. This was followed by one about the Elkhart-LaGrange, Indiana settlement, written by Thomas Meyers in volume 3, issue 1; and also in this same issue is a profile of the Greater Lancaster County settlement by Joe Donnermeyer.

Joe and Henry Troyer have now collaborated to write one about the Greater Holmes County settlement. Titled “A Population Profile of the Greater Holmes County Amish Settlement: Ohio’s Oldest and Largest Amish Community”, and [appearing in volume 6, issue 2](https://plainanabaptistjournal.org/article/id/6835/) of JPAC, it presents information on a variety of demographic characteristics.

The Greater Holmes County settlement began in 1808 with the arrival of its first permanent settler, Jonas “Weiss” Stutzman who also built an extra-large chair for Jesus, expecting his second coming at any time.

[That chair](https://amishamerica.com/journal-of-plain-anabaptist-communities-jpac-issue-4-now-available/) is now on display at Behalt (Amish & Mennonite Heritage Center), located near Berlin. The chair itself is in the large room with the 10′ by 265′ painting of Anabaptist history by Heinz Gaugel.

![Image 4](https://amishamerica.com/images/holmes-county-amish-schoolhouse-behalt.jpg)

This is one of the oldest school buildings in Holmes County. After a new facility was built, it was relocated to the grounds of Behalt (the Amish & Mennonite Heritage Center) and is now used to educate tour groups about Amish education, and give them an opportunity to ring the school bell. Photo by Joe Donnermeyer

## A Pessimistic Outlook…Proven Wrong

One of the earliest studies of the Greater Holmes County settlement comes from a thesis published in 1932 and written by Lyle Fletcher, a student then in the Department of Geography at The Ohio State University.

Even though it is a solid piece of scholarship, he assumes that geographic isolation is essential to Amish survival, and thereby concludes on the final three pages:

> “With the coming of the automobile and the subsequent good roads, conditions have changed…So we leave the Amish with great admiration for their social system but with sincere doubts as to its capacity for continuity.”

Wow! He sure did get that one wrong! The Greater Holmes County settlement has grown from only 13 church districts (about 25-35 families in each district) in 1920 to nearly 270 today.

The Greater Holmes County settlement is a mecca for hundreds of thousands of tourists each year and the eastern half of the county is considered as one of the most densely populated areas of Amish anywhere in North America.

Over-all, **about 46 percent of Holmes County is Amish**, and this does not include Beachy Amish and various Amish-Mennonite groups who do not prohibit the ownership of motor vehicles. The settlement is so large that it spills out into four other counties (Wayne, Stark, Tuscarawas, and Coshocton).

![Image 5: Rear view of a black horse-drawn buggy on a wet rural road; red triangular slow-vehicle sign visible at rear.](https://amishamerica.com/images/holmes-county-amish-buggy-rainy-day.jpg)

Even with reflectors, a slow-moving vehicle sign and tail lights, it can be hard to see a buggy on a rainy day, especially in an area like Holmes County, with a terrain of rolling hills. This picture was taken from inside my car. Photo by Joe Donnermeyer

## Six Holmes County Amish Population Facts

Here are a half dozen population facts from the Donnermeyer and Troyer study. These population characteristics are based on a statistical study from a one-in-five sample of households found in the 2025 directory for this settlement.

### Fact #1: Bishops’ Average Age

The **average age of ordination** of bishops is 45.6 years. Men are younger when ordained as ministers (35.8 years) and deacons (38.5 years). This makes sense because almost all bishops are first selected as ministers, and occasionally as deacons.

### Fact #2: Occupations of Ordained Amish Men

There is no better way to illustrate the Amish transition out of agriculture than to examine the **occupations of ordained men**. During earlier times, it could be assumed that men who farm are preferred for the ministry. Not today. In the Greater Holmes County settlement, only 19.5% of bishops listed an agricultural occupation, compared to about 22% for ministers and only 9.3% of deacons.

When considering all heads of households who listed an occupation in the 2025 directory, the **percent engaged in agricultural pursuits is down to 11.4%**.

![Image 6: Red barn and farm buildings sit among green fields under a gray sky, with trees on the left and a fence in the foreground.](https://amishamerica.com/images/holmes-county-amish-farm-layout.jpg)

This picture shows a typical layout of an Amish farm in Holmes County. On the right, either side of the big tree, can be seen both the main house and the dawdyhaus. The dawdyhaus is a place for retired parents to live after one of their adult children takes over operation of the farm and begins to raise their own children there. Photo by Joe Donnermeyer

Back in the 1965 directory for this same settlement, fully 71% of men were farmers or farm laborers. Of the three biggest settlements, only 5.5% of men from the Greater Geauga County settlement are agriculturalists and in Elkhart-LaGrange, the percentage was about 15.

However, the proportion in the Greater Lancaster County settlement is substantially higher, at 41%. Not all settlements are alike.

### Fact #3: Most Common Occupations For Amish Men

The **most frequent occupation** of men in the Greater Holmes County settlement today is some sort of carpentry work or occupations associated with construction (33.7%).

### Fact #4: Average Marriage Age For Amish Men & Women

The **average age of marriage** in the Greater Holmes County settlement was 23.5 years for husbands and 22.1 years for wives. This has not changed much over the years.

Plus, the average age for men to first become fathers is 24.9 years and for women to become mothers is 23.5 years. In other words, on average, first born children enter this world about 16 months after marriage.

### Fact #5: Most Common Marriage Months

**Month of marriage** in the Greater Holmes County community is, in order of popularity, May (19.6%), September (19.2%), October (13.5%), June (13.2%), and August (10.2%).

It used to be that marriages waited until the conclusion of harvesting, but with the transition out of agriculture, that pattern in the Greater Holmes County settlement has changed.

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1IWS-u7bLtI)

There are now two marriage seasons — one in the late Spring and one in the Autumn. What has not changed over the many decades is a preference to be married during the middle of the week, with an overwhelming choice for Thursday.

### Fact #6: Total Fertility in Different Amish Groups Varies Greatly

**Total fertility** is the number of offspring born to women who have completed their reproductive period. Total fertility remains high for almost all Amish, no matter if they live in a large or a small settlement. There are, however, substantial differences by fellowship.

Among the three major fellowships found in the Greater Holmes County settlement directory of 2025, total fertility is 7.8 live births for women in the Dan affiliation, compared to 6.1 for Old Order wives, and 5.8 for New Order wives.

An earlier study published in JPAC (Troyer, 2022) of the Swartzentruber fellowship within the Greater Holmes County settlement is even higher, topping out at 10.4.

With the rapid growth of the Amish population and the number of settlements increasing just as fast (Donnermeyer, 2021), population studies will remain an important way to examine issues associated with social and cultural changes in Amish society.
